chunks: Contrast & weighting: the exam synthesis.
Image contrast in conventional spin echo is set by two knobs: TR governs how much T1 weighting you get, and TE governs how much T2 weighting.
Combine them:.
Short TR / short TE → T1-weighted.
Fat and white matter bright; fluid (CSF) dark.
Long TR / long TE → T2-weighted.
Fluid bright.
This is where most pathology (extra water) shows.
Long TR / short TE → proton density.
Both weightings minimized; signal tracks tissue water content.
One brain slice, three weightings: only TR and TE change between panels.
Watch the CSF in the ventricles: dark on T1, mid-gray on PD, bright on T2.Inversion recovery adds a preparatory 180° pulse and a TI.
Choosing TI at a tissue's null point suppresses it: STIR (short TI ≈ 0.69·T1 of fat) nulls fat; FLAIR (long TI ≈ 2000-2500 ms) nulls CSF so periventricular lesions aren't hidden.
Gradient echo uses a flip angle instead of a 180° refocuser and is sensitive to T2* (susceptibility).
Gadolinium shortens T1, so enhancing tissue is bright on T1, which marks blood-brain-barrier breakdown.
The fastest read: find the fluid (ventricles, eyeballs).
Dark fluid → T1.
Bright fluid → T2.
Dark CSF but lesions still bright → FLAIR.
Key point: TR controls T1 weighting; TE controls T2 weighting..
Key point: Short TR/short TE = T1; long TR/long TE = T2; long TR/short TE = PD..
Key point: STIR nulls fat (TI ≈ 0.69·T1 fat); FLAIR nulls CSF (long TI)..
Key point: Gradient echo → flip angle, T2* sensitive..
Key point: Gadolinium shortens T1 → bright on T1 at BBB breakdown..
Worked example.
You pull up a lumbar spine protocol and see a sagittal sequence with TR 500 ms and TE 20 ms alongside a second sagittal sequence with TR 3500 ms and TE 110 ms.
The first is T1-weighted: the short TR gives longitudinal magnetization little time to recover between excitations, so tissue with a short T1, like fat and marrow,
regrows the most magnetization and looks bright, while CSF, with its long T1, stays dark.
The second is T2-weighted: the long TR lets essentially every tissue fully recover before the next pulse, which erases T1 differences, and the long TE then lets transverse magnetization decay,
so tissue with a long T2, like CSF and edema, still has signal left and looks bright.
A disc herniation with surrounding edema can be easy to miss on the T1 image, where fat dominates the contrast, but it stands out against the dark disc and cord on the T2 image.
If a third sequence paired a long TR with a short TE, both T1 and T2 weighting would be minimized and the image would instead track proton density,
the raw concentration of mobile hydrogen in each tissue.
Memory hook: Short TR and short TE favor fat, long TR and long TE favor fluid.
Find the CSF: dark is T1, bright is T2..
Memory hook: TR controls how much T1 shows through and TE controls how much T2 shows through.
Cancel both (long TR, short TE) and what's left is proton density..
Memory hook: A nulling TI is about 0.69 times the T1 of the tissue being suppressed, which is why STIR (short TI, nulls fat) and FLAIR (long TI, nulls CSF) use such different TI values..
Exam trap: STIR nulls anything with fat's short T1, not just fat.
Gadolinium shortens T1 into that same range, so STIR will null enhancement too, which is why STIR is not paired with contrast..
Exam trap: Long TR alone does not make a sequence T2-weighted.
Long TR with a short TE removes T1 weighting but adds proton density weighting instead, not T2..
Exam trap: A gradient echo image looks T2-like but its susceptibility blooming from blood products comes from T2 star, which includes local field inhomogeneity on top of true T2 decay, not T2 alone..
Image quality: SNR, CNR, resolution & the trade-offs.
SNR (signal-to-noise) rises with voxel volume (bigger voxels = more signal), with √NEX (averages), with lower receiver bandwidth, with field strength, and with better coils.
CNR (contrast-to-noise) is the difference in signal between two tissues over the noise, and it is what actually makes a lesion visible.
Spatial resolution is set by voxel size: a finer matrix or smaller FOV or thinner slice = smaller voxels = more detail, but each holds less signal, so SNR falls.
That is the fundamental resolution ↔ SNR trade at fixed scan time.
Same slice, same scan time, only the acquisition matrix changes.
Finer matrix means smaller voxels and more detail, but each voxel holds less signal, so the 512 image is grainier: the resolution to SNR trade.Scan time (2D SE) = TR × phase-encode steps × NEX.
So doubling the phase matrix doubles both resolution-in-that-axis and scan time.
Everything is a four-way balance of SNR, resolution, coverage, and time.
Two efficiency levers: the Ernst angle maximizes GRE signal for a given TR/T1, and parallel imaging (SENSE/GRAPPA) buys speed at an SNR cost of g·√R (the g-factor, worst centrally).
Key point: SNR ∝ voxel volume × √NEX; lower bandwidth and higher field raise it..
Key point: Finer matrix / smaller FOV / thinner slice = more resolution, less SNR..
Key point: Scan time (2D SE) = TR × phase steps × NEX..
Key point: CNR (not raw SNR) determines lesion conspicuity..
Key point: Parallel imaging costs SNR by g·√R (g-factor)..
Worked example.
You are imaging a small joint with a 3 mm slice, a 256 phase-encode matrix, 1 NEX, and the images are noisy.
Thinning the slice to 2 mm to reduce partial-volume blur cuts voxel volume by a third, and since SNR is proportional to voxel volume, SNR falls by roughly that same fraction.
To claw some signal back you average twice, going to 2 NEX.
Because SNR improves only with the square root of the number of averages, that recovers about the square root of 2, not a full doubling, and it doubles scan time,
since 2D spin echo scan time equals TR times phase-encode steps times NEX.
If instead you had doubled the phase matrix to 512 steps to gain in-plane resolution, you would halve the phase-encode pixel dimension, taking another SNR hit from the smaller voxel,
while also doubling scan time directly, because phase steps multiply straight into the scan-time formula.
Resolution, SNR, and time are locked together: buying back one always costs one of the other two.
Memory hook: SNR scales directly with voxel volume but only with the square root of NEX.
Halve the voxel and you lose a full factor of SNR; you need four times the averages to win it back..
Memory hook: For 2D spin echo, scan time equals TR times phase-encode steps times NEX.
Only the phase direction adds time; more frequency-encode samples sharpen resolution for free..
Memory hook: CNR, not raw SNR, is what makes a lesion visible.
A high-SNR image with poor tissue contrast can still hide pathology that a noisier, higher-contrast image shows clearly..
Exam trap: Increasing the frequency-encode matrix does not add scan time, but increasing the phase-encode matrix does, directly and linearly.
Don't confuse the two directions..
Exam trap: Parallel imaging (SENSE or GRAPPA) buys speed by skipping phase-encode lines, but the SNR cost is the g-factor times the square root of the acceleration R,
and the g-factor penalty is worst at the center of the FOV, not spread evenly..
Exam trap: Raising receiver bandwidth shortens scan time and reduces chemical-shift artifact, but it lowers SNR because a wider bandwidth admits more noise per sample.
It is not a free efficiency gain..
MR safety: the exam-focused overview.
MRI has no ionizing radiation, but it uses three magnetic fields, and only the static field is always on.
Its danger is the projectile (missile) effect on ferromagnetic objects, plus benign transient bioeffects (dizziness and a metallic taste) at high field.
The gradients switch fast: their dB/dt can cause peripheral nerve stimulation, and their acoustic noise (up to ~120 dB) mandates hearing protection.
The RF deposits energy as heat (SAR, W/kg), risking burns from looped cables or skin-to-skin contact.
Facilities use four zones (I public → IV magnet room, most restricted).
Everyone is screened; implants are checked against MR-safe / MR-conditional / MR-unsafe labeling (an MR-conditional device is safe only under the stated field/SAR/slew limits).
A quench boils off helium, which is vented outside, but a failed vent risks oxygen displacement (asphyxiation) and frostbite.
Gadolinium in severe renal impairment carries a risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.
Key point: Three fields: static (projectile), gradient (PNS + acoustic), RF (SAR/burns)..
Key point: Zone IV = magnet room, most restricted; no ferromagnetic items..
Key point: MR-conditional = safe ONLY under the stated conditions..
Key point: Quench → helium boil-off → possible oxygen displacement..
Key point: Gadolinium + severe renal impairment → NSF risk..
Worked example.
A patient in a wheelchair with a small pocketknife left in a jacket pocket is brought toward the scanner room by a family member who was never screened.
The knife is drawn toward the bore and becomes a projectile, the classic ferromagnetic missile effect from the always-on static field.
The correct workflow is that everyone entering Zone III or IV, staff, patients, and visitors alike,
is screened with a ferromagnetic detection system and a verbal/written questionnaire before crossing into Zone IV, and only MR-trained, screened staff supervise anyone in Zone IV.
The static field is never off, even during a power outage, so screening has to happen at the zone boundary every single time, not just once at intake.
Memory hook: Four zones, increasing restriction: Zone I public access, Zone II screening/reception, Zone III controlled (screened persons only), Zone IV the magnet room itself..
Memory hook: Three fields, three hazards: static field causes the projectile effect (always on), gradients cause peripheral nerve stimulation and loud acoustic noise (dB/dt, switching fast),
RF deposits heat measured as SAR and can burn from loops or skin contact..
Memory hook: MR Safe, MR Conditional, MR Unsafe are the only three labels; MR Conditional is safe only under the specific field strength, SAR, and gradient slew-rate conditions on its label,
so you verify the label and the scanner parameters every time, never assume from a similar device..
Exam trap: A quench vents helium outside the building by design; the danger is a failed or blocked vent path leading to oxygen displacement (asphyxiation risk) and cold burns in the magnet room,
so a quench is a planned safety response, not a routine event and not itself the hazard..
Exam trap: SAR-related burns most often come from looped cables or skin-to-skin contact points completing a conductive loop,
not from the implant itself; padding cables away from skin and preventing loops is basic technologist practice on every patient..
Exam trap: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is a gadolinium contrast risk tied to severe renal impairment, not a static-field or RF hazard; it belongs with screening for renal function,
not with zone or projectile safety..
Patient care: screening to monitoring.
Screen before every scan (status changes): implants, pacemakers, aneurysm clips, cochlear implants, neurostimulators, and metal.
A history of metalwork/grinding needs orbital radiographs to exclude an intra-orbital fragment.
Prepare the patient: remove all ferromagnetic items, gown as needed, explain the loud noise, and give hearing protection.
Position for signal and comfort: center the anatomy in the coil at isocenter, immobilize to reduce motion, and hand over the call/squeeze device.
For contrast, screen for renal risk and prior reactions, obtain consent, and know the plan for an acute reaction (hives/wheeze/hypotension → stop, help, ABCs, epinephrine for anaphylaxis).
Routine eGFR screening is no longer required before the Group II macrocyclic agents in common use,
since their NSF risk is very low; confirm renal function for older linear agents or when impairment is likely, and follow facility policy.
Avoid gadolinium in pregnancy unless essential; after gadolinium, breastfeeding may continue without interruption because very little reaches breast milk,
though an anxious mother may choose to pump and discard for 24 hours.
Monitor throughout: keep verbal contact, manage claustrophobia (reassurance, call system, wide/open bore, sedation), and use only MR-safe monitoring equipment for sedated or unstable patients.
Key point: Screen before every scan; orbital radiographs for metal-in-eye history..
Key point: Hearing protection for every patient..
Key point: Contrast: consent and reaction management (epinephrine for anaphylaxis); eGFR screening is risk-based, not routine before Group II macrocyclic agents..
Key point: Avoid gadolinium in pregnancy unless essential..
Key point: Monitor continuously; MR-safe equipment only..
Worked example.
A patient scheduled for a contrast-enhanced lumbar spine MRI reports a history of working with a metal grinder years ago and has never had an orbital X-ray to clear metal fragments.
Screening also turns up reduced kidney function on a recent lab result.
The correct sequence is to hold the contrast-enhanced order and first obtain orbital radiographs to rule out a retained intra-orbital metallic fragment,
since an occult fragment near the globe can move or heat during scanning; separately,
the technologist checks the patient's eGFR against facility policy for gadolinium and discusses the finding with the ordering provider,
because severe renal impairment raises the risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.
Screening is not a one-time chart review, it is repeated before this specific scan because implant and health status can change between visits.
Memory hook: Screen every single time, not just once: implants, devices, pregnancy status, renal function, and metal exposure history can all change visit to visit..
Memory hook: Metalworking or grinding history plus no prior orbital imaging means get orbital radiographs before scanning, to rule out an intra-orbital metallic fragment..
Memory hook: For a contrast reaction, start with the basics: stop the injection, get help, support airway-breathing-circulation, and give epinephrine for anaphylaxis; know this sequence cold,
it is the first-line response..
Exam trap: Claustrophobia management (reassurance, call/squeeze device, open or wide-bore magnet, sedation when needed) is a comfort and completion issue,
not a contraindication to scanning by itself..
Exam trap: Gadolinium is avoided in pregnancy unless the information is essential to care and cannot wait, because it crosses the placenta; this is a risk-benefit decision with the ordering provider,
not an absolute rule against ever scanning a pregnant patient..
Exam trap: Only MR-safe or MR-conditional monitoring equipment, matched to the specific scanner conditions,
may enter the magnet room for a sedated or unstable patient; standard ward monitors and infusion pumps are not substitutes..
Pulse sequences: SE, FSE, GRE, EPI and how they are built.
A pulse sequence is a timed recipe of RF pulses and gradients that fills k-space line by line.
The families you must recognize:.
Spin echo (SE): a 90° excitation then a 180° refocusing pulse.
The 180° cancels static field inhomogeneity, so SE is T2 (not T2*) weighted and robust to susceptibility, though one echo per TR makes it slow.
Fast/turbo spin echo (FSE/TSE): multiple 180° pulses after each excitation collect an echo train (ETL).
Scan time drops by roughly the ETL factor.
The effective TE is set by when the center of k-space is filled, not by the first echo.
Long trains blur and make fat stay bright.
Gradient echo (GRE): a single flip angle with no 180°; the echo is formed by a gradient reversal, so residual field inhomogeneity is not refocused and GRE is T2* weighted.
Spoiled GRE gives T1/T2* contrast, while balanced SSFP keeps transverse magnetization for a bright-fluid T2/T1 ratio image.
Echo-planar imaging (EPI): fills all (or many) k-space lines after a single excitation, the basis of DWI and fMRI.
It is extremely fast but very sensitive to susceptibility, causing geometric distortion and signal dropout near air and bone.
Diffusion (DWI) adds paired motion-probing gradients scaled by the b-value; tissue where water cannot move (acute stroke) stays bright while the ADC map is dark.
The single organizing idea is that how you refocus the echo (180° versus gradient) and how many lines you read per excitation together set the contrast, the speed, and the artifacts.
Key point: SE uses a 180 refocuser for true T2: susceptibility-robust but slow..
Key point: FSE reads an echo train (ETL), cutting time by the ETL factor; effective TE is when the k-space center is filled..
Key point: GRE has no 180, so it is T2* weighted; spoiled gives T1/T2*, balanced SSFP gives bright fluid..
Key point: EPI fills k-space in one shot: fast (DWI and fMRI) but prone to geometric distortion..
Key point: DWI: restricted diffusion is bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map..
Worked example.
A patient has a hip replacement and you must choose between a fast spin echo and a gradient echo proton density sequence to evaluate the bone next to the hardware.
Gradient echo has no 180 degree refocusing pulse, so the local field distortion the metal creates around it is never cancelled,
and the image shows a large signal void with visible geometric warping near the implant.
Fast spin echo runs a whole train of 180 degree pulses, and each one refocuses the dephasing that metal induced since the last pulse, so the artifact shrinks dramatically.
The right choice for periprosthetic imaging is fast spin echo, or a dedicated metal artifact reduction sequence built on it,
because the refocusing pulse train is what tames the T2 star dephasing that a gradient echo sequence cannot correct.
Memory hook: Spin echo and fast spin echo both refocus with a 180, so both read out true T2.
Gradient echo skips the 180, so it reads out T2 star instead..
Memory hook: EPI is the one shot sequence: one excitation fills most or all of k-space, which is why it is fast for diffusion and functional imaging but also the most distortion prone sequence..
Memory hook: Effective TE in fast spin echo is set by whichever echo fills the center of k-space, not by the first echo in the train..
Exam trap: Do not confuse T2 with T2 star.
T2 star is always shorter than T2 because it includes magnet inhomogeneity dephasing that the 180 degree pulse in spin echo and fast spin echo cancels out; gradient echo has no way to cancel it..
Exam trap: A longer echo train shortens fast spin echo scan time, but it also blurs detail and lets fat stay bright even at a long effective TE,
which is different from conventional spin echo where fat is dark at long TE..
Exam trap: Diffusion weighted imaging and the ADC map read oppositely: restricted diffusion, such as acute stroke, is bright on the DWI image but dark on the ADC map.
Mixing those two up reverses the clinical read..
Reading pathology: where lesions hide and what lights them up.
Most pathology adds water (edema, inflammation, many tumors), so it is bright on T2 and on FLAIR.
Because FLAIR nulls CSF, periventricular and cortical lesions no longer hide in bright fluid.
A short checklist of the sequences that reveal specific disease:.
DWI and ADC: restricted diffusion is bright on DWI and dark on ADC.
This is the signature of acute infarct, and also of abscess and hypercellular tumor.
Beware T2 shine-through: always check the ADC to confirm true restriction.
Post-gadolinium T1: enhancement marks blood-brain-barrier breakdown such as tumor, active demyelination, or infection.
Patterns matter (a ring-enhancing lesion suggests abscess, glioblastoma or metastasis).
GRE and SWI: blooming (exaggerated dark signal) reveals blood products, calcium and iron through susceptibility.
Finally, know what is bright on T1 without contrast: fat, subacute hemorrhage (methemoglobin), melanin (melanoma metastases), proteinaceous or highly concentrated fluid, and slow flow.
Recognizing these keeps you from mistaking intrinsic T1 brightness for enhancement.
Key point: Most pathology is extra water, so it is bright on T2 and FLAIR (FLAIR nulls CSF)..
Key point: Restricted diffusion is bright on DWI and dark on ADC: acute stroke, abscess, dense tumor..
Key point: Post-gadolinium enhancement marks blood-brain-barrier breakdown..
Key point: GRE and SWI blooming reveals blood, calcium and iron..
Key point: Intrinsically T1-bright: fat, subacute blood, melanin, proteinaceous fluid..
Worked example.
A 68-year-old presents with sudden left-sided weakness three hours from symptom onset.
The right MCA territory shows a focal area that is bright on DWI and dark on ADC, confirming true restricted diffusion rather than T2 shine-through, which is the signature of acute infarct.
The FLAIR sequence in the same region is still nearly normal, because vasogenic edema and FLAIR hyperintensity typically lag several hours behind the diffusion abnormality,
so a DWI-FLAIR mismatch supports that the stroke is still within an early treatment window.
A GRE or SWI sequence is added to exclude hemorrhage before any decision about thrombolysis, since blooming susceptibility artifact there would mean a bleed rather than a candidate for lytic therapy.
No enhancement is expected yet on post-gadolinium T1, because blood-brain-barrier breakdown from infarct typically takes a few days to appear.
Memory hook: Bright on DWI and dark on ADC is true restriction.
Bright on DWI with a normal or bright ADC is T2 shine-through, not a true acute infarct..
Memory hook: DWI lights up within minutes of stroke onset, but FLAIR takes hours to catch up, so a DWI-FLAIR mismatch is a clue to how fresh the stroke is..
Memory hook: Blooming on GRE or SWI means blood, calcium, or iron, and the dark spot on the image is always bigger than the true lesion..
Exam trap: T2 shine-through: a chronic lesion can look bright on DWI simply because it is bright on T2, not because diffusion is restricted.
Always confirm with the ADC map, which should be dark for a true acute infarct..
Exam trap: A ring-enhancing lesion is not specific to one diagnosis.
Abscess, glioblastoma, and metastasis can all show this pattern, so additional clues such as restricted diffusion in the abscess cavity are needed to tell them apart..
Exam trap: T1 brightness without contrast, from fat, subacute blood, melanin, or concentrated proteinaceous fluid, can be mistaken for enhancement.
Always compare to the pre-contrast T1 or use fat saturation to confirm true enhancement..
Flow, function and artifacts: MRA methods and the artifacts to name.
Imaging flow.
Three ways to see vessels without catheters:.
Time-of-flight (TOF) MRA: stationary tissue is saturated by rapid RF, while fresh inflowing blood is unsaturated and bright (flow-related enhancement).
It fails for in-plane flow because those spins saturate, so use thin slabs perpendicular to the vessel.
A saturation band on one side selects arteries versus veins.
Phase-contrast (PC) MRA: bipolar gradients give moving spins a net phase proportional to velocity.
You set a VENC (encoding velocity); if the true velocity exceeds VENC, the phase wraps and you get velocity aliasing.
PC also quantifies flow and direction.
Contrast-enhanced MRA: gadolinium shortens blood T1 for a fast, flow-independent angiogram, where timing the bolus to the arterial phase is everything.
Artifacts to recognize by name: motion produces ghosting along the phase-encode direction (pulsatile flow ghosts too,

so a saturation band or gating helps); chemical shift lies along the frequency direction (worse at high field or low bandwidth); aliasing or wraparound occurs when the FOV is smaller than the object in
the phase direction; Gibbs or truncation appears as parallel ringing lines at high-contrast borders (reduce with a finer matrix); susceptibility distorts near metal or air,
worst on GRE and EPI; and the zipper comes from stray RF.
Chemical shift runs along the frequency (readout) axis and grows as bandwidth drops: at low bandwidth the fat signal is misregistered,

giving bright and dark bands at fat/water borders.Gibbs (truncation) ringing appears as parallel lines just inside high-contrast borders when k-space is cut off; a k-space filter (apodization) trades a
little sharpness to suppress it.
Key point: TOF MRA: inflowing unsaturated spins are bright; it fails for in-plane flow..
Key point: Phase contrast: velocity above VENC gives aliasing; PC also quantifies flow direction..
Key point: Motion and pulsatile-flow ghosts propagate along the PHASE-encode direction..
Key point: Chemical shift is in the FREQUENCY direction; worse at high field or low bandwidth..
Key point: Gibbs or truncation is ringing at sharp borders; reduce it with a higher matrix..
Worked example.
An axial T2-weighted image of the abdomen shows a bright band of ghosting running across the whole image in the anterior to posterior direction,
overlapping the aorta and repeating at regular intervals.
The phase-encode direction for this acquisition is anterior to posterior, and the pattern repeats with a spacing tied to the cardiac cycle,
so this is pulsatile flow ghosting from the aorta: the periodic motion of arterial inflow between phase-encode steps mismaps signal along phase, not frequency.
The fix is a saturation band placed over the vessel proximal to the imaging slab, or gating the acquisition to the cardiac cycle, not a bandwidth change,
because bandwidth only helps chemical shift and noise, which sit along the frequency axis.
Memory hook: Motion and pulsatile flow ghost along PHASE.
Chemical shift is strictly along FREQUENCY.
Gibbs truncation ringing is usually worst along PHASE, because that axis often has fewer encoding steps, so raise the phase matrix to reduce it..
Memory hook: TOF is bright because it is unsaturated inflow; the same physics means TOF goes dark whenever flow lies in-plane long enough to get repeatedly hit by RF and saturate..
Memory hook: A traveling or walking saturation band sits on one side of the slab to null the vessel you do not want: proximal placement suppresses arterial signal for a venogram,
distal placement suppresses venous signal for an arteriogram..
Exam trap: Aliasing (wraparound) comes from an FOV smaller than the anatomy in the phase direction; it is fixed by enlarging phase FOV or using phase oversampling, not by changing bandwidth..
Exam trap: Susceptibility artifact is worst on GRE and EPI (no 180 degree refocusing pulse to correct field inhomogeneity) and mildest on spin echo..
Exam trap: The zipper artifact runs across the image from stray RF (a door left open, a light left on) and is unrelated to flow or motion..
Fat suppression: STIR, spectral, Dixon and water excitation.
Fat is bright on most sequences and can hide pathology, so suppressing it raises the conspicuity of edema, enhancement and marrow disease.
Four methods dominate:.
STIR (short-TI inversion recovery) nulls fat by its T1.
Because it acts on T1 and not frequency, it is uniform even in a poor field (off-isocenter, near metal), but it is not fat-specific and will null anything with fat's short T1,
including gadolinium-enhancing tissue, so it is not combined with contrast.
Spectral (chemical-shift) saturation uses a frequency-selective pulse to saturate fat before readout.
It is fat-specific and contrast-compatible but fails where the field is inhomogeneous, and it is harder at lower field where the fat-water frequency gap is smaller.
Dixon acquires in-phase and opposed-phase echoes and computes separate water-only and fat-only images, robustly and quantitatively.
Water excitation tips only the water protons, used in high-resolution cartilage imaging.
Choosing among them trades uniformity (STIR) against specificity and contrast compatibility (spectral, Dixon) and speed.
Key point: STIR nulls fat by T1: uniform in a poor field, but not contrast-compatible..
Key point: Spectral fat-sat is fat-specific and contrast-compatible but needs a homogeneous field..
Key point: Dixon uses in-phase and opposed-phase echoes for robust water-only and fat-only images..
Key point: Water excitation tips only water, used in high-resolution cartilage imaging..
Key point: Suppressing bright fat raises conspicuity of enhancement, edema and marrow disease..
Worked example.
You are protocoling a shoulder MRI and the coil placement puts the joint off isocenter, near the edge of the magnet's homogeneous volume, close to surgical hardware.
You want fat suppression so labral fluid and marrow edema stand out.
A frequency-selective spectral fat-sat pulse depends on a clean, uniform separation between the fat and water resonance peaks; off isocenter, and worse near metal,
the local field varies enough that the pulse partly saturates water in some spots and misses fat in others, giving patchy, unreliable suppression.
Switching to STIR solves the uniformity problem because it nulls tissue by T1 relaxation rather than by resonance frequency, so it does not care how homogeneous the local field is.

The trade-off shows up later in the same exam: if a contrast-enhanced sequence is planned, STIR cannot be used for that part, because gadolinium shortens the T1 of enhancing tissue down near fat's T1,
and STIR would null the enhancement right along with the fat.
For that portion of the exam, spectral fat-sat closer to isocenter, or Dixon, is used instead.
Memory hook: STIR nulls by T1, so it is field-uniform but not contrast-safe.
Spectral fat-sat is frequency-selective, so it is contrast-safe but field-sensitive..
Memory hook: Off isocenter, near metal, or at low field where the fat-water frequency gap is small: reach for STIR, not spectral fat-sat..
Memory hook: Dixon separates water and fat by acquiring in-phase and opposed-phase echoes and solving for both signals,
which keeps it reliable and quantitative where a single saturation pulse would fail..
Exam trap: STIR contrast is not purely a fat-null overlay.
TE still contributes T2 weighting underneath, so fluid can be bright from T2 on a STIR image, which is easy to misread as pure T1 behavior..
Exam trap: Spectral fat-sat depends on field strength: the fat-water chemical shift is a fixed 3.5 ppm, but that translates to a wider frequency gap at higher field,
so it is easier at 3T and harder at 1.5T or below, especially over a large FOV..
Exam trap: Water excitation is not the same technique as fat saturation.
It selectively excites water protons at the outset rather than suppressing fat afterward, which is why it suits very short TR, high-resolution cartilage sequences..
Data acquisition: k-space, encoding and the Fourier transform.
MRI does not measure the image directly; it fills k-space, a grid of spatial-frequency data, and the Fourier transform converts that into the picture.
Two gradients encode position within a slice: frequency encoding is applied during readout, mapping position to signal frequency,
and phase encoding is stepped once per TR to fill successive k-space lines.
Because each line needs its own TR, the phase matrix (not the frequency matrix) drives scan time.
The center of k-space carries bulk signal and contrast; the periphery carries edges and fine detail (resolution).

This explains many techniques: partial Fourier samples just over half of k-space using its symmetry; centric ordering fills the center first to capture contrast at a chosen instant (dynamic MRA); paral
lel imaging skips lines and uses coil sensitivities to unfold the result; and zero-filling interpolates to a finer display matrix without adding true resolution.
A true 3D acquisition adds a second phase-encode (partition) gradient through the slab.
Key point: MRI fills k-space; the Fourier transform makes the image..
Key point: Frequency encoding is during readout; phase encoding steps once per TR..
Key point: The phase matrix drives scan time; the frequency matrix is essentially free..
Key point: k-space center = contrast and signal; periphery = resolution and edges..
Key point: Partial Fourier, parallel imaging and centric ordering all manipulate how k-space is filled..
Worked example.
You are running a 2D sequence with a TR of 500 ms, a phase matrix of 192, and 1 excitation (NEX).
Scan time is TR multiplied by the number of phase encoding steps multiplied by NEX, so 500 ms times 192 times 1 comes out to about 96 seconds.
If you drop the phase matrix to 128 and keep TR and NEX the same, scan time falls to about 64 seconds because you are now filling fewer k-space lines.
If instead you had reduced the frequency matrix from 256 to 192, scan time would not change at all, since frequency encoding is sampled entirely within a single readout window during each TR.
This is exactly why the phase matrix, not the frequency matrix, is the lever technologists pull to cut acquisition time.
Memory hook: Frequency encoding is essentially free: it all happens inside one readout window per TR.
Phase encoding is the expensive one: every step needs its own TR..
Memory hook: The center of k-space carries signal and contrast, the edges carry resolution and fine detail, so losing central lines hurts contrast and losing peripheral lines hurts sharpness..
Memory hook: k-space is a map of spatial frequencies, not a map of anatomy.
The Fourier transform is what turns that spatial frequency data into the picture you actually read..
Exam trap: Do not confuse which encoding drives scan time.
It is the phase encoding matrix, not the frequency encoding matrix, because phase encoding needs a fresh TR for every step while frequency encoding is captured entirely within a single readout..
Exam trap: Zero filling, sometimes called a zip, interpolates the image onto a finer display matrix and can look sharper,
but it adds no true spatial resolution because no new spatial frequencies were actually acquired..
Exam trap: Partial Fourier uses k-space's conjugate symmetry to skip roughly half the phase encoding steps, saving time or shortening TE,
but it comes at some SNR cost since fewer real lines are averaged into the final image..
MRI instrumentation: magnet, gradients, RF and coils.
An MRI scanner is four subsystems working together.
The main magnet provides the strong static field, usually a superconducting magnet cooled by liquid helium; its homogeneity is fine-tuned by shim coils, and its fringe field extends beyond the bore,
bounded by the 5-gauss line.
Gradient coils (x, y, z) superimpose linear field variations for slice selection and spatial encoding; their fast switching makes the acoustic noise and can cause peripheral nerve stimulation.
The RF system uses a transmit coil to excite spins (the B1 field) and receive coils (often phased arrays) to detect the tiny returning signal and enable parallel imaging.
Supporting these, the RF (Faraday) shield around the room blocks external radio interference, and higher field strength (for example 3 T versus 1.5 T) raises SNR but also raises SAR,
chemical shift and susceptibility.
A quench is the sudden loss of superconductivity that boils off helium, which is why the room has an oxygen monitor and a vent.
Key point: Superconducting magnets are cooled by liquid helium; shims optimize homogeneity..
Key point: Gradient coils encode position and cause the acoustic noise and PNS..
Key point: The RF transmit coil excites spins; receive (phased-array) coils detect signal..
Key point: The Faraday shield blocks external RF (zipper); the 5-gauss line bounds the fringe field..
Key point: Higher field raises SNR but also SAR, chemical shift and susceptibility..
Worked example.
During a scan the technologist sees a bright, repeating linear band of noise crossing the image that has nothing to do with the patient's anatomy,
and traces the cause to the scan room door being left open.
The room's copper Faraday shield only blocks stray radiofrequency energy from entering or leaving the room when the enclosure is completely sealed.
With the door ajar, ambient radiofrequency signals leak in and beat against the scanner's own frequency, producing the classic zipper artifact.
Once the door is closed the shield is intact again and the artifact disappears, which confirms the room shielding, not the scanner hardware, was the cause.
Memory hook: Superconducting magnets stay at field with liquid helium cooling, because once resistance drops to zero the current keeps circulating without any power input..
Memory hook: Gradient coils do the spatial encoding and make the loud switching noise.
RF coils do the exciting (transmit) and the listening (receive)..
Memory hook: Higher field strength buys more SNR, but it also raises SAR and widens the chemical shift artifact.
Nothing about going up in tesla is free..
Exam trap: Do not confuse the transmit coil's job, exciting spins with the B1 field, with the receive coil's job, detecting the tiny returning signal.
Phased array coils are about receive sensitivity and enabling parallel imaging, not about excitation..
Exam trap: A quench is a sudden, uncontrolled loss of superconductivity that rapidly boils off the helium, not a routine event.
It is why the magnet room has an oxygen monitor and a quench pipe vented outside..
Exam trap: Do not confuse the 5 gauss line, the fringe field safety boundary around the magnet, with the Faraday shield, the room enclosure that blocks external radiofrequency interference.
One concerns the static magnetic field, the other concerns RF noise..
3D imaging and reconstruction: volumes, MIP and reformats.
A 2D acquisition excites one slice at a time; a 3D volumetric acquisition excites a whole slab and phase-encodes through it, yielding thin, contiguous (gapless) partitions with high SNR.
When the voxels are isotropic (equal in all directions), the volume can be reformatted (MPR) into any plane without loss of resolution, so one acquisition serves every viewing angle.
Volumes are also shown as projections: a maximum-intensity projection (MIP) keeps the brightest voxel along each ray to show bright vessels in MR angiography,
while a minimum-intensity projection (MinIP) keeps the darkest voxel to show veins on susceptibility imaging or air.
The trade-offs to remember: 3D gives thin slices and high SNR but is more motion-sensitive and can take longer, while thick 2D slices are fast but suffer partial-volume averaging.
Adjacent 2D slices can also cross-talk through imperfect slice profiles, reduced by an interslice gap or interleaving.
Key point: 3D excites a slab and partition-encodes it: thin gapless slices, high SNR..
Key point: Isotropic voxels allow multiplanar reformatting in any plane..
Key point: MIP displays bright vessels; MinIP displays dark veins or air..
Key point: Thick 2D slices are fast but blur small findings (partial volume)..
Key point: Slice cross-talk is reduced with an interslice gap or interleaving..
Worked example.
A 3D time-of-flight MR angiogram of the circle of Willis is acquired as a thin slab with isotropic voxels,
and a maximum-intensity projection is generated by casting rays through the volume and keeping only the brightest voxel along each ray, producing a single angiogram-like image.
Because a MIP collapses a 3D volume into a 2D projection,
an overlapping vessel or an adjacent bright structure such as fat or a draining vein can project onto the artery of interest and mimic a stenosis or obscure a real one,
so the thin source partitions must always be reviewed to confirm any narrowing seen only on the MIP.
Because the acquisition used isotropic voxels, the same volume can also be reformatted with MPR into a coronal or oblique plane that follows the vessel's course, without reacquiring any data.
Memory hook: MIP keeps the brightest voxel along each ray, and MinIP keeps the darkest.
MIP shows arteries, MinIP shows veins or air..
Memory hook: Isotropic voxels are the ticket to free reformats: one acquisition, any plane, no loss of resolution..
Memory hook: A finding seen only on the MIP is not confirmed until it is checked against the thin source images..
Exam trap: A MIP can hide a true stenosis or mimic a false one, because overlapping vessels and venous contamination project onto the same pixels.
Always correlate with the source images before calling a stenosis..
Exam trap: Time-of-flight MRA signal is contaminated by anything with a short T1 or fast in-plane inflow, such as fat, subacute blood, or slow venous flow,
which can masquerade as vessel signal on the MIP.
Fat suppression or saturation bands help control this..
Exam trap: Thin contiguous 3D slices give high SNR per unit volume, but at the cost of longer scan time and greater motion sensitivity than thick 2D slices,
so 3D is not automatically the better choice for every exam..
Regional anatomy: planes and sequences by body part.
Each body part has a preferred plane and sequence chosen to display its key structures.
A few high-yield examples:.

Neuro: the internal auditory canals are screened with thin heavily T2-weighted images (CISS/FIESTA) for the vestibulocochlear nerve; the pituitary with thin dynamic post-contrast coronal T1; the tempor
al lobes with thin oblique coronals through the hippocampi.
Musculoskeletal: the rotator cuff (supraspinatus) on oblique coronal; the ACL on sagittal oblique; the menisci on short-TE (proton-density) sagittal and coronal.

Body: MRCP uses heavily T2-weighted sequences so static bile and pancreatic fluid are bright; the liver is characterized with multiphase dynamic post-gadolinium T1; the prostate with high-resolution T2
plus diffusion and dynamic contrast; the breast with fat-suppressed dynamic T1 and subtraction.
The recurring logic: pick the plane that lies along or across the structure of interest, and the contrast that makes its pathology stand out (fluid-sensitive, fat-suppressed, or dynamic enhancement).
Key point: Choose the plane along or across the structure of interest..
Key point: Neuro: thin T2 for cranial nerves; dynamic coronal T1 for the pituitary..
Key point: MSK: oblique coronal for the cuff, sagittal for the ACL, short-TE for menisci..
Key point: Body: MRCP is heavily T2; liver, prostate and breast rely on dynamic contrast..
Key point: Match the contrast (fluid-sensitive, fat-sat, dynamic) to the pathology sought..
Worked example.
A referral requests MRI of the shoulder to evaluate a suspected rotator cuff tear.
The technologist plans oblique coronal images angled parallel to the supraspinatus tendon rather than a true anatomic coronal,
because a plane that cuts across the tendon obliquely can create the illusion of a tear or underestimate a real one.
Oblique sagittal images, angled perpendicular to the cuff, are added to assess tendon retraction and muscle atrophy.
A fat-saturated proton-density or T2 sequence is chosen over plain T1, because fluid within a tear needs to appear bright against suppressed fat,
so a full-thickness tear shows as a fluid-bright gap through the tendon.
The same logic explains why the knee is imaged with short-TE sequences angled along the meniscal anatomy, rather than a single generic axial scan.
Memory hook: Plane follows the structure: oblique coronal for the cuff, oblique sagittal for the ACL.
A plain anatomic plane will not do..
Memory hook: Fat-saturated fluid-sensitive sequences catch the tear because fluid is bright and fat is dark; plain T1 alone can hide it..
Memory hook: MRCP is heavily T2-weighted because static fluid such as bile and pancreatic juice stays bright while everything else fades..
Exam trap: An anatomic, non-oblique coronal through the shoulder can mimic or obscure a cuff tear.
The oblique plane parallel to the supraspinatus is required for accurate assessment..
Exam trap: Dynamic post-contrast timing matters as much as plane for the pituitary.
A microadenoma enhances less avidly and later than the normal gland, so it shows up as a relatively dark focus against the brightly enhancing gland only on the early dynamic images..
Exam trap: Tendons and menisci oriented near 55 degrees to the main field can show artifactual increased signal on short-TE sequences, the magic angle effect, which can mimic tendinosis or a tear.
A longer-TE sequence helps confirm whether the finding is real..
Building a protocol: why each sequence is there.
A protocol is a deliberate sequence of acquisitions, each present for a reason.
A routine brain study typically includes T1 (anatomy), T2 and FLAIR (fluid-sensitive pathology, with FLAIR nulling CSF), and DWI (acute ischemia),
with post-gadolinium T1 added when enhancement is relevant.

Disease-specific protocols tune this base: acute stroke leans on DWI/ADC; multiple sclerosis emphasizes FLAIR plus post-contrast T1; a brain tumor adds perfusion to grade vascularity; the temporal lobe
s get thin hippocampal coronals for epilepsy.
Body and vascular protocols follow the same logic: cardiac viability uses late gadolinium enhancement, enterography distends bowel and images dynamically,
and non-contrast angiography uses time-of-flight or phase contrast.
The technologist also builds in artifact control: flow compensation, gating and saturation bands for pulsatile flow, and metal-artifact-reduction choices (spin echo over gradient echo,
high bandwidth) around hardware.
Key point: Routine brain: T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI, plus post-gadolinium T1 when needed..
Key point: Each sequence answers a specific question; disease tunes the base protocol..
Key point: Stroke leans on DWI; MS on FLAIR; tumor adds perfusion..
Key point: Angiography uses TOF, phase contrast or timed contrast..
Key point: Protocols build in artifact control (gating, sat bands, metal-reduction)..
Worked example.
Ordering a routine brain protocol for suspected multiple sclerosis, the technologist starts with a three-plane localizer to plan slice angles, then sagittal FLAIR to screen the corpus callosum,
where MS plaques classically radiate outward from the ventricles.
Axial FLAIR and T2 survey the rest of the brain, since plaques are bright on both, and post-gadolinium T1 separates active demyelination, which enhances, from old inactive plaques, which do not.
DWI is included as a routine safety net for a silent acute infarct, even though MS plaques themselves do not typically restrict diffusion.
Each sequence answers one question: T1 for anatomy, T2 and FLAIR for the fluid-sensitive lesion burden, and post-contrast T1 for activity,
so no sequence is present without a reason and none of the reasons duplicate each other.
Memory hook: Every sequence in a protocol answers a different question.
If two sequences answer the same question, one of them may not be needed..
Memory hook: Localizer sets the angles, T1 shows anatomy, T2 and FLAIR show fluid-sensitive pathology, and post-contrast T1 shows activity or blood-brain-barrier breakdown..
Memory hook: Disease tunes the base protocol: stroke leans on DWI, MS leans on FLAIR plus post-contrast T1, and tumor adds perfusion..
Exam trap: Adding a post-contrast sequence does not remove the need for a pre-contrast T1.
Without it, intrinsically T1-bright material such as fat, blood, or melanin cannot be told apart from true enhancement..
Exam trap: Flow compensation, gating, and saturation bands are artifact-control choices added to existing sequences, not sequences of their own,
and they are built in specifically to suppress pulsatility and flow artifact..
Exam trap: Metal-artifact-reduction choices favor spin echo over gradient echo and a higher receiver bandwidth,
since gradient echo and low bandwidth both increase susceptibility artifact around hardware..
MR angiography and venography: TOF, PC and contrast methods.
MR angiography shows vessels three ways.
Time-of-flight (TOF) saturates stationary tissue so fresh inflowing blood is bright (flow-related enhancement); it needs thin slabs perpendicular to flow and fails for in-plane flow.
Phase contrast (PC) encodes velocity as phase, so it not only depicts vessels but quantifies flow velocity and direction; its VENC must exceed the true velocity or the phase aliases.
Contrast-enhanced MRA shortens blood T1 with gadolinium for a fast, flow-independent angiogram,
where bolus timing to the arterial phase is everything (peripheral run-off uses a moving-table bolus chase, and time-resolved methods trade spatial for temporal resolution).
MR venography assesses the dural sinuses or deep veins with 2D TOF, PC or post-contrast venography.
For patients who cannot receive gadolinium, non-contrast techniques (TOF, PC, and ECG-gated fresh-blood or quiescent-interval methods) provide angiograms with no contrast at all.
Key point: TOF: inflowing unsaturated blood is bright; it fails for in-plane flow..
Key point: Phase contrast quantifies velocity and direction; VENC must exceed peak flow..
Key point: CE-MRA is fast and flow-independent but depends on arterial bolus timing..
Key point: MR venography uses TOF, PC or post-contrast to assess sinuses and deep veins..
Key point: Non-contrast MRA (TOF, PC, fresh-blood) serves patients who cannot have gadolinium..
Worked example.
You are planning a phase-contrast MRA of the carotids and need to pick a VENC.
Peak systolic velocity in a normal carotid is roughly 60 to 100 cm per second.
If you set VENC at 20 cm per second, velocities above that wrap around and alias, showing as artifactually reversed or wrong-magnitude flow in the vessel center.
If you set VENC at 150 cm per second to be safe, you avoid aliasing but the phase signal for the actual flow is now a small fraction of the encode range,
so the velocity measurement is noisy and less sensitive.
The right move is to set VENC just above the expected peak velocity for that vessel, around 80 to 100 cm per second here, so you get maximum phase sensitivity without wrapping.
Memory hook: VENC is a ceiling: set it just above the expected peak velocity.
Too low wraps (aliases), too high wastes sensitivity..
Memory hook: TOF is qualitative and anatomic; PC is quantitative, giving both velocity and direction because it literally encodes phase to speed..
Memory hook: CE-MRA trades flow-dependence for T1-shortening: it is fast and not affected by in-plane flow or saturation, but only as good as bolus timing..
Exam trap: TOF fails for slow or in-plane flow because those spins sit in the slab long enough to become saturated like stationary tissue; thinner slabs, or multiple overlapping thin slabs (MOTSA),
limit this saturation..
Exam trap: For patients who cannot receive gadolinium (severe renal impairment, prior reaction), non-contrast options exist: TOF, PC,
and ECG-gated fresh-blood or quiescent-interval single-shot techniques for venography and lower-extremity angiography..

Exam trap: Time-resolved contrast-enhanced MRA trades spatial resolution for temporal resolution to catch the arterial phase before venous contamination; a single mistimed acquisition can overlap arter
ial and venous signal..
MRI contrast agents: gadolinium, safety and special agents.
The workhorse MRI contrast agents are gadolinium chelates.
Gadolinium is paramagnetic and shortens the T1 of nearby tissue, so where it accumulates the tissue brightens on T1-weighted images.
In the brain it reaches tissue only where the blood-brain barrier is broken, so enhancement flags tumor, active demyelination or infection.

Agents are excreted by the kidneys, so eGFR is used to flag the severe renal impairment linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF): routine screening is no longer required before the stable macrocyc
lic agents, but older, less-stable linear agents with poor renal function are the classic NSF setting, so macrocyclic agents at the lowest effective dose are preferred, or contrast is avoided.

Why we give gadolinium: on pre-contrast T1 the mass is nearly invisible; post-gadolinium it lights up because Gd shortens T1 where the blood-brain barrier has broken down.Reactions range from mild (hiv
es, treated with antihistamines and observation) to rare anaphylaxis, whose first-line treatment is epinephrine.
Gadolinium is avoided in pregnancy unless essential; after gadolinium, breastfeeding may continue without interruption because very little reaches breast milk,
though an anxious mother may pump and discard for 24 hours.
Beyond standard extracellular agents, hepatobiliary agents aid liver characterization, iron-based agents can act as blood-pool agents, and negative oral agents darken bowel fluid for MRCP.
Key point: Gadolinium is paramagnetic, shortens T1, and brightens tissue on T1 images..
Key point: Brain enhancement marks blood-brain-barrier breakdown..
Key point: eGFR is risk-based, not routine before Group II macrocyclic agents; NSF links less-stable linear agents to severe renal failure..
Key point: Prefer stable macrocyclic agents at the lowest effective dose; avoid in pregnancy unless essential..
Key point: Mild reactions get antihistamines; anaphylaxis is treated first with epinephrine..
Worked example.
A patient is scheduled for a contrast-enhanced brain MRI and the eGFR comes back at 25 mL per minute per 1.73 square meters,
in the range associated with nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk from gadolinium exposure.
Gadolinium itself is the toxic part once it is released from its chelate, so agents are engineered to hold it tightly.
Linear chelates bind gadolinium less securely than macrocyclic chelates, so more free gadolinium can be released and deposited in tissue, including skin,
and in patients with poor renal clearance this is the mechanism behind NSF.
Because gadolinium is cleared through the kidneys, poor renal function means the agent, and any gadolinium it releases, stays in the body far longer, raising both exposure and risk.
The response is not to skip a clinically indicated scan but to use a stable macrocyclic agent at the lowest dose that answers the clinical question, with the decision documented.
If the goal instead were biliary imaging to look for a bile leak, a hepatobiliary agent, partly excreted through the liver into bile rather than only through the kidneys,
would be chosen over a standard extracellular agent.
Memory hook: Gadolinium is the toxic part; the chelate is what makes it safe to inject.
Macrocyclic chelates cage it more tightly than linear ones, which is why NSF risk concentrates in linear agents..
Memory hook: Renal function matters for contrast because poor kidney function means gadolinium lingers longer,
raising tissue retention and NSF risk; eGFR is checked in at-risk patients rather than routinely..
Memory hook: Special-purpose agents to keep straight: hepatobiliary agents for liver and bile, iron-based agents for blood-pool vascular imaging, negative oral agents to darken bowel fluid for MRCP..
Exam trap: NSF risk depends on chelate stability and renal function together.
Group II macrocyclic agents are very low risk, and current ACR guidance no longer requires routine eGFR screening before them,
though many facilities still confirm renal function before any gadolinium and no agent is truly risk-free..
Exam trap: A prior allergic-type reaction to iodinated CT contrast or a shellfish allergy does not predict a gadolinium reaction; that cross-reactivity belief is a myth even for iodinated contrast,
though any prior contrast reaction of any kind raises general risk..
Exam trap: Anaphylaxis is treated first with epinephrine, not antihistamines or steroids.
Antihistamines are for milder urticarial reactions, not the airway and cardiovascular compromise of true anaphylaxis..
Flip angle: the Ernst angle and the SAR trade-off.
The flip angle is the angle by which the RF pulse tips the net magnetization away from the main field.
It is one of the most useful contrast knobs in MRI, and what it does depends on the sequence family.
90 degrees puts all the magnetization into the transverse plane, giving the maximum signal from a single excitation.
This is the classic spin-echo excitation.
Gradient echo usually uses less than 90 degrees.
With short TRs there is no time for full longitudinal recovery, so a smaller flip angle yields more steady-state signal.
The Ernst angle is the flip that maximizes signal for a given TR and tissue T1, following cos(Ernst angle) = exp(-TR / T1); a shorter TR or a longer T1 means a smaller Ernst angle.
In gradient echo the flip angle also steers contrast: a larger flip leans toward T1 weighting, while a smaller flip leans toward proton density and T2*.
The catch is SAR: flip angle scales with RF power, so a bigger flip deposits more heat, which is why fast, high-flip, short-TR sequences can reach SAR limits, especially at higher field strength.
Key point: The flip angle is how far the RF pulse tips the magnetization from the main field..
Key point: 90 degrees gives maximum single-excitation signal (classic spin echo)..
Key point: Gradient echo uses a smaller flip; the Ernst angle maximizes signal for a given TR and T1..
Key point: Larger flip leans to T1 weighting; smaller flip leans to proton density and T2*..
Key point: Flip angle scales with RF power, so a larger flip raises SAR..
Worked example.
You are running a T1-weighted spoiled gradient echo of the brain with a short TR of 8 ms.
At a 90 degree flip the longitudinal magnetization barely recovers between pulses, so the signal is weak.
Lowering the flip toward the Ernst angle for white matter, roughly 8 to 10 degrees at that TR, restores signal.
The Ernst angle is the flip that maximizes steady-state signal for a given TR and T1, where cos(Ernst) equals exp(-TR/T1).
A short TR pushes the Ernst angle small, which is why fast gradient echo uses low flip angles.
Memory hook: Short TR wants a small flip.
As TR drops, the Ernst angle drops with it..
Memory hook: cos of the Ernst angle equals E1, and E1 is exp(-TR over T1)..
Exam trap: SAR scales with the square of the flip angle and with the square of field strength, so trimming the flip angle is the fastest way to cut SAR..
Exam trap: The Ernst angle maximizes signal, not contrast.
A higher flip can give stronger T1 weighting even though total signal is lower..
Contrast reactions: recognition and management.
How common, and what is not a reaction.
Adverse reactions to a gadolinium-based contrast agent occur in roughly 0.07 to 2.4 percent of patients, and the vast majority are mild.
True anaphylaxis is rare, on the order of 0.001 to 0.01 percent, and fatal reactions are rarer still.
A transient feeling of warmth or flushing during injection is not a true reaction; reassurance is usually all it needs,
and calming an anxious patient before the injection can prevent symptoms from escalating.
The three severity tiers.
Reactions are graded in three tiers:.
Mild: nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, itching, and limited hives.
The radiologist evaluates the patient, vitals are taken, and the patient is observed for up to 30 minutes.
Moderate: diffuse erythema, bronchospasm, wheezing, hypotension, or a vasovagal episode.
Not immediately life threatening but can progress, so medical treatment and monitoring until resolution are required.
Severe: laryngeal edema, unresponsiveness, seizures, arrhythmia, and anaphylaxis.
These demand immediate treatment.
Telling the two low blood pressure pictures apart.
A vasovagal reaction, often triggered by anxiety around IV placement, produces hypotension with bradycardia, pallor, nausea,
and sweating; the first maneuver is to elevate the legs or use the Trendelenburg position to restore blood flow to the brain, then recheck vitals until the patient improves.
Anaphylaxis produces hypotension with tachycardia, typically alongside hives, facial or laryngeal swelling, or wheezing, and it is the clear indication for epinephrine.
Extravasation.
A separate problem is extravasation, where contrast enters the soft tissue instead of the vein, causing swelling, redness, burning, and pain.
A warm compress promotes reabsorption and circulation, a cold compress relieves pain, and a radiologist should assess the site before the patient leaves.
The rapid response sequence.
When a reaction occurs: remove the patient from the scanner and assess breathing, pulse, and consciousness; alert the covering radiologist and, if needed,
the emergency response team; prepare the emergency equipment and medication box in a safe zone outside the magnetic field; inform responders of the study type, the agent given,
and when the reaction began; then deliver medications exactly as the physician directs.
The medication box.
Each drug pairs with an indication:.
Albuterol for wheezing.
Atropine for bradycardia.
Diphenhydramine for mild urticaria.
Dextrose for hypoglycemia.
Furosemide for pulmonary edema.
Epinephrine for anaphylaxis.
Epinephrine and disposition.
Per department protocol, the epinephrine auto-injector is the one drug a technologist may give decisively: 0.3 mg for patients 30 kg and over, 0.15 mg for 15 to 30 kg,
pressed firmly against the lateral thigh until it clicks and held for several seconds.
Every patient who receives an auto-injector goes to the emergency department for monitoring.
Premedication and monitoring reference points.
Patients with a prior severe reaction are premedicated, commonly prednisone 50 mg by mouth 13, 7, and 1 hour before contrast plus diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before.
While monitoring: SpO2 above 95 percent is normal and 92 percent or less suggests hypoxemia; normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and 80 diastolic.
Key point: Reactions to gadolinium-based agents are uncommon and mostly mild; anaphylaxis occurs in roughly 0.001 to 0.01 percent of patients..
Key point: Vasovagal means hypotension with bradycardia, pallor, and sweating; anaphylaxis means hypotension with tachycardia plus hives or airway involvement..
Key point: For extravasation, a warm compress promotes reabsorption, a cold compress relieves pain, and a radiologist assesses the site before discharge..
Key point: In an emergency: remove the patient from the scanner, alert the radiologist and response team, prepare equipment and the med box outside the field, inform responders,
and deliver drugs as directed..
Key point: The epinephrine auto-injector is the one drug a technologist may give per department protocol: 0.3 mg at 30 kg and above, 0.15 mg for 15 to 30 kg,
and every recipient goes to the emergency department..
Worked example.
Five minutes after a gadolinium-based contrast injection, a patient develops spreading hives and begins to wheeze, with a heart rate of 118.
Skin and airway involvement together meet anaphylaxis criteria, so this is treated as a severe reaction rather than a mild one.
The technologist removes the patient from the scanner, checks breathing and pulse, alerts the covering radiologist,
and moves the patient to a safe zone outside the magnetic field with the medication box and emergency equipment ready.
Because both skin and airway are involved, the radiologist directs intramuscular epinephrine into the lateral thigh without delay, with albuterol as an adjunct for the wheeze,
and the patient is monitored and sent to the emergency department.
Memory hook: Slow and pale points vagal, fast with hives points anaphylaxis..
Memory hook: Compresses for extravasation: warm to clear it, cold to calm it..
Memory hook: The response flow spells RAPID: Remove, Alert, Prepare, Inform, Deliver..
Exam trap: Both vasovagal reactions and anaphylaxis drop the blood pressure; the heart rate separates them, slow for vasovagal and fast for anaphylaxis..
Exam trap: Warmth or flushing during injection is an expected sensation, not a true reaction, so the answer is reassurance rather than medication..
Exam trap: Diphenhydramine treats mild urticaria only; epinephrine, not an antihistamine, is the drug for anaphylaxis, and premedication reduces but does not eliminate repeat risk..
Brain MRI: routine protocol and when to enhance.
A routine brain study uses the head coil and covers from the skull base to the vertex, roughly one slice above the top of the skull.
Axial slices are angled along the AC-PC line, drawn through the anterior and posterior commissures, so that anatomy is displayed in a reproducible plane.
Many departments now acquire 3D sagittal volumes (T1, FLAIR, and T2) and reformat them into axial and coronal planes, which reduces repeat scanning and gives isotropic detail.
The non-contrast set is built around a signal triad.
Diffusion detects acute infarct: true restriction is bright on the high b-value image (for example b1000) and dark on the ADC map.
SWI (susceptibility-weighted imaging) shows hemorrhage and cerebral microbleeds in trauma and microhemorrhage.
FLAIR is a fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequence that nulls CSF so CSF appears dark, and it highlights multiple sclerosis and other white-matter disease.
The spine equivalent for demyelination is STIR.
Gadolinium is dosed by body weight per department protocol.
Structures that normally enhance confirm that contrast was delivered: the pituitary gland and infundibulum, choroid plexus, nasal mucosa and turbinates, dural venous sinuses, and vessels.
Contrast is added by indication, such as infection, tumor follow-up, pre-operative and immediate post-operative studies, metastatic or meningioma work-up in a patient with a cancer history,
and demyelinating disease.
Isolated memory loss usually does not receive contrast.
Key point: Head coil, coverage skull base to vertex, axial slices angled on the AC-PC line..
Key point: Diffusion restriction means bright on high b-value AND dark on ADC..
Key point: SWI shows hemorrhage and microbleeds; FLAIR nulls CSF and shows MS..
Key point: 3D sagittal volumes are reformatted into axial and coronal planes..
Key point: Gadolinium is weight-based; pituitary, choroid plexus, mucosa, sinuses, and vessels normally enhance..
Worked example.
A patient arrives with sudden left-sided weakness.
On the high b-value diffusion image a right frontal region is bright, and the same region is dark on the ADC map.
That combination confirms an acute infarct with true restricted diffusion, so the finding is reported as acute stroke rather than dismissed as an artifact.
Memory hook: Diffusion for stroke, SWI for blood, FLAIR for plaques..
Memory hook: True restriction is bright high-b, dark ADC..
Memory hook: AC to PC keeps every brain in the same plane..
Exam trap: FLAIR nulls CSF so CSF is dark, unlike T2 where CSF is bright..
Exam trap: High b-value brightness alone is not restriction without a dark ADC; bright high-b with bright ADC is T2 shine-through..
Specialized neuro studies: pituitary, IAC, and stereotactic planning.
The dynamic pituitary study uses the head coil and full-dose contrast.
A microadenoma is smaller than 10 mm and a macroadenoma is 10 mm or larger.
A dynamic contrast-enhanced sequence acquires rapid repeated images just after injection to catch microadenomas, which enhance later than the normal gland.
On early dynamic frames the lesion therefore looks relatively dark against the briskly enhancing normal pituitary.
Do not alter the dynamic sequence parameters.
The gland has an anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and a posterior lobe (neurohypophysis), the posterior lobe is often intrinsically T1-bright, and the gland sits in the sella turcica.
The internal auditory canal study also uses the head coil and full-dose contrast.
The IAC carries cranial nerves VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear).
Indications include sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo or balance problems, tinnitus, and acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma).
Technique combines thin-section heavily T2-weighted cisternal imaging, a steady-state CISS or FIESTA type sequence that outlines the nerves within bright CSF,
plus thin post-contrast T1 with fat saturation.
A related variant targets trigeminal neuralgia or facial-nerve problems such as facial pain or Bell's palsy involving CN VII.
Stereotactic or neuronavigation planning is a pre-surgical study.
Keep the head straight and do not angle the slice packages, and acquire an isotropic 3D volume with full coverage.
Do not clip the nose, ears, or back of the head, because the surgical navigation system registers the whole head surface.
Sub-variants add perfusion for tumor grading or a dynamic sequence for metastases and meningioma, and a seizure pre-operative study angles coronals perpendicular to the hippocampus.
Key point: Microadenoma is under 10 mm, macroadenoma is 10 mm or larger..
Key point: Dynamic pituitary catches microadenomas by their delayed enhancement, dark early against the normal gland..
Key point: IAC carries CN VII and VIII; indications include hearing loss and acoustic neuroma..
Key point: IAC uses thin-section CISS or FIESTA cisternal imaging plus post-contrast T1 fat-sat..
Key point: Stereotactic studies keep the head straight, do not angle packages, and never clip nose, ears, or occiput..
Worked example.
A patient with a rising prolactin level has a normal-looking sella on routine images.
The dynamic pituitary sequence is run, and on the earliest post-injection frames a small 6 mm region stays dark while the rest of the gland enhances briskly.
That delayed enhancement pattern identifies a microadenoma that a single delayed image would have missed.
Memory hook: Micro is under 10, macro is ten or more..
Memory hook: Seven and Eight run through the IAC gate..
Memory hook: Straight head, full head for navigation..
Exam trap: A microadenoma enhances later than the gland, so it looks dark early, not bright early..
Exam trap: Do not angle or crop the stereotactic packages; clipping the nose, ears, or occiput breaks surface registration..
Spine MRI protocols: cervical, thoracic, and lumbar.

The cervical spine is imaged with a combined head and neck coil for indications such as neck pain, herniated disc (HNP), degenerative disc disease (DDD), radiculopathy, stenosis, cord compression, MS,
tumor, Chiari malformation, syrinx, and radiating arm pain.
Sagittal coverage runs from the pons and fourth ventricle down to about T2 to T3, pedicle to pedicle, and axials extend from C2 to C3 through C7 to T1, angled to each disc space.
Core sequences are Sag T2 and Sag T1 for herniation, DDD, lesions, tumor, and syrinx, plus Sag STIR for MS, metastases, fracture, and infection.
Axial GRE displays the nerve roots and osteophytes, and Ax T2 shows cord lesions and syrinx.
An anterior saturation band placed in front of the vertebral bodies suppresses swallowing, cardiac, and breathing motion and also reduces CSF pulsation artifact.
The thoracic spine covers roughly C7 to L1 for mid back pain and the same degenerative and cord indications.
Because the thoracic levels are hard to count, a vitamin E capsule (a common skin or table marker) is placed to help count vertebral bodies so the correct level is localized.
Sag STIR is the best sequence for MS, infection, fracture, and bony metastases.
Add Cor T2 for scoliosis and Cor STIR when neurofibromatosis (NF1 or NF2) is suspected.
Axials may use right to left phase encoding to push breathing motion artifact away from the cord.
The lumbar spine covers about T12 to S2 with axials from L1 to S1 for low back pain, HNP, DDD, radiculopathy, stenosis, tumor, radiating leg pain, prior surgery, and tethered cord.
Use an odd number of slices per disc (for example 5) so one slice runs through the disc center.
Contrast is required for infection, post-operative scarring, and tumor.
After back surgery, contrast separates enhancing scar (fibrosis) from non-enhancing recurrent disc.
Tethered cord studies extend coverage down to the coccyx.
Key point: Cervical uses a head and neck coil; sagittals run from the pons and fourth ventricle to about T2 to T3..
Key point: Sag STIR is best for MS, metastases, fracture, and infection in every region of the spine..
Key point: Axial GRE shows nerve roots and osteophytes but blooms near metal, so avoid it there..
Key point: An anterior saturation band suppresses swallowing, cardiac, and breathing motion plus CSF pulsation..
Key point: A vitamin E capsule marker counts thoracic levels; lumbar covers about T12 to S2 with odd slices per disc..
Worked example.
A patient returns with recurrent leg pain one year after an L4 to L5 discectomy.
A plain non-contrast study cannot tell whether the epidural soft tissue is scar or a new disc fragment.
Contrast is given, and the tissue enhances uniformly, which identifies fibrosis rather than recurrent disc.
Because scar enhances while recurrent disc does not, the post-operative lumbar spine is protocoled with contrast from the start.
Memory hook: STIR lights up the bad marrow: MS, mets, fracture, infection..
Memory hook: Vitamin E dot lets you count the vertebral bodies and find the level..
Memory hook: Post-op scar glows, recurrent disc stays dark..
Exam trap: Do not run GRE near spinal hardware, because metal blooms and hides the anatomy..
Exam trap: The post-operative lumbar spine gets contrast because scar enhances while recurrent disc does not..
Total spine and technique: bone versus neuro, drop metastases, and metal reduction.
A total spine is assembled from two sagittal packages, an upper and a lower set, that overlap by about two disc spaces, using 3 mm slices with no gap.
The field of view for each package is set to the habitus it covers, not by a fixed rule.
Always use the smallest field of view that still covers the anatomy, and adjust resolution whenever the FOV changes.
Remember the counts: the spine has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, and 5 lumbar vertebrae.
Metastatic disease splits into two patterns.
Drop metastases seed down the CSF from a primary brain tumor, so the study images the whole thecal sac including the entire sacrum and typically omits the pre-contrast axials.
Bony metastases arise from primary cancers such as lung, prostate, or breast, usually need no contrast, and an in and out of phase sequence can help characterize marrow.
Cor STIR is added when neurofibromatosis is suspected.
For post-contrast technique, use a fat-saturated T1 to improve differentiation of enhancing tissue, and do not substitute a STIR sequence for the post-contrast series,
because gadolinium shortens T1 toward STIR's null point and can suppress the very enhancement you want to show.
Near hardware, a metal reduction toolkit recovers the image.
Use TSE (turbo spin echo) rather than gradient echo, increase the receive bandwidth, and raise the turbo or echo train factor.
Decrease the slice thickness, switch fat-saturated T2 to STIR for more uniform fat suppression, and decrease the TE.
Raise the resolution, change the phase encode direction, and increase the number of signal averages to recover lost signal.
Key point: Total spine sagittals use two packages overlapping by about two disc spaces, using 3 mm slices with no gap..
Key point: Drop mets seed from a brain tumor and require imaging the whole thecal sac including the entire sacrum..
Key point: Bony mets from lung, prostate, or breast usually need no contrast; in and out of phase can help..
Key point: Near metal, use TSE not gradient echo, raise bandwidth, and switch fat-sat T2 to STIR..
Worked example.
A patient with a known posterior fossa primary is sent for spine imaging to look for CSF seeding.
Because drop metastases fall through the CSF and collect at the bottom of the thecal sac, the coverage is extended to include the entire sacrum,
and the pre-contrast axials are omitted so the post-contrast series does the work.
A patient with lung cancer and back pain, by contrast, is worked up for bony metastases, usually without contrast, and an in and out of phase sequence helps confirm marrow replacement.
Memory hook: Drop mets fall to the floor, so scan all the way to the sacrum..
Memory hook: Fight metal with TSE, wide bandwidth, and STIR..
Exam trap: Near metal, prefer STIR over fat-saturated T2 and use TSE rather than gradient echo..
Brain MRA and MRV: time-of-flight, coverage, and reconstructions.
Brain MRA is usually a non-contrast time-of-flight (TOF) study.
The bright vessel signal comes from fresh, unsaturated blood flowing into the imaging slab, while the stationary background tissue is repeatedly saturated by the rapid pulses and stays dark.
No gadolinium is needed for this contrast.
A TOF angiogram can be added to a routine brain study or run on its own, and typical indications include aneurysm, brain hemorrhage, and arteriovenous malformation (AVM),
which may need extra coverage to include the feeding and draining vessels.
Coverage for the arterial study runs from about the top of the corpus callosum down to the skull base, and the TOF acquisition should be kept isotropic so reformats are clean in any plane.
To extend coverage, do not raise the number of slices per slab much above 40, because too many slices per slab causes the Venetian blind artifact, a stripe of signal drop at the slab boundaries.
Instead, add more slabs.
Reconstructions include rotating maximum intensity projections (MIPs) of the Circle of Willis plus targeted MIPs of the bilateral and individual carotid arteries.
An aneurysm and an AVM are best shown on TOF or contrast MRA, which display the aneurysm sac or the AVM nidus with its feeding and draining vessels.
A cavernoma, being low-flow and angiographically occult, is better characterized on SWI.
Brain MRV is the venous half of the vascular study and evaluates dural venous sinus thrombosis and venous sinus stenosis.
Venous coverage runs from the top of the skull down to below the foramen magnum.
A non-contrast venogram uses a straight sagittal and a straight coronal 2D TOF acquisition, while a contrast venogram uses an axial fast 3D T1 gradient echo planned along the AC-PC line.
For a contrast MRV, the pre and post series must match exactly so a MIP subtraction removes the background tissue, and the nose is cropped out of the reconstruction.
Key point: TOF is bright because inflowing blood is unsaturated while background tissue is saturated dark, with no contrast used..
Key point: Arterial brain MRA coverage runs from the top of the corpus callosum down to the skull base and is kept isotropic..
Key point: Extend TOF coverage by adding more slabs, not more slices per slab, to avoid the Venetian blind artifact..
Key point: Aneurysm and AVM are best shown on TOF or contrast MRA; a cavernoma is better shown on SWI because it is angiographically occult..
Key point: Brain MRV evaluates dural sinus thrombosis; contrast MRV needs matched pre and post series for MIP subtraction..
Worked example.
A technologist needs to extend a TOF brain MRA superiorly to capture the upper branches of an AVM.
Rather than increasing the slices per slab to 60, which would leave dark horizontal bands where the slabs meet,
the technologist keeps each slab near 40 slices and adds a second and third slab to reach the added coverage.
The Circle of Willis and the malformation are then reconstructed as rotating MIPs without slab-boundary signal loss.
Memory hook: TOF glows because inflowing blood is fresh and unsaturated, not because of dye..
Memory hook: More coverage means more slabs, not more slices..
Memory hook: Aneurysm and AVM on MRA; cavernoma on SWI..
Exam trap: To extend TOF coverage, add more slabs rather than more slices per slab, because too many slices per slab causes the Venetian blind artifact at the slab boundaries..
Exam trap: TOF vessels are bright because inflowing blood is unsaturated, not because contrast was given..
Neck MRA and carotid technique: contrast timing, saturation bands, and dissection.
Neck MRA indications include prior stroke or CVA, carotid stenosis or occlusion, and carotid dissection.
A limited non-contrast TOF of the neck can cover just above and below the carotid bifurcation, while a full non-contrast neck MRA covers from the skull base down to the aortic arch.
As with brain MRA, coverage is extended by adding slabs rather than slices per slab.
