Contrast-enhanced neck MRA uses a thin coronal 3D gradient echo, on the order of 1.5 mm, covering from the top of the Circle of Willis down to the aortic arch and including both carotids.
Gadolinium is weight-based, and the acquisition is timed to the arterial bolus using a test bolus or a bolus-tracking method so the arteries are captured before venous contamination.
Saturation band direction sets which vessels are displayed.
A saturation band placed superior to the slab, a "sat up," suppresses inflow from above and displays arterial flow, while a band placed inferior to the slab, a "sat down," displays venous flow.
This is how subclavian steal is demonstrated, a condition where vertebral artery flow reverses because of a compromised subclavian artery, so the vertebral fills from the wrong direction.
Carotid dissection is a tear that lets blood track into the vessel wall.
It is best shown on a pre-contrast fat-saturated T1, typically a coronal 3D T1, or an axial T1 fat-sat if the coronal fails, covering the carotids and the entire aortic arch.
The classic sign is a normally dark flowing vessel with a crescent of bright signal in the wall, the intramural hematoma, at the site of the dissection.
Because the finding lives in the wall and not the lumen, it is imaged before contrast is given.
Key point: Neck MRA indications include prior stroke, carotid stenosis or occlusion, and carotid dissection..
Key point: Full non-contrast neck MRA covers from the skull base to the aortic arch, extended by adding slabs..
Key point: Contrast neck MRA is weight-based and timed to the arterial bolus so arteries fill before veins..
Key point: A superior saturation band (sat up) shows arterial flow, an inferior band (sat down) shows venous flow..
Key point: Carotid dissection is best shown on pre-contrast fat-sat T1 as a bright crescent of intramural hematoma..
Worked example.
A patient presents with neck pain and stroke symptoms after a fall, and the radiologist suspects a carotid dissection.
Before any gadolinium is given, the technologist runs a coronal 3D fat-saturated T1 covering the carotids from the skull base through the aortic arch.
On the images the normally dark carotid shows a bright crescent along its wall, the intramural hematoma, confirming the dissection while the lumen still appears patent.
Memory hook: Sat up sees arteries, sat down sees veins..
Memory hook: Steal means the vertebral runs backward from a bad subclavian..
Memory hook: Dissection is a bright crescent in the wall on fat-sat T1, done before dye..
Exam trap: A superior saturation band (sat up) shows arterial flow, while an inferior saturation band (sat down) shows venous flow..
Exam trap: Carotid dissection shows a bright crescent of intramural hematoma on fat-saturated T1 and is imaged before contrast..
MSK MRI protocols: shoulder, knee, hip, wrist, and foot.
The shoulder is imaged for rotator cuff tear, bursitis, and arthritis.
Position the arm at the side, palm up, in external rotation supported by a sandbag, which moves the bicipital groove out of the way for a cleaner view of the rotator cuff,
especially the supraspinatus tendon.
The arm should lie parallel to the chest without sagging, and if the patient cannot externally rotate, image in neutral.
Coverage runs from above the acromioclavicular joint to below the glenoid.
The coronal is angled perpendicular to the glenohumeral joint and the sagittal is parallel to it.
The four rotator cuff muscles are Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, and Subscapularis (SITS).
The knee is imaged for pain, ACL or PCL tear, meniscal tear, torn cartilage, arthritis, and internal derangement.
Center the laser at the inferior border of the patella (the apex), not the joint center.
Coverage runs from the quadriceps femoris attachment above to the patellar tendon and fat pad below.
The hip is imaged for pain, bursitis, avascular necrosis (AVN), and labral tear.
Place the phased-array coil with its top at the iliac crest and the hip joint over a posterior coil element, and locate the hip midway between the ASIS and the greater trochanter.
Tie the feet together with toes in and heels apart to hold gentle internal rotation.
Axial coverage runs from a few inches above the hip joint to below the lesser trochanter.
The wrist is imaged for triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear, carpal fracture, carpal tunnel syndrome, ganglion cyst, and ligament tear.
Position with the hand overhead (the superman position) or head-first supine, and cover all the carpal bones from the carpometacarpal joints to the wrist joint.
The foot and ankle protocols are forefoot or midfoot, ankle or hindfoot, and whole foot, using a foot and ankle coil, feet-first supine.
Indications include pain, fracture, ligament tear, Morton neuroma, bone infection, edema, Lisfranc injury, and Achilles tendon tear.
Key point: Shoulder: arm at the side, palm up in external rotation on a sandbag for a clean view of the supraspinatus tendon..
Key point: The four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis (SITS)..
Key point: Knee laser centers on the inferior border of the patella (the apex), not the joint center..
Key point: Hip coil top sits at the iliac crest; feet are tied for gentle internal rotation..
Key point: Wrist uses the superman position covering all carpals; foot and ankle coil runs feet-first supine..
Worked example.
A patient with shoulder pain and suspected rotator cuff tear is positioned with the arm at the side, palm turned up so the shoulder sits in external rotation, and a sandbag holds the position.
Because external rotation swings the bicipital groove out of the way, the bicipital groove swings clear and the supraspinatus tendon is seen along its length.
If the patient cannot tolerate external rotation, the arm is left neutral rather than forced.
Coverage extends from above the acromioclavicular joint to below the glenoid.
Memory hook: SITS spells the four rotator cuff muscles: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis..
Memory hook: Palm up turns the biceps groove out of the way to profile the supraspinatus tendon..
Memory hook: Knee laser sits on the point of the patella, its inferior apex..
Exam trap: The knee laser is centered at the inferior border of the patella (the apex), not the joint center..
Exam trap: The four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis..
MSK technique: fat suppression, metal reduction, and arthrograms.
Fat suppression choice matters when the field is inhomogeneous.
Spectral fat-saturated T2 fails in a distorted field, so use STIR instead of fat-saturated T2 when there is metal near the area of interest, when the fat suppression looks inhomogeneous,
or when unsuspected metal is causing inhomogeneity.
STIR nulls fat by inversion time and is far more uniform in a distorted field.
Metal reduction escalates with the amount of metal.
A small amount such as a single screw can be handled with a routine metal-reduction protocol, often at 1.5T because susceptibility artifact is smaller at lower field.
A large metal implant such as a joint replacement (hip or knee) needs a dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequence (a SEMAC or MAVRIC type) that corrects through-plane and in-plane distortion.
An in and out of phase sequence is added when a bone tumor or marrow replacement is the question.
An MR arthrogram is a two-part procedure.
First, contrast is injected directly into the joint (an intra-articular injection), then the joint is imaged.
Distending the joint with fluid outlines the cartilage, labrum, and ligaments so tears and degeneration are seen.
Arthrograms are performed on the shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, and ankle, and they help decide whether arthroscopy, surgery, or joint replacement is needed.
Key point: Switch fat-saturated T2 to STIR when metal or inhomogeneous fat suppression is present..
Key point: STIR nulls fat by inversion time and stays uniform even in a distorted field..
Key point: A single screw needs routine metal reduction, often done at 1.5T for smaller susceptibility..
Key point: A joint replacement needs a dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequence (a SEMAC or MAVRIC type)..
Key point: An MR arthrogram injects contrast directly into the joint, then images the distended joint..
Worked example.
A patient with a prior hip screw is scanned and the fat-saturated T2 images show patchy, uneven fat suppression around the metal.
The technologist switches to STIR, which nulls fat by inversion time rather than by frequency, so the suppression becomes uniform despite the field distortion.
If the same patient had a full hip replacement instead of a single screw, the routine metal-reduction protocol would not be enough,
and a dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequence (a SEMAC or MAVRIC type) would be used to correct the larger distortion.
Memory hook: Metal or messy fat-sat, reach for STIR every time..
Memory hook: One screw is routine; a whole joint replacement needs SEMAC or MAVRIC..
Memory hook: Arthrogram means inject into the joint first, then image..
Exam trap: Switch from fat-saturated T2 to STIR when metal or inhomogeneous fat suppression is present..
Exam trap: An MR arthrogram injects contrast directly into the joint (intra-articular), not into a vein..
Body MRI protocols: liver, MRCP, and abdomen/pelvis coverage.
Dedicated liver MRI is ordered for suspected hepatocellular carcinoma, cirrhosis surveillance, hemangioma characterization, fatty liver, and hepatitis.
The patient lies supine with the liver positioned over the posterior spine coil elements and an anterior phased-array body coil placed on top.
Whatever the indication, the prescribed slices must cover the entire liver, from the dome down past the inferior tip.
A lesion you cannot see is a lesion you cannot report.
MRCP targets the biliary tree and pancreatic duct in patients with gallstones, pancreatitis, a pancreatic mass, or biliary obstruction.
Axial coverage runs from the dome of the liver to below the ampulla of Vater, so a distal common bile duct stone at the ampulla is never cut off the bottom of the stack.
The patient is NPO for 4 to 6 hours so the gallbladder is distended and the stomach is empty.
Coverage landmarks separate the abdominal exams on the boards.
A screening abdomen and pelvis runs from the top of the liver to below the pubic symphysis, usually as two overlapping packages.
A renal mass protocol runs from the top of the adrenal gland to the pubic symphysis.
MR enterography for Crohn disease covers the dome of the liver through the anus, because small bowel and perianal disease can coexist.
Female pelvis MRI evaluates fibroids, endometriosis, adnexal masses and ovarian cysts, cervical pathology, and congenital uterine anomalies.
The patient is head first and supine with an anterior phased-array coil over the pelvis, after a fast of about 4 hours.
Packages are straight by default; only the small field-of-view high-resolution T2 package is angled, and only when a specific organ is the target.
Key point: Liver MRI covers the entire liver; core indications are HCC, cirrhosis, hemangioma, fatty liver, and hepatitis.
Key point: Position the liver over the posterior spine elements with the anterior phased-array body coil on top.
Key point: MRCP axial coverage: dome of the liver to below the ampulla of Vater, NPO 4 to 6 hours.
Key point: Screening abdomen/pelvis: top of the liver to below the pubic symphysis, often two overlapping packages; renal mass: top of the adrenal to the symphysis.
Key point: Enterography covers the dome of the liver through the anus.
Key point: Female pelvis: head-first supine, anterior phased-array coil, roughly a 4-hour fast; packages are straight by default.
Worked example.
You are setting up an MRCP on a patient with suspected choledocholithiasis.
You confirm the patient has been NPO for at least 4 hours so bile fills a distended gallbladder.
You place the anterior body coil so the phased-array elements span from above the liver dome to the lower abdomen.
Prescribing the axial stack, you start above the dome of the liver and extend below the ampulla of Vater, because the stone you are hunting is most likely impacted in the distal duct.
Stopping at the pancreatic head would risk missing exactly the finding the exam was ordered for.
Memory hook: MRCP goes Dome to Duodenum: the ducts drain down to the ampulla, so cover below it.
Memory hook: Screening abdomen/pelvis is Liver to Landing: top of the liver down to the pubic symphysis.
Memory hook: Enterography eats everything: dome of the liver all the way through the anus.
Exam trap: Stopping MRCP coverage at the pancreatic head instead of extending below the ampulla of Vater.
Exam trap: Mixing up renal-mass coverage (top of adrenal to symphysis) with screening abdomen/pelvis (top of liver to symphysis).
Exam trap: Angling female pelvis packages by default; they stay straight unless the small-FOV T2 package is targeting the uterus or cervix.
Body MRI technique: contrast agents, breath-hold vs navigator, MRCP, and orientation.
Weight-based extracellular gadolinium is the default agent for contrast-enhanced body MRI.
Switch to a hepatobiliary contrast agent for focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) and for the living-liver-donor protocol: functioning hepatocytes take the agent up and excrete it into bile,
which produces delayed hepatobiliary-phase images.
FNH contains functioning hepatocytes, so it retains the agent while most other lesions wash out to darkness.
Respiratory strategy is a protocol decision, not an afterthought.
A cooperative patient can breath-hold a 3D T1 gradient echo.
A poor breath-holder gets respiratory-triggered or navigator-gated sequences plus single-shot fast spin echo and free-breathing radial 3D T1 gradient echo acquisitions instead of long breath-holds.
Quantitative sequences have their own rules: proton density fat fraction (PDFF) quantifies hepatic fat and supports iron and hemochromatosis workups, and it must run before contrast.

MR elastography maps liver stiffness; elastography and donor patients fast about 4 hours; for elastography this mainly prevents a postprandial rise in portal flow that would falsely raise liver stiffne
ss, and it also reduces bowel motion.
MRCP is heavily T2 weighted, so static bile and pancreatic-duct fluid stay bright while flowing blood and solid tissue go dark.
Before the scan the patient swallows a dilute oral agent, such as an iron-oxide or manganese-based solution, which shortens the T2 of bowel fluid and darkens it so it does not overlie the ducts.
This is not IV contrast.
Secretin transiently dilates the pancreatic duct and stimulates exocrine output, improving duct visualization and allowing dynamic assessment for chronic pancreatitis, strictures,
and obstructing duct stones.
Timing and orientation round out the technique.
Routine post-contrast abdominal imaging uses an empiric scan delay of about 30 seconds, and enterography uses a free-breathing dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) acquisition with a short inject delay.
Hematuria or bladder work adds a delayed excretory-phase acquisition several minutes after injection, sometimes with a diuretic, to opacify the collecting system and show filling defects.
In the female pelvis, angle the small field-of-view high-resolution T2 package to the uterus for endometrial cancer and congenital uterine anomalies, and to the cervix for cervical cancer.
An antispasmodic (anti-peristaltic) agent can be given to quiet bowel motion.
Key point: Weight-based extracellular gadolinium is the default; use a hepatobiliary agent for FNH and the living-donor protocol.
Key point: Poor breath-holder: respiratory-triggered or navigator-gated sequences plus single-shot and free-breathing radial acquisitions.
Key point: PDFF quantifies fat and supports iron/hemochromatosis workups; it must be acquired pre-contrast.
MR elastography maps stiffness.
Key point: MRCP is heavily T2 weighted; the dilute oral iron-oxide or manganese drink darkens bowel fluid and is not IV contrast.
Key point: Routine post-contrast uses an empiric 30 second delay; enterography uses free-breathing DCE; hematuria or bladder work adds a delayed excretory phase.
Key point: Angle the small-FOV T2 package to the uterus for endometrial cancer and anomalies, to the cervix for cervical cancer.
Worked example.
A patient arrives for lesion characterization and the report question is whether a 3 cm mass is FNH.
You select a hepatobiliary contrast agent rather than the routine extracellular agent, because hepatocyte uptake and biliary excretion give you a delayed hepatobiliary phase.
FNH keeps functioning hepatocytes, so it should retain contrast and stay bright on that phase while most other masses go dark.
You also confirm the PDFF map is scheduled before injection, since gadolinium would corrupt the fat quantification.
The whole protocol hinges on picking the right agent before the needle goes in.
Memory hook: FNH = Functioning hepatocytes, Needs Hepatobiliary agent.
Memory hook: PDFF: Pre-contrast, and Fat fraction is what it measures; the same multi-echo scan supports iron assessment.
Memory hook: Uterus for uterine (endometrial) cancer, Cervix for cervical cancer: angle to the organ that has the disease.
Exam trap: Crediting IV gadolinium for dark bowel fluid on MRCP; the swallowed dilute oral agent does that by shortening bowel-fluid T2.
Exam trap: Choosing routine extracellular gadolinium for an FNH workup; only a hepatobiliary agent gives the delayed hepatobiliary phase.
Exam trap: Running PDFF after injection; gadolinium changes the signal, so fat and iron quantification must come pre-contrast.
MRI coils: field coils, RF coil types, and coil selection.
Every MR system relies on a chain of coils.
The main field coil produces the static B0 field.
Shim coils carry small correction currents that improve B0 homogeneity across the imaging volume.
Gradient coils temporarily vary the field strength with position so signal can be spatially encoded: X along right-left, Y along anterior-posterior, and Z along head-foot.
The RF transmit coil produces the B1 field, perpendicular to B0, that tips protons out of alignment, and receive coils detect the returning MR signal.
Coils on the patient side come in three functional types.
Transmit-only coils are built into the bore wall; this built-in body coil transmits for surface-coil exams and acts as a T/R coil when used alone.
Receive-only surface coils, such as the head/neck, spine, foot/ankle, shoulder, wrist, and body phased arrays, are placed on or around the patient and can be combined with each other.
Local transmit-receive (T/R) coils, such as a circularly polarized (CP) head coil or a knee coil, need a T/R switch and are used alone, not combined with another coil.
The built-in body coil is the exception: it transmits while a receive-only surface coil receives, so it does pair with other coils.
Because a local T/R coil such as the head or knee coil transmits over a small volume, it carries a lower RF heating risk and is preferred for some implant cases.
Element count and fit drive image quality.
More elements concentrate sensitivity and raise SNR over a local region,
and arrays support parallel imaging for faster scans and broad coverage; the trade-offs are wrap or aliasing artifact and burn risk from elements and cables.
Fill factor describes how much of the coil's sensitive volume the imaged part occupies, so fitting the coil closely to the anatomy raises SNR and image quality.
Key point: B0 coil makes the static field; shim coils smooth it; gradient coils vary it with position for spatial encoding.
Key point: Gradient axes: X is right-left, Y is anterior-posterior, Z is head-foot.
Key point: The RF transmit coil produces B1 perpendicular to B0 to excite protons; receive coils detect the signal.
Key point: Receive-only surface coils can be combined; a local T/R coil (CP head, knee) is used alone, though the body coil transmits for receive-only coils.
Key point: More elements raise local SNR; a close fit raises fill factor and SNR.
Worked example.
A shoulder MRI is ordered on a 3T system.
You choose the dedicated shoulder array rather than the flexible body array because it fits the joint closely and raises the fill factor.
You seat the coil directly over the humeral head, strap it so it cannot shift, and connect it as a receive-only coil while the body coil in the bore wall transmits.
Because it is receive-only, you could add the spine array if the protocol needed more coverage.
Memory hook: Shim smooths, gradients steer, RF tips, receive listens.
Memory hook: A local T/R coil (head, knee) travels alone; the body coil transmits for receive-only coils.
Memory hook: Fill the coil with anatomy and you fill the image with signal.
Exam trap: Shim coils correct field homogeneity; gradient coils deliberately vary the field.
Questions often swap these roles.
Exam trap: The CP head coil and knee coil are local T/R coils used alone; receive-only arrays can be combined, and the body coil transmits for them.
Exam trap: More elements mean more local SNR, not automatically fewer artifacts; wrap and burn risk are the array's weak points.
Coil positioning by region: landmarks and setup.
Landmarks make coil positioning repeatable.
For brain exams the head coil is centered at the glabella; when the head coil is used for spine work the landmark moves to the chin.
The knee coil markings center at the inferior patella.
For a dedicated pelvis exam, the top of the body phased array sits at the iliac crest, and for abdomen, pelvis, or composed exams the array is centered over the abdomen first.
The body phased array works together with the spine coil, so the region of interest must lie within the spine coil's sensitive volume as well as under the anterior array.
Extremity coils such as the foot/ankle, shoulder, and wrist coils should fit closely and be padded and strapped to limit motion.
When positioning the wrist, keep its tendons from lying near 54.7 degrees to B0.
Near that orientation the magic angle effect alters T2 decay in tendon and ligament fibers,
raising their signal most conspicuously on short-TE sequences and inviting a faulty diagnosis; the effect is a peak that fades as the fibers move away from 54.7 toward 0 or 90 degrees.
For multi-station protocols, receive-only coils are combined: head plus spine for brain and spine, foot/ankle plus spine for the Achilles region, neck and chest arrays for the brachial plexus,
and peripheral angio arrays plus phased arrays plus spine for runoff studies.
A T/R coil cannot be added to any of these combinations.
Key point: Head coil: center at the glabella for brain, at the chin for spine.
Key point: Knee coil: center at the inferior patella per the coil markings.
Key point: Pelvis: top of the body array at the iliac crest; keep the part within the spine coil.
Key point: Wrist: keep tendons away from about 54.7 degrees to B0, the peak of the magic angle effect in tendons and ligaments.
Key point: Combine receive-only coils for brain plus spine, Achilles, brachial plexus, and runoff exams; a T/R coil cannot join.
Worked example.
A pelvis MRI is ordered.
You place the patient supine with the spine coil sections under the pelvis, then lay the body phased array so its top edge sits at the iliac crest.
You confirm the whole pelvis lies within both the array and the spine coil coverage, strap the array so it cannot slide,
and landmark midway between the crest and the symphysis before sending the patient to isocenter.
Memory hook: Brow for brain, chin for spine.
Memory hook: The knee coil kneels to the lower patella.
Memory hook: Around 54.7 degrees, tendons lie: keep the wrist tendons off the magic angle.
Exam trap: Glabella and chin are both head coil landmarks; which one applies depends on whether the exam is brain or spine.
Exam trap: The knee centers at the inferior patella, not the joint line or the superior pole.
Exam trap: Magic angle is a positioning error, not a metal artifact; it brightens tendons near 54.7 degrees and can mimic a tear.
RF heating and coil safety: SAR, B1+rms, and burns.
SAR, the specific absorption rate, is the rate at which the body absorbs RF power, in watts per kilogram (W/kg).
It depends on the patient's habitus, weight, and tissue as well as the sequence, so the height and weight entered at registration must be accurate.
SAR roughly quadruples when a protocol moves from a 1.5T to a 3T system.
Normal operating mode allows less than 2 W/kg whole body and less than 3.2 W/kg to the head; first level controlled mode allows less than 4 W/kg whole body.
When a sequence exceeds the limit, reduce RF deposition: lower the flip angle, choose a low-SAR RF pulse, shorten the turbo or echo train factor, run fewer slices,
split the scan into more concatenations, and remove saturation bands that are not needed.
Removing blankets and fanning air into the bore keep the patient comfortable but do not reduce SAR.
B1+rms is the average effective RF field of the transmit coil for a sequence, in microtesla.
Unlike SAR it is patient-independent: it is set by the system, the sequence, and the parameters, and the scanner reports it directly,
so it is a more consistent condition to verify than a patient-dependent SAR estimate.
Implants often carry a B1+rms condition; a deep brain stimulator (DBS) with whole-body eligibility, for example, may require every sequence to stay at or below 2 microtesla,
checked before each sequence runs.
Burn prevention is positioning work.
Never let the patient touch the bore wall or a bare coil or cable, and pad skin-to-skin contact points such as crossed hands or touching knees with a pad or pillowcase.
When a metal implant causes severe artifact or its conditions demand a lower field, a 1.5T system is the better choice.
For an implant without leads that sits entirely within a local transmit-receive coil, that coil can lower RF exposure elsewhere,
but a leaded implant such as a pacemaker or neurostimulator may constrain which transmit coil is permitted, often a body-coil B1+rms limit and sometimes a local transmit/receive coil,
because near-field coupling to the lead is hard to predict.
Key point: SAR is the rate of RF power absorption in W/kg; it depends on patient habitus, weight, and the sequence.
Key point: Normal mode: under 2 W/kg whole body and 3.2 W/kg head; first level: under 4 W/kg whole body.
Key point: SAR roughly quadruples from a 1.5T to a 3T system.
Key point: Reduce SAR: lower flip angle, low-SAR pulse, shorter echo train, fewer slices, more concatenations, drop unneeded saturation bands.
Key point: B1+rms is patient-independent, reported in microtesla, and governs many implant conditions such as a 2 microtesla DBS limit.
Worked example.
A patient with a whole-body eligible DBS arrives for a lumbar spine MRI.
You verify the device conditions, which require every sequence to run at or below a B1+rms of 2 microtesla, and confirm the entered height and weight are correct so the SAR estimate is valid.
Before starting each sequence you check the reported B1+rms and lower the flip angle on one sequence that reads high.
You pad between the patient's hands so no skin touches skin and confirm no part of the patient rests against the bore.
Memory hook: SAR is watts per kilogram of patient; B1+rms is microtesla of transmit field.
Memory hook: 1.5 to 3: the field doubles, SAR quadruples.
Memory hook: No skin on skin, no patient on bore, no bare cable on patient.
Exam trap: B1+rms does not change with patient weight; SAR does.
Questions test both the units and the patient dependence.
Exam trap: 2 W/kg is normal mode whole body, 3.2 W/kg is the head limit, 4 W/kg is first level.
Keep the three straight.
Exam trap: Adding saturation bands raises SAR; removing unneeded ones lowers it.
Comfort measures like fanning do not reduce SAR.
MR image quality: SNR, scan time, and spatial resolution tradeoffs.
Every protocol is a negotiation between three things: signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), scan time, and spatial resolution.
SNR is the mean signal intensity divided by the standard deviation of the noise.
Some of its drivers are fixed once the patient is on the table: field strength, the sequence design, and the tissue itself.
The rest are yours at the console: voxel size, TR and TE, the number of signal averages (NEX), receiver bandwidth, and the coil.
Voxel size is the central lever.
Signal comes from tissue, so a bigger voxel holds more of it.
A larger FOV, a smaller matrix, or a thicker slice all enlarge the voxel and raise SNR; the price is coarser detail.
Shrink the voxel for sharper images and the noise floor rises to meet you.
The master tradeoff directions are worth committing to memory:.
TR up: SNR up, scan time up.
TE up: SNR down, with the loss growing at longer TE as T2 decay continues.
Flip angle up (toward the optimum): SNR up.
NEX up: SNR up, scan time up.
FOV up: SNR up, resolution down.
Phase matrix up: resolution up, SNR down, scan time up.
Frequency matrix up: resolution up, SNR down, scan time unchanged.
Slice thickness up: SNR up, fewer slices needed, resolution down.
Bandwidth up: SNR down, shorter minimum TE and TR, less chemical shift.
Parallel imaging: scan time down, SNR down.
Receiver bandwidth deserves a second look because it moves in the opposite direction from intuition.
Opening the bandwidth samples more noise, so SNR falls, but the readout finishes sooner, which permits shorter TE and TR, and the fat-water chemical shift spans fewer pixels,
so that artifact shrinks along with susceptibility effects near metal.
Nothing on this list is free: every gain in signal, speed, or sharpness is paid for somewhere else.
Key point: SNR is the mean signal divided by the standard deviation of the noise.
Key point: Fixed factors: field strength, sequence design, tissue.
Operator factors: voxel size, TR and TE, NEX, receiver bandwidth, coil choice.
Key point: Bigger voxels (larger FOV, smaller matrix, thicker slices) raise SNR at the cost of resolution.
Key point: Raising the phase matrix sharpens the image but lowers SNR and lengthens the scan; the frequency matrix sharpens with no time cost.
Key point: Higher receiver bandwidth lowers SNR but reduces chemical shift and allows a shorter minimum TE and TR.
Worked example.
A lumbar spine T2 at 3 mm slices with a 512 matrix comes back grainy.
Dropping the matrix to 384 enlarges each pixel and buys back signal, and moving to 4 mm slices adds more.
If the radiologist wants the fine detail kept, you add an average instead: same voxel, more signal, and a longer scan is the price you quote before you commit.
Memory hook: Signal lives in tissue: bigger voxel, brighter image.
Memory hook: Bandwidth wider, noise louder, fat shift smaller.
Memory hook: Nothing is free: every SNR gain is paid in time or detail.
Exam trap: Raising the phase matrix improves resolution but lowers SNR and lengthens the scan; raising the frequency matrix adds no time.
Neither raises SNR.
Exam trap: Higher bandwidth lowers SNR, yet it reduces chemical shift and shortens the minimum TE and TR.
Exam trap: SNR is defined with the standard deviation of the noise, not the mean of the noise.
Acquisition parameters and k-space: matrix, FOV, NEX, and acceleration.
Each echo fills one phase-encoding line of k-space, and the scan ends when every line has been collected.
That is why, for a conventional non-echo-train sequence, 2D scan time is a simple product: TR times NEX times the number of phase-encoding steps,
and a turbo or fast spin echo divides that by its echo train length.
Geometry comes from the same parameters.
In-plane voxel size is FOV divided by matrix in each direction, and slice thickness supplies the third dimension.
The distance factor, the slice gap set as a percent of thickness, trims cross-talk and the number of slices needed, but a generous gap can skip small pathology.
NEX repeats each line and averages the copies.
Because the noise is re-sampled along with the signal,
doubling NEX raises SNR by only about 40 percent (the square root of two) while the scan time fully doubles; the bonus is smoother motion and pulsatile-flow artifact.
Phase resolution shortens a scan differently, by acquiring a reduced percentage of the phase lines and accepting rectangular voxels.
FOV phase adjusts coverage in the phase direction without touching resolution, since the line count scales in proportion.
Three techniques change how k-space itself is filled.
Partial Fourier acquires part of k-space and calculates the rest from symmetry: faster, with some SNR loss and possible blurring.
Oversampling collects data beyond the prescribed FOV so anatomy outside the edge cannot wrap in; in the frequency direction it is essentially free, while in the phase direction it adds scan time.
Parallel imaging undersamples k-space and unfolds the result using the sensitivity maps of multiple coil elements,
cutting scan time by the acceleration factor while lowering SNR by roughly its square root; run it with too small an FOV and an aliasing band can appear in the center of the image.
Key point: 2D scan time = TR x NEX x number of phase-encoding steps.
Key point: Doubling NEX gives about 40 percent more SNR (square root of 2) and doubles the scan time.
Key point: Voxel = FOV/matrix in plane by slice thickness; the distance factor is the slice gap as a percent of thickness.
Key point: Partial Fourier acquires part of k-space and estimates the rest: faster, lower SNR, possible blurring.
Key point: Oversampling samples beyond the FOV to prevent wrap; parallel imaging undersamples k-space to save time at an SNR cost.
Worked example.
An abdominal breath-hold sequence runs 24 seconds and the patient cannot manage it.
Applying parallel imaging with a factor of two brings it near 12 seconds at a known SNR cost.
If that is still too long, reducing phase resolution or narrowing the phase FOV drops more lines, and you check that the smaller FOV still clears the flanks so no wrap folds into the liver.
Memory hook: Time = TR x NEX x phase steps: only three knobs stretch a 2D scan.
Memory hook: NEX pays double for a 40 percent raise.
Memory hook: Oversample to stop wrap; undersample (parallel imaging) to save time.
Exam trap: Doubling NEX raises SNR about 40 percent (square root of 2), not 100 percent, and it doubles the scan time.
Exam trap: Parallel imaging cuts time at the cost of SNR and can leave aliasing in the center of the image if the FOV is too small.
Exam trap: FOV phase changes coverage in the phase direction, not resolution.
TR, TE, TI, and flip angle: setting image contrast.
Two clocks set the contrast of a spin echo image.
TR is the time between excitation pulses: it decides how much longitudinal recovery happens before the next pulse, how many slices fit in the acquisition, and how long the scan runs.
TE is the time from excitation to the echo, when the data for one phase-encoding line is collected: it decides how much T2 decay is allowed to separate the tissues.
The classic weighting table follows from those two clocks.
T1 weighting uses a short TR and a short TE, catching tissues mid-recovery.
T2 weighting uses a long TR and a long TE, letting recovery finish and decay do the talking.
Proton density uses a long TR with a short TE, silencing both relaxation effects so proton content carries the contrast.
Inversion recovery adds a third clock, TI: FLAIR pairs a long TR and long TE with a long TI so CSF crosses its null at excitation, while STIR uses a short TI to catch fat at its null.
The flip angle is the excitation angle that tips magnetization away from B0.
For any given TR and tissue there is one angle that yields the most steady-state signal, the Ernst angle.
Sequence families keep to characteristic ranges: spin echo and turbo spin echo use a 90 degree excitation with 180 degree refocusing pulses,
gradient echo excites below 90 degrees so its short TRs still leave usable longitudinal magnetization, and inversion recovery opens with a 180 degree inversion followed by a 90.
Key point: T1: short TR, short TE.
T2: long TR, long TE.
PD: long TR, short TE.
Key point: FLAIR: long TR and TE with a long TI to null CSF.
STIR: short TI to null fat.
Key point: TR sets slice count and scan time; TE sets how much T2 decay shapes the contrast.
Key point: The Ernst angle is the flip angle that gives maximum SNR for a given TR.
Key point: Spin and turbo spin echo use 90 then 180 degree pulses; gradient echo stays under 90; inversion recovery starts with a 180 then a 90.
Worked example.
A brain FLAIR comes back with CSF that is not fully dark and the periventricular lesions are hard to separate from the ventricles.
Checking the protocol, the TI was left near the short value used for fat nulling.
Restoring the long TI appropriate for CSF at that field strength nulls the fluid, and the lesions stand out against dark ventricles again.
Memory hook: T1 short and short, T2 long and long, PD long TR with short TE.
Memory hook: TI targets: short TI kills fat (STIR), long TI kills CSF (FLAIR).
Memory hook: TR grows slices and time; TE grows T2 contrast.
Exam trap: PD pairs a long TR with a short TE; choosing a long TE turns the image into T2 weighting.
Exam trap: FLAIR and STIR both null a tissue with TI, but FLAIR uses a long TI for CSF and STIR uses a short TI for fat.
Exam trap: Gradient echo excites below 90 degrees; spin echo families use 90 and 180 degree pulses.
Making an MR signal: protons, B0, Larmor, and resonance.
Clinical MRI images the hydrogen nucleus (1H), a single proton found in abundance in water and fat.
A proton is a spinning charged particle, and a moving charge creates a magnetic field, so each proton behaves like a tiny bar magnet.
Outside the scanner these tiny magnets point in random directions and cancel out.
Inside the bore, the static field B0 forces each proton into one of two states: parallel (low energy) or anti-parallel (high energy).
A slight majority sits in the low-energy parallel state, and that small excess adds up to the net magnetization vector (NMV) pointing along B0, the z axis.
This longitudinal magnetization cannot be measured directly; it has to be tipped into the transverse plane before it can give a signal.
The protons do not sit still.
Each one precesses about B0 like a wobbling top, at the Larmor frequency: fo = gamma x B0.
Gamma, the gyromagnetic ratio, is 42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen, so protons precess at about 63.9 MHz at 1.5T and about 127.7 MHz at 3T.
Higher field means faster precession.
To tip the NMV, a radiofrequency pulse (B1) is applied perpendicular to B0 at (or very near) the Larmor frequency.
Because the RF matches the protons' own precession rate, energy transfers by resonance and the NMV rotates toward the transverse plane.
RF at the wrong frequency transfers almost no energy.
Once the pulse ends, the rotating transverse magnetization sweeps past the receive coil and induces a small current in it (Faraday induction): that current is the MR signal.
Key point: Hydrogen (1H) is the imaged nucleus: a spinning charged proton acts like a tiny magnet..
Key point: In B0, a slight excess of protons aligns parallel (low energy); the excess sums to the NMV along the z axis..
Key point: Protons precess at the Larmor frequency: fo = gamma x B0, with gamma = 42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen (about 63.9 MHz at 1.5T, 127.7 MHz at 3T)..
Key point: The RF pulse (B1) must be perpendicular to B0 and at the Larmor frequency; resonance is what lets energy transfer and tip the NMV..
Key point: Only rotating transverse magnetization induces a current in the receive coil; longitudinal magnetization gives no measurable signal..
Worked example.
During prescan on a 3T system the scanner searches for the center frequency and settles near 127.7 MHz.
The same patient scanned last week on the department's 1.5T magnet ran near 63.9 MHz.
Nothing about the patient changed: fo = gamma x B0, so doubling the field doubles the precession frequency,
and the transmitter must follow it exactly or the excitation pulse will not resonate with the spins.
Memory hook: Larmor ladder: 42.58 per tesla, so roughly 64 at 1.5T and 128 at 3T..
Memory hook: No resonance, no signal: the RF must match the spins' own precession frequency..
Memory hook: The coil is deaf to the z axis: signal only comes from magnetization rotating in the transverse plane..
Exam trap: Gamma for hydrogen is 42.58 MHz/T, so the Larmor frequency scales with field strength: 63.9 MHz at 1.5T and 127.7 MHz at 3T..
Exam trap: B1 must be applied perpendicular to B0 and at (near) the Larmor frequency; off-resonance RF does not transfer energy..
Exam trap: Longitudinal magnetization along B0 cannot be measured directly; it must be tipped into the transverse plane first..
Relaxation: T1 spin-lattice and T2 spin-spin.
After the RF pulse ends, the tipped magnetization returns to equilibrium by two separate processes that run at the same time.
T1 relaxation is the recovery of longitudinal magnetization along B0.
It is called spin-lattice relaxation because the protons hand their absorbed RF energy back to the surrounding molecular environment, the lattice, as heat.
T1 is defined as the time for a tissue to recover 63% of its longitudinal magnetization.
How fast that hand-off works depends on how the lattice molecules move.
Energy transfers efficiently only when the molecular tumbling rate is close to the Larmor frequency.
Free water is made of small molecules that tumble far too fast, so the transfer is poor and free water has a long T1.
Fat's carbon-bond structure tumbles near the proton's Larmor frequency, transfers energy efficiently, and so has a short T1.
T2 relaxation is the decay of transverse magnetization.
It is called spin-spin relaxation because each proton sits in a slightly different local field created by its neighbors, so the spins precess at slightly different rates and drift out of phase.
As phase coherence is lost, the net transverse magnetization shrinks.
T2 is the time for the transverse magnetization to fall to 37% of its starting value.
For any given tissue T1 is always longer than T2: typical soft-tissue T1 values run about 300 to 2000 ms while T2 values run about 30 to 150 ms, and free water such as CSF runs longer than both.
Water, and most pathology because of its raised water content, has a long T1 and a long T2.
Fat has a short T1 and a short T2.
Key point: T1 = longitudinal (spin-lattice) relaxation: energy is released as heat to the lattice; T1 is the time to recover 63% of longitudinal magnetization..
Key point: T1 efficiency depends on molecular motion near the Larmor frequency: free water tumbles too fast (long T1), fat tumbles near it (short T1)..
Key point: T2 = transverse (spin-spin) relaxation: neighboring spins' local fields cause dephasing; T2 is the time to fall to 37% of the initial transverse magnetization..
Key point: T1 is always longer than T2 in a given tissue (typical soft tissue T1 about 300-2000 ms, T2 about 30-150 ms; free water runs longer)..
Key point: Water and most pathology: long T1 and long T2.
Fat: short T1 and short T2..
Worked example.
Right after an excitation pulse, think about CSF and scalp fat in the same head.
The fat protons hand their energy to a lattice that tumbles near the Larmor frequency, so fat's longitudinal magnetization is largely back within a few hundred milliseconds.
CSF is nearly pure free water: its tiny fast molecules accept energy poorly, so its recovery drags on for seconds.
That difference in energy hand-off, not any scanner setting, is why the two tissues recover at such different rates.
Memory hook: 1 lattice, 2 spins: T1 is spin-LATTICE (longitudinal), T2 is spin-SPIN (transverse)..
Memory hook: 63 up, 37 left: T1 marks 63% recovered, T2 marks 37% remaining..
Memory hook: Water is a bad listener: it tumbles too fast to catch the Larmor beat, so its T1 is long..
Exam trap: T1 is the time to 63% recovery, not full recovery; T2 is the time to 37% remaining, not zero..
Exam trap: T1 is always longer than T2 for a given tissue; they never swap order..
Exam trap: Free water has a LONG T1: its small fast molecules transfer energy poorly at the Larmor frequency..
Dephasing, T2 vs T2*, and the spin-echo refocusing pulse.
Once the RF pulse switches off, the spins in the transverse plane start to fan out.
Two things drive this dephasing.
The first is the true tissue process: spin-spin interactions, where each proton feels slightly different local fields from its neighbors.
That alone would make the signal decay with the tissue's T2.
The second is the magnet itself: no main field is perfectly uniform, so spins in slightly stronger regions precess faster than spins in slightly weaker ones.
Add the two together and the free induction decay dies away faster than true T2.
This combined, faster decay is T2*.
T2* is always shorter than T2 because it includes everything T2 does plus the external field inhomogeneity.
Left alone, the signal would be gone before a useful echo could be sampled.
The spin-echo sequence rescues it with a 180 degree refocusing pulse.
Picture runners on a track: after the 90 degree pulse they all start together, then the fast ones pull ahead.
The 180 flips everyone over, so the fast spins now sit behind and the slow spins sit ahead.
Precessing at their same rates, the fast ones catch up and all the spins come back into phase, forming an echo at the echo time TE.
For the rephasing to land exactly at TE, the 180 must be applied at TE/2.
This trick only repairs the dephasing caused by the static field inhomogeneity, because that error is the same before and after the flip.
The random spin-spin dephasing is not reversible, so the echo amplitude still decays with true T2.
A gradient-echo sequence has no 180 pulse, so it cannot recover the inhomogeneity losses and its signal decays with T2*.
Key point: Transverse dephasing has two sources: true spin-spin interactions (T2) and main field inhomogeneity..
Key point: T2* combines both sources, so T2* decay is always faster (shorter) than T2 decay..
Key point: The spin-echo 180 degree pulse flips the spins so fast ones fall behind and catch up, rephasing into an echo at TE..
Key point: The 180 degree refocusing pulse is applied at TE/2 so the echo forms exactly at TE..
Key point: Spin echo recovers the static field inhomogeneity dephasing (the part that makes T2* shorter than T2); true T2 decay remains, and gradient echo recovers neither..
Worked example.
A patient with fixed dental braces needs a brain scan.
On the gradient-echo localizer the frontal region shows large signal voids: the metal distorts the local field, spins dephase rapidly,
and with no refocusing pulse the signal decays at the very short local T2*.
The fast spin-echo series looks far cleaner through the same region, because each 180 degree pulse rephases the dephasing caused by that static distortion.
The braces did not change; the sequence's ability to refocus static inhomogeneity did.
Memory hook: The star burns out faster: T2* is always shorter than T2..
Memory hook: Turn the runners around at half time: the 180 sits at TE/2 so everyone finishes together at TE..
Memory hook: Spin echo forgives the magnet's flaws; gradient echo has to live with them..
Exam trap: T2* is shorter than T2 because it adds external field inhomogeneity on top of spin-spin dephasing..
Exam trap: The refocusing pulse is 180 degrees and sits at TE/2, not at TE..
Exam trap: Spin echo recovers the static field inhomogeneity dephasing (not true T2); gradient echo does not..
Spatial encoding: slice, phase, and frequency gradients into k-space.
An MR signal on its own carries no address.
Three gradients, switched on at three different moments of each TR, stamp position onto the signal.
The slice-select gradient runs at the same time as the RF pulse.
It makes the Larmor frequency vary along its axis, so only the plane of tissue whose local frequency matches the RF pulse gets excited.
Slice thickness follows from two things: the RF bandwidth and the steepness of the gradient.
A steeper gradient, or a narrower bandwidth, gives a thinner slice.
After excitation, the phase-encode gradient switches on briefly.
Spins at different positions along its axis precess at different rates while it is on, and when it switches off they keep a position-dependent phase shift.
The gradient is stepped to a different amplitude every TR, and each step writes one line of the raw data matrix.
Finally the frequency-encode (readout) gradient runs during the echo itself, so that signal frequency encodes position along the third axis while the echo is digitized.
That raw data matrix is k-space.
It is a map of spatial frequencies, not a picture.
The central lines hold the low spatial frequencies: bulk signal, overall brightness, and contrast.
The peripheral lines hold the high spatial frequencies: edges and fine detail.
Every point in k-space contains signal from the entire slice.
Once every planned line is filled, a two-dimensional Fourier transform converts k-space into the image, turning spatial frequencies into pixel intensities.
Excite, encode, sample, repeat per TR, transform: that is how every 2D image is built.
Key point: The slice-select gradient is on during the RF pulse; only spins whose local Larmor frequency matches the RF are excited..
Key point: Slice thickness is set by the RF bandwidth and the steepness of the slice-select gradient..
Key point: The phase-encode gradient is a brief pulse after excitation, stepped to a new amplitude every TR; each step fills one line of k-space..
Key point: The frequency-encode (readout) gradient is on during the echo, so frequency encodes position while the echo is sampled..
Key point: k-space center holds contrast and bulk signal (low spatial frequencies); the periphery holds edges and fine detail; a 2D Fourier transform reconstructs the image..
Worked example.
You run an axial brain series with 192 phase-encode steps.
Each TR, the z gradient switches on with the RF pulse to excite the chosen slice, a phase-encode blip along right-left takes a new amplitude,
and the readout gradient along anterior-posterior runs while the echo is sampled.
After 192 TRs the 192 lines of k-space are full and the scanner Fourier transforms them into the image.
The patient coughs halfway through, right when the central lines are being acquired.
Because those lines carry the low spatial frequencies for the whole slice, the result is not a smudge at one spot but degraded contrast and ghosting across the entire image.
Memory hook: Slice with the RF, phase in between, frequency while you listen..
Memory hook: Center of k-space = contrast; corners = crisp edges..
Memory hook: One TR, one phase step, one line..
Exam trap: The slice-select gradient is on during the RF pulse and the readout gradient is on during the echo; swapping the two is the classic error..
Exam trap: k-space center = contrast and signal, periphery = fine detail.
Exams love to reverse them..
Exam trap: k-space is raw spatial-frequency data, not a scrambled photo: no single k-space point maps to a single pixel..
The image-formation pipeline: excite, encode, sample, reconstruct.
Every MR image, whatever the sequence name on the console, is built by the same loop.
Excite the chosen slice with an RF pulse while the slice-select gradient is on.
Encode the signal spatially: a phase-encode step, then frequency encoding during the readout.
Sample the echo into one line of k-space.
Repeat every TR with a new phase-encode amplitude until k-space is full, then reconstruct with the Fourier transform.
Sequences differ mainly in how they form the echo that gets sampled.
A gradient echo sequence forms its echo by reversing the polarity of the readout gradient: the first lobe dephases the spins, the flipped lobe rephases them.
There is no 180 degree pulse, so the signal decays with T2*, and the excitation typically uses a flip angle under 90 degrees,
which leaves longitudinal magnetization in reserve and allows a very short TR.
A spin echo sequence forms its echo with a 180 degree refocusing pulse applied after the excitation.
Inversion recovery adds a different 180: a preparatory inversion pulse placed before the excitation.
After the inversion, the sequence waits a chosen time so that one tissue's longitudinal magnetization is crossing zero at the moment of excitation, and that tissue gives no signal.
STIR uses this to null fat, FLAIR to null CSF.
Keep the two 180s apart: the inversion 180 prepares the magnetization before excitation, while the spin-echo 180 refocuses it afterward.
And whatever the echo mechanism, they all end the same way: fill k-space, then reconstruct with a Fourier transform.
A conventional scan fills one phase-encode line per TR; a fast or turbo scan fills several lines per TR (an echo train), which is how it saves time.
Key point: Pipeline: excite the slice, phase then frequency encode, sample the echo into k-space, repeat per TR, Fourier transform to reconstruct..
Key point: Gradient echo forms its echo by reversing the readout gradient: no 180 degree pulse, T2* decay, flip angle usually under 90 degrees..
Key point: Spin echo forms its echo with a 180 degree refocusing pulse applied after the excitation..
Key point: Inversion recovery adds a preparatory 180 degree inversion before the excitation; the nulled tissue is excited at its zero crossing (STIR nulls fat, FLAIR nulls CSF)..
Key point: Whatever the echo mechanism, the filled k-space is reconstructed with a Fourier transform; a conventional scan fills one phase-encode line per TR,
a fast or turbo scan several (an echo train)..
Worked example.
You start a brain exam with a gradient-echo localizer: no refocusing pulse and a small flip angle let the TR drop to a few milliseconds, so the scout finishes in seconds,
though the patient's dental work blooms because nothing refocuses the local field errors.
Next comes a spin echo series, where a 180 degree pulse after each excitation forms the echo.
Then the FLAIR: now a 180 degree inversion goes in before each excitation, with the wait time chosen so CSF is at its zero crossing and comes out black.
Three different echo mechanisms, yet all three fill the same k-space matrix line by line and hand the filled matrix to the Fourier transform.
Memory hook: GRE flips gradients, SE flips spins, IR flips first..
Memory hook: Excite, encode, sample, repeat, transform..
Exam trap: Gradient echo forms its echo by gradient reversal; there is no refocusing pulse in it to remove..
Exam trap: The inversion 180 comes before the excitation as preparation; the spin-echo 180 comes after it to refocus.
Two different pulses, two different jobs..
Exam trap: One phase-encode line per TR is only the conventional case: a fast or turbo spin echo fills several lines per TR (an echo train), which is how it shortens the scan..
Patient positioning and coil setup: centering, comfort, and image quality.
Good images begin before the first pulse, at how the patient and coil are set up.
The goal is to place the region of interest at the magnet isocenter, where the field is most uniform and the gradients most linear,
because that is where fat suppression works best and geometry is truest.
The technologist lands the coil and table on the target anatomy rather than on the patient's overall center.
The receive coil should be the smallest one that still covers the anatomy, brought as close as comfort allows, because coil sensitivity and therefore signal to noise fall off quickly with distance.
Positioning is also the main defense against motion, the commonest cause of a repeated scan: a neutral relaxed posture, padding at pressure points, and immobilization all help the patient hold still.
The same padding keeps conductive parts of the coil and cables off bare skin, which prevents an RF heating loop, and hearing protection guards against the loud gradient noise.
Key point: Center the region of interest at isocenter for the best field uniformity, fat suppression, and geometry..
Key point: Use the smallest coil that covers the anatomy and place it close, because SNR falls off with distance..
Key point: Positioning is the main defense against motion, the commonest cause of repeats..
Key point: Padding and cable routing keep conductors off skin to prevent RF heating loops..
Worked example.
A lumbar spine study is set up by landing the coil on the L3 region so the mid lumbar spine sits at isocenter, not by centering on the patient's waist.
A spine array is chosen over the body coil for its higher local signal, foam pads are placed under the knees to flatten the lordosis and ease the back, and cushions immobilize the pelvis.
Ear plugs go in, the cable is routed clear of the skin, and the patient is given a squeeze ball, which together cut both motion repeats and heating risk.
Memory hook: Center the anatomy, not the patient, at isocenter..
Memory hook: Smallest covering coil, placed close, wins on signal to noise..
Memory hook: Pad for comfort, immobilization, and to keep conductors off skin..
Exam trap: Do not center on the patient's body midpoint; off-center anatomy loses fat suppression and distorts..
Exam trap: A larger coil or one held away from the part wastes signal and can fold in distant tissue..
Exam trap: STIR is not a substitute for correct centering; poor positioning still degrades every sequence..
MR safety: the static field, zones and projectiles.
The static magnetic field is always on, even when no scan is running, and it never turns off between patients.
That single fact drives the biggest hazard in the suite: any ferromagnetic object brought too close becomes a projectile that accelerates toward the bore.
Oxygen cylinders, mop buckets, scissors, and IV poles have all caused serious incidents.
Access is controlled by a four zone scheme.
Zone I is public space, Zone II is the screening area, Zone III is the controlled area around the control room, and Zone IV is the magnet room itself.
Only screened people and MR safe or verified conditional equipment cross into Zone IV.
The field strength falls off with distance but does so steeply, so the dangerous region is close to the bore.
A quench is the sudden loss of superconductivity that boils off the cryogen and can vent helium into the room.
It is rare, drops the field, and is an emergency because the room can lose oxygen.
The quench button is a last resort, not a way to stop a scan.
Key point: The static field is always on, including overnight and between patients..
Key point: Ferromagnetic objects become projectiles near the bore..
Key point: The four zone scheme controls who and what reaches the magnet..
Key point: A quench boils off cryogen and is an oxygen emergency..
Worked example.
A porter wheels a standard steel oxygen cylinder toward a patient in Zone IV.
As it passes the bore opening the field grips it and pulls it into the magnet at speed.
The lesson is procedural, not physical: MR safe aluminum cylinders and screened equipment are the only gas supplies allowed past Zone III, and the fix is screening at the door,
not reflexes at the bore.
Memory hook: Always on means always dangerous: the field does not wait for a scan..
Memory hook: Four zones, one rule: nothing crosses into Zone IV unscreened..
Exam trap: Thinking the field is off when no scan runs; it is superconducting and permanent..
Exam trap: Confusing the quench button with a scan stop; a quench is an emergency, not a pause..
MR safety: acoustic noise, nerve stimulation and monitoring.
Beyond the static field, the changing gradients create their own hazards.
Switching gradients push against the static field and vibrate the coil, which produces the loud knocking of a scan.
Levels routinely exceed the threshold where hearing protection is required, so earplugs or headphones are mandatory for every patient, including the sedated and the very young.
Fast gradient switching can also cause peripheral nerve stimulation, felt as a twitch or tingle in the skin.
Scanners limit the gradient slew rate to stay below this threshold, which is why very fast sequences are constrained.
It is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, but it signals that the hardware is near its regulatory ceiling.
Because many patients cannot be watched directly inside the bore, monitoring matters.
Sedated or unstable patients need MR conditional pulse oximetry and the means to communicate.
A patient who can squeeze a call ball and hear the intercom is a patient who can report a problem before it becomes an incident.
Key point: Gradient switching drives the acoustic noise of a scan..
Key point: Hearing protection is required for every patient, no exceptions..
Key point: Fast gradients can cause peripheral nerve stimulation, so slew rate is limited..
Key point: Sedated patients need MR conditional monitoring and a way to signal..
Worked example.
A sequence is sped up by raising the gradient slew rate.
The patient reports a tingling twitch across the abdomen.
That is peripheral nerve stimulation, the body reaching the gradient limit before any imaging harm occurs.
The operator backs off the slew rate; the scanner would otherwise cap it automatically to stay within the regulatory bound.
Memory hook: Loud comes from the gradients, not the magnet..
Memory hook: A twitch means the gradients are at the edge; the fix is to slow the switching..
Exam trap: Blaming acoustic noise on the static field; it comes from gradient switching..
Exam trap: Assuming nerve stimulation is dangerous; it is a comfort limit that flags the gradient ceiling..
Motion and flow artifacts: ghosting, wrap and the fixes.
Most artifacts that streak an image trace back to something that moved or something that flowed.
Both express themselves along the phase encoding direction, because phase is measured across many separate repetitions and any change between them is misread as position.
Breathing, pulsing vessels, and swallowing all print faint copies, called ghosts, spread across that axis.
Flowing blood is a special case.
Spins that move between excitation and readout can be mismapped, producing bright or dark ghosts that march across the image in step with the heartbeat.
This is why a pulsing artery can smear a line right through the anatomy of interest.
The fixes follow the cause.
Swapping the phase and frequency directions moves a ghost off the anatomy.
Saturation bands blank the moving tissue.
Flow compensation rephases moving spins, and cardiac or respiratory gating ties the acquisition to the cycle so each line is captured at the same moment.
Wrap, or aliasing, is a related trap: anatomy outside a too small field of view folds back onto the image, fixed by enlarging the field or oversampling.
Left: a clean image.
Middle: motion prints ghost copies along the phase axis.
Right: a phase field of view smaller than the anatomy makes the edges wrap back onto the image.
Key point: Motion and flow artifacts appear along the phase encoding axis..
Key point: Pulsatile flow ghosts march across the image with the heartbeat..
Key point: Swapping phase and frequency moves a ghost off the anatomy..
Key point: Wrap folds outside anatomy back in and is fixed by a larger field or oversampling..
Worked example.
A knee scan shows a pulsing artery ghosting a bright line across the meniscus.
Two independent fixes help: swap phase and frequency so the ghost lands outside the joint, and add flow compensation so the moving blood is rephased.
Either can rescue the study; combining them is common when the vessel sits right over the target.
Memory hook: Ghosts always ride the phase axis..
Memory hook: If it moved or it flowed, look along phase encoding..
Exam trap: Expecting motion ghosts along the frequency direction; they follow phase encoding..
Exam trap: Confusing flow ghosting with wrap; wrap is field of view too small, not motion..
3D acquisition: isotropic voxels and the sequences that make them.
A 3D acquisition encodes a whole slab at once with a second phase encoding along the slice direction, rather than exciting one thin slice at a time.
The payoff is thin, contiguous partitions with high signal and, when the voxel is equal in all three dimensions, true isotropic data.
Isotropic data can be reformatted into any plane after the fact without a loss of detail.
The named sequences reflect this.
A spoiled gradient echo volume such as MPRAGE gives sharp T1 brain anatomy for surgical planning and reformats.
A long echo train spin echo volume, called SPACE or CUBE depending on the vendor, delivers T2 or FLAIR contrast across a whole region in one scan that can be sliced any way the reader needs.
The cost is time and a sensitivity to motion, since the whole slab is spoiled by movement rather than a single slice.
That is the tradeoff behind choosing 3D: pay in scan time and motion risk, receive isotropic data that reformats freely and reconstructs cleanly into MIP and curved views.
Key point: 3D encodes a whole slab with a second phase encode along slice..
Key point: Isotropic voxels reformat into any plane without losing detail..
Key point: MPRAGE gives T1 volumes; SPACE or CUBE give T2 or FLAIR volumes..
Key point: The tradeoff is longer scans and greater motion sensitivity..
Worked example.
A surgeon needs the same brain data viewed axially, sagittally, and coronally for planning.
A single isotropic MPRAGE volume is acquired once, then reformatted into all three planes from one dataset.
Acquiring three separate 2D stacks would cost more time and would not align voxel for voxel the way one isotropic volume does.
Memory hook: Isotropic means slice it any way you like, later..
Memory hook: One 3D volume beats three 2D stacks when reformats are the goal..
Exam trap: Assuming 3D is always better; it costs time and punishes motion across the whole slab..
Exam trap: Forgetting that only isotropic voxels reformat without a loss of resolution..
Choosing a fat suppression method: strengths and pitfalls.
There is no single best way to suppress fat; each method trades robustness against precision.
Spectral fat saturation targets the fat resonance directly and gives clean, selective suppression, but it depends on a uniform field.
Off center and at low field it fails unevenly, leaving bright fat on one side of the image.
STIR suppresses fat by its short T1 using an inversion pulse, so it is robust where the field is imperfect, including large fields of view and the extremities.
The catch is that it also suppresses anything with a fat like T1, such as some contrast enhancement, which is why STIR and gadolinium are a poor pair.
Dixon methods separate water and fat by their signal phase and produce both suppressed and combined images from one acquisition, which is robust and informative but needs the reconstruction.
Water excitation only excites water in the first place.
The exam relevant skill is matching the method to the situation: uniform small field favors spectral, difficult field favors STIR,
and the need for reliable uniform suppression plus in and out of phase data favors Dixon.
Key point: Spectral saturation is selective but needs a uniform field..
Key point: STIR is field robust but also nulls fat like T1, so avoid it with gadolinium..
Key point: Dixon separates water and fat and yields several image sets from one scan..
Key point: The skill is matching the method to field strength and uniformity..
Worked example.
A large field of view ankle at the edge of the magnet shows patchy failed fat saturation with spectral suppression.
Switching to STIR fixes it because STIR relies on T1, not on a uniform fat resonance.
If the same study needed post contrast imaging, STIR would be wrong, since it would also suppress the enhancing tissue, and Dixon would be the better robust choice.
Memory hook: Uniform field favors spectral; difficult field favors STIR..
Memory hook: STIR plus gadolinium is a trap: it nulls the enhancement too..
Exam trap: Using STIR after contrast; it suppresses enhancing tissue along with fat..
Exam trap: Expecting spectral saturation to work off center or at low field..
Diffusion in disease: stroke, abscess and cellular tumors.
Diffusion weighted imaging measures how freely water moves.
Where movement is hindered, the DWI image stays bright and the ADC map goes dark, the pattern called restricted diffusion.
Reading the pair together is essential, because bright DWI alone can be a T2 effect rather than true restriction.
Confirming a low ADC is what proves the finding.
The clinical value is in what restricts.
Acute ischemic stroke restricts within minutes as the sodium pump fails and cells swell, which makes DWI the earliest and most sensitive sign of infarct.
A pus filled abscess restricts because its thick contents trap water, which helps separate it from a necrotic tumor whose center usually does not.
Densely cellular tumors restrict because tightly packed cells leave little room for water to move.
The exam skill is to pair the sequences and know the differential.
Restricted diffusion is a strong, early, specific sign, but only when DWI bright is matched by ADC dark.
The trap, called T2 shine through, is bright DWI with a normal or high ADC, which is not restriction at all.
Key point: Restricted diffusion is DWI bright with ADC dark, read as a pair..
Key point: Acute stroke restricts within minutes, so DWI is the earliest infarct sign..
Key point: Abscess and densely cellular tumor also restrict; necrotic tumor centers usually do not..
Key point: T2 shine through is bright DWI with normal ADC, which is not restriction..
Worked example.
A ring enhancing brain lesion could be an abscess or a necrotic tumor.
DWI shows a bright center; the ADC map confirms the center is dark.
Restricted diffusion in the cavity favors abscess, because pus traps water, whereas a necrotic tumor center typically does not restrict.
The ADC map is what settles it.
Memory hook: Real restriction is bright DWI and dark ADC together..
Memory hook: Stroke lights up on DWI first, before T2 and FLAIR catch up..
Exam trap: Calling any bright DWI restriction; check the ADC to exclude T2 shine through..
Exam trap: Assuming a ring enhancing lesion is always tumor; a restricting center suggests abscess..
Perfusion by DSC: first-pass bolus tracking.
Dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) MRI tracks a rapid bolus of gadolinium as it first passes through brain tissue,
using fast T2*-weighted (or T2-weighted) echo-planar imaging repeated every one to two seconds.
Gadolinium is not being watched for its usual T1 brightening here; instead its local magnetic susceptibility disturbs the field around vessels and causes a transient,
sharp drop in signal intensity as the bolus passes through the capillary bed, an effect that grows with tissue vascularity.
Plotting signal loss over time yields a concentration-time curve, whose shape drives the postprocessing.
Integrating the curve gives relative cerebral blood volume (CBV), deconvolving it against an arterial input function yields cerebral blood flow (CBF),
and dividing CBV by CBF gives mean transit time (MTT).
A second, smaller signal dip often follows as contrast recirculates through the systemic circulation, and this recirculation must be modeled out or it will bias the curve.
Because the whole technique depends on catching a sharp bolus, a fast,
tight power-injector bolus and rapid whole-brain coverage are essential; a slow or spread-out injection blurs the curve and degrades the maps.
Key point: DSC uses a fast gadolinium bolus and T2*-weighted EPI, imaged every 1 to 2 seconds..
Key point: Susceptibility from the bolus causes a transient signal drop, not enhancement..
Key point: Postprocessing yields CBV, CBF, and MTT maps from the concentration-time curve..
Key point: Recirculation produces a second, smaller signal dip that must be corrected for..
Key point: Requires a tight, fast power-injector bolus for reliable curves..
Worked example.
A patient with a suspected high-grade glioma undergoes DSC perfusion as part of the brain tumor protocol.
As the gadolinium bolus arrives, the tumor region shows a much deeper and faster signal drop than normal white matter, reflecting its dense, leaky neovasculature.
The resulting relative CBV map shows a hot spot with values several times normal gray matter,
a pattern that correlates with higher tumor grade and helps guide the biopsy target toward the most aggressive-appearing region.
Memory hook: DSC: Drop in Signal, Contrast bolus, on T2*.
Signal goes down as gadolinium passes..
Memory hook: CBV from the area under the curve, CBF from how fast and how high it rises, MTT equals CBV divided by CBF..
Memory hook: Think stroke and tumor grade: DSC is the fast bolus-chasing sequence..
Exam trap: DSC signal drops during the bolus (T2* susceptibility effect); do not confuse this with the signal rise seen on T1-weighted DCE enhancement curves..
Exam trap: CBV, CBF, and MTT are all derived from the same DSC acquisition; they are not three separate scans..
Exam trap: A slow or poorly timed injection ruins the first-pass curve; DSC is uniquely sensitive to bolus technique compared with DCE..
Perfusion by DCE: permeability and Ktrans.
Dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI uses repeated T1-weighted acquisitions before, during, and after a gadolinium injection to watch tissue enhance over several minutes,
in contrast to the seconds-long bolus tracking of DSC.
Because gadolinium shortens T1, tissue that takes up contrast brightens, and the shape of the resulting signal-time (enhancement) curve, how steeply it rises, how high it peaks,
and whether it plateaus or washes out, characterizes the underlying tissue.
Pharmacokinetic modeling of this curve produces quantitative maps of capillary permeability.
The key parameter is Ktrans, the transfer constant describing how quickly contrast leaks from plasma into the extravascular extracellular space; a related parameter, ve,
describes the size of that extravascular extracellular space.
Tumors with immature, leaky neovasculature typically show high Ktrans and rapid washout, so DCE is used for tumor characterization, distinguishing benign from malignant lesions,
and for monitoring treatment response, since effective antiangiogenic therapy can lower Ktrans before a tumor visibly shrinks.
Where DSC is a T2* bolus-tracking technique built around CBV, DCE is a T1 permeability technique built around Ktrans.
Key point: DCE uses repeated T1-weighted imaging over minutes to track contrast uptake and washout..
Key point: The enhancement curve shape (rise, peak, washout) reflects tissue vascularity and permeability..
Key point: Ktrans is the transfer constant quantifying capillary permeability; ve is the extravascular extracellular space fraction..
Key point: High Ktrans and fast washout suggest aggressive, leaky tumor vasculature..
Key point: DCE (T1, permeability) is distinct from DSC (T2*, first-pass bolus)..
Worked example.
A patient with a suspicious prostate lesion undergoes multiparametric MRI including DCE.
The lesion shows early, rapid enhancement followed by washout on the signal-time curve, a pattern with high Ktrans consistent with the leaky, disorganized vasculature of prostate cancer,
whereas benign tissue nearby shows slow, progressive enhancement without washout.
Combined with the anatomic and diffusion sequences, this DCE pattern raises suspicion and supports targeting that region for biopsy.
Memory hook: DCE: Dynamic Contrast Enhancement, T1-weighted, minutes-long curve, tissue signal goes up..
Memory hook: Ktrans equals transfer constant equals how fast contrast leaks out of the vessel into tissue..
Memory hook: DSC drops on T2* in seconds; DCE rises on T1 over minutes..
Exam trap: Do not swap DCE and DSC: DCE is T1-weighted enhancement over minutes, DSC is T2*-weighted signal drop over seconds..
Exam trap: Ktrans measures permeability, not blood volume; CBV is a DSC parameter, not a DCE parameter..
Exam trap: Rapid washout on DCE suggests malignancy, but curve shape must be read alongside anatomic and diffusion findings, not in isolation..
Arterial spin labeling: perfusion without contrast.
Arterial spin labeling (ASL) measures brain perfusion without any injected contrast agent.
Instead, an inversion pulse is applied to arterial blood water proximal to the imaging slab, magnetically labeling it as it flows toward the brain.
After a delay that lets the labeled blood reach the tissue of interest, a label image is acquired; a second control image is acquired without labeling.
Subtracting the label image from the control image removes static tissue signal and leaves a small residual signal proportional to blood delivered to tissue, the perfusion-weighted image,
from which quantitative cerebral blood flow (CBF) maps are calculated.
Two main labeling schemes are used: pulsed ASL (PASL), which inverts a thick slab in a single short pulse, and pseudo-continuous ASL (pCASL),
which labels for one to two seconds using a train of rapid pulses and generally gives higher SNR and is now the more widely recommended approach.
The post-label delay (PLD), the time between labeling and image acquisition,
must be long enough for labeled blood to reach the tissue but short enough that the label has not decayed; too short a PLD in a patient with slow or collateral flow can underestimate perfusion.
Because the label and control difference is only a percent or two of brain signal, ASL is inherently low SNR and requires many repeated averages to build an adequate image.
Its major advantages are that it needs no gadolinium, useful in renal impairment, pediatric patients, and anyone needing repeated serial follow-up, and that it is fully quantitative,
yielding CBF in physical units directly rather than only relative maps.
Key point: ASL labels arterial blood water with an inversion pulse instead of using injected contrast..
Key point: The label image is subtracted from the control image to isolate the small perfusion signal..
Key point: pCASL generally gives higher SNR than PASL and is the more widely recommended technique..
Key point: Post-label delay (PLD) must be tuned to transit time; too short a PLD underestimates flow in slow-flow states..
Key point: ASL is contrast-free and gives quantitative CBF, at the cost of inherently low SNR requiring many averages..
Worked example.
A child needs a follow-up brain MRI for a known low-grade lesion and gadolinium is best avoided given the number of anticipated repeat scans over years.
An ASL sequence is added instead of DSC perfusion.
The label and control images are acquired and subtracted to generate a quantitative CBF map, showing no significant increase in perfusion within the lesion compared with the prior study,
which is reassuring against transformation to a more aggressive, hypervascular tumor, all without any contrast injection.
Memory hook: ASL: no injection, the blood itself is the contrast agent, magnetically tagged, then subtracted out..
Memory hook: Control minus label equals perfusion signal; pCASL beats PASL for SNR..
Memory hook: No gadolinium needed: think ASL for renal failure, kids, and repeat serial scans..
Exam trap: ASL uses no injected contrast at all; do not confuse it with DSC or DCE, both of which require gadolinium..
Exam trap: Too short a post-label delay underestimates perfusion in slow-flow or collateral-dependent territories, it is not simply a fixed universal setting..
Exam trap: ASL's low intrinsic SNR is compensated by averaging many repetitions, not by increasing labeling duration indefinitely..
Choosing a perfusion method: DSC, DCE, or ASL.
All three perfusion techniques answer different physiological questions, and picking the right one depends on what is being asked.
