DSC uses a fast gadolinium bolus imaged with T2*-weighted echo-planar sequences, tracking the first pass of contrast to generate CBV, CBF,
and MTT maps; it is the workhorse for acute stroke (identifying the ischemic penumbra) and for tumor grading (high CBV correlating with higher-grade, more vascular tumors).
DCE uses repeated T1-weighted imaging over several minutes to watch contrast slowly leak out of vessels,
generating Ktrans and ve maps of capillary permeability; it is favored for tumor characterization and for monitoring treatment response to antiangiogenic or chemotherapy regimens.

ASL needs no contrast at all, magnetically labeling arterial blood and subtracting the labeled image from a control to generate quantitative CBF maps directly; it is preferred whenever gadolinium shoul
d be minimized or avoided, such as renal impairment, pediatric patients, or serial follow-up imaging, and it is increasingly used in dementia and neurodegenerative disease workups,
where regional hypoperfusion patterns (for example, parietotemporal hypoperfusion in Alzheimer disease) support the diagnosis without repeated contrast exposure.
In practice, stroke and tumor-grading protocols often still favor bolus contrast techniques for their higher SNR, while ASL is the default when contrast is contraindicated, undesirable,
or when only a quick, quantitative CBF check is needed.
Key point: DSC (T2*, bolus, CBV/CBF/MTT) is the classic choice for stroke and tumor grading..
Key point: DCE (T1, Ktrans, ve) targets capillary permeability for tumor characterization and treatment response..
Key point: ASL needs no contrast and is preferred for renal impairment, pediatrics, and serial follow-up..
Key point: ASL is increasingly used in dementia and neurodegenerative disease workups for regional hypoperfusion patterns..
Key point: Choice depends on the clinical question: flow and volume (DSC), permeability (DCE), or contrast-free quantitative CBF (ASL)..
Worked example.
A patient with progressive memory loss is being evaluated for possible Alzheimer disease.
Rather than adding a gadolinium-based perfusion sequence, the protocol includes ASL,
which shows the classic pattern of reduced perfusion in the posterior cingulate and parietotemporal cortex with relative sparing of primary sensorimotor and occipital cortex,
supporting the clinical diagnosis.
Because ASL requires no injection, it can be repeated at a future visit to track disease progression without any added contrast burden.
Memory hook: Volume and flow: DSC.
Permeability: DCE.
No contrast at all: ASL..
Memory hook: Stroke and grading lean DSC; characterization and treatment response lean DCE; renal failure, kids, and repeats lean ASL..
Memory hook: Three letters, three questions: DSC asks how much blood, DCE asks how leaky, ASL asks how much flow without any dye..
Exam trap: Higher tumor grade correlates with higher CBV on DSC, not with a specific Ktrans value; do not merge the DSC and DCE parameters..
Exam trap: ASL being contrast-free does not make it universally superior; its lower SNR means bolus techniques are still preferred when maximum spatial detail is needed..
Exam trap: Dementia perfusion patterns are regional (parietotemporal in Alzheimer disease), not just globally reduced flow; the distribution pattern is diagnostically relevant..
Phase contrast MRA and velocity encoding (VENC).
Phase contrast MRA works by applying a bipolar flow-encoding gradient along one axis.
Stationary spins accrue no net phase because the two lobes cancel, but spins moving along that axis accrue a phase shift proportional to their velocity.
The operator sets a single parameter, VENC (velocity encoding), the velocity that produces exactly 180 degrees of phase shift.
This scales the phase-to-velocity relationship for the vessel being studied.
Choosing VENC is a trade-off.
If true velocity exceeds VENC, the phase shift exceeds 180 degrees and wraps (aliases), displaying as an artifactually reversed or truncated velocity in the fastest part of the vessel,
typically the center of a jet or stenosis.
If VENC is set much higher than the expected peak velocity, aliasing is avoided but the true phase signal occupies only a small fraction of the encoding range,
so the velocity measurement becomes noisy and less sensitive to slow flow.
The correct VENC sits just above the expected peak velocity for the vessel and clinical question.
Because each spatial direction can be encoded independently, PC can measure velocity in a single through-plane direction or in all three directions for a full flow vector.
Through-plane acquisitions with a region of interest drawn over the vessel allow flow quantification: multiplying mean velocity by cross-sectional area gives volumetric flow, used for shunt ratios,
regurgitant fraction in valve disease, and CSF flow studies.
A separate background phase correction step removes phase offsets from gradient nonlinearity and eddy currents that would otherwise bias the flow measurement.
Key point: VENC is the velocity that produces 180 degrees of phase shift on the bipolar flow-encoding gradient..
Key point: Velocities above VENC wrap around and alias, appearing as reversed or truncated flow..
Key point: Setting VENC too high above true peak velocity reduces sensitivity to slow flow and adds noise..
Key point: Through-plane PC with an ROI over the vessel yields volumetric flow: mean velocity times cross-sectional area..
Key point: Background phase correction removes gradient and eddy-current offsets that would otherwise bias flow measurements..
Worked example.
A patient with known aortic regurgitation is referred for phase-contrast quantification of regurgitant fraction.
The technologist places a through-plane PC acquisition just above the aortic valve and sets VENC at 150 cm per second.
Peak systolic velocity is about 120 cm per second, comfortably under VENC, so forward flow is captured cleanly,
and 150 also leaves enough range to resolve the lower-velocity diastolic reverse flow without wrapping the systolic peak or burying the reverse-flow signal in noise.
Forward and reverse flow volumes are then integrated across the cardiac cycle to calculate the regurgitant fraction.
Memory hook: VENC is a ceiling, not a target: set it just above the expected peak velocity to use most of the phase range without wrapping..
Memory hook: Aliasing in PC looks like a reversed sign or truncated value in the fastest part of the vessel, not signal dropout like TOF saturation..
Exam trap: Aliased PC flow can mimic a jet reversal or stenosis; the fix is repeating with a higher VENC, not reinterpreting the direction as real..
Exam trap: A single VENC must accommodate both the fastest and slowest velocities of interest in one acquisition; too narrow a range sacrifices one or the other..
Time-of-flight MRA: inflow, saturation, and pitfalls.
Time-of-flight MRA relies on flow-related enhancement: a short TR, high flip angle sequence rapidly saturates stationary tissue in the imaging slab,
so it produces little signal by the time it is sampled again.
Blood flowing into the slab from outside has not experienced the prior saturation pulses and enters fully magnetized, giving it much brighter signal than the saturated background,
an effect strongest for blood entering perpendicular to the slab and moving quickly through it.
The same mechanism creates the main pitfall.
Blood traveling in-plane, parallel to or within the imaging slab, or moving slowly,
remains inside the excited volume long enough to receive repeated RF pulses and becomes saturated like stationary tissue, causing signal loss that can mimic stenosis or occlusion.
Thin slabs and multiple overlapping thin-slab acquisition (MOTSA) reduce transit time through any one slab and limit this effect,
though MOTSA introduces its own stair-step or venetian-blind artifact at the seams between slabs.
Because TOF depends on direction of entry rather than vessel identity,
a spatial saturation band placed just outside the slab on one side nulls signal from blood entering from that direction: the band goes on the side the unwanted flow enters from, so in a head study,
where arteries flow up from below, a superior band nulls the descending venous inflow for an arterial-only study; because leg arteries flow downward, that pairing reverses there,
as in the venogram example below.
Ramped RF excitation or TONE (tilted optimized nonsaturating excitation) pulses vary flip angle across the slab to compensate for progressive saturation as blood travels deeper into it.
A separate pitfall is that any inherently T1-bright material, such as fat, subacute (methemoglobin) hemorrhage, or residual gadolinium,
can mimic flow-related enhancement because the sequence cannot distinguish true inflow from any other source of T1 shortening.
Key point: TOF signal comes from unsaturated inflowing blood entering a slab of saturated stationary tissue..
Key point: In-plane or slow flow becomes saturated like background tissue, causing pseudo-stenosis or pseudo-occlusion..
Key point: Thin slabs and MOTSA reduce saturation but MOTSA adds a stair-step artifact at slab overlaps..
Key point: A saturation band on one side of the slab nulls inflow from that direction, isolating arteries or veins..
Key point: T1-bright material (fat, subacute blood, residual gadolinium) can mimic flow on TOF..
Worked example.
A 2D TOF venogram of the lower legs is planned to evaluate for deep vein thrombosis.
Because leg arterial flow runs downward and enters from above, a superior saturation band is placed above each imaging slice to null arterial inflow, so only venous flow remains bright.
If the band were mistakenly placed inferior to the slice instead, arterial signal would appear bright and venous signal would be nulled,
producing a study that looks falsely occluded for the veins the exam was meant to assess.
Memory hook: TOF signal is about direction of entry, not vessel type: the saturation band decides whether you see arteries or veins..
Memory hook: Slow or in-plane flow saturates like stationary tissue on TOF: it is stuck in the slab too long and loses its edge..
Exam trap: A TOF signal void from in-plane or slow flow can be mistaken for true stenosis or occlusion; correlate with another technique before calling a lesion..
Exam trap: Fat, subacute hemorrhage, or residual gadolinium can produce a T1-bright false positive on TOF that mimics a vessel..
Contrast-enhanced MRA: bolus timing and technique.
Contrast-enhanced MRA (CE-MRA) does not depend on inflow or velocity at all.
Gadolinium shortens the T1 of blood dramatically, so a fast, heavily T1-weighted 3D gradient echo sequence makes contrast-filled vessels bright regardless of flow direction or velocity,
eliminating the saturation and in-plane flow pitfalls that limit TOF.
This makes the technique flow-independent, but it shifts the challenge to bolus timing.
Image contrast in a 3D acquisition is set almost entirely by which data fills the center of k-space,
since that region carries overall contrast and signal while the periphery carries fine spatial detail.
With centric k-space ordering, the center is acquired first, so timing needs only to get the leading edge of the bolus into the vessel at the start of the scan.
With sequential (linear) ordering, the center of k-space is acquired partway through the scan,
so the technologist must predict when peak arterial gadolinium concentration will coincide with that middle portion of acquisition.
Three common strategies fix the timing.
A test bolus injects a small dose and times a single-slice dynamic series to measure the true transit time from injection to the artery of interest before the diagnostic bolus is given.
Bolus tracking (commercially SmartPrep or CareBolus) monitors signal in the target vessel in real time and automatically triggers the diagnostic acquisition once a threshold is reached.
Time-resolved techniques acquire many undersampled 3D volumes in rapid succession through the injection,
trading spatial resolution for temporal resolution so at least one frame captures the pure arterial phase.
If the acquisition is mistimed and the center of k-space is sampled too early, the study shows weak enhancement or ringing artifact from a still-rising bolus; if sampled too late,
contrast has already reached the veins, producing venous contamination that obscures the arterial anatomy.
Key point: CE-MRA is flow-independent: gadolinium T1-shortening makes vessels bright regardless of velocity or direction..
Key point: Whichever data fills the center of k-space sets overall image contrast; centric order front-loads it, sequential order places it mid-scan..
Key point: Test bolus and bolus tracking (SmartPrep or CareBolus) measure or detect true arrival time to trigger the diagnostic acquisition..
Key point: Time-resolved MRA trades spatial resolution for temporal resolution to guarantee a pure arterial-phase frame..
Key point: Mistimed acquisitions cause either ringing from a rising bolus or venous contamination from a late acquisition..
Worked example.
A CE-MRA of the runoff vessels is ordered for a patient with peripheral arterial disease.
Using a test bolus, the technologist measures a 14-second transit time from the antecubital injection site to the popliteal artery.
The diagnostic sequence uses centric k-space ordering, so the scan starts roughly 14 seconds after the diagnostic bolus begins,
ensuring the leading edge of gadolinium is in the artery right as the center of k-space, and therefore the image contrast, is being acquired.
Had the scan instead started too late, the calf veins would already be enhancing by the time distal arterial images are acquired,
contaminating the study with venous signal that can obscure arterial pathology.
Memory hook: CE-MRA contrast is decided at the center of k-space: centric order means get there first, sequential means get there in the middle..
Memory hook: Test bolus measures transit time in advance; bolus tracking watches for arrival in real time; time-resolved just keeps shooting through the whole thing..
Exam trap: A CE-MRA acquired too early shows weak or ring-like arterial signal from a still-rising bolus, not true pathology; a repeat with adjusted delay is needed..
Exam trap: Venous contamination from delayed acquisition can obscure an arterial stenosis or mimic shunting; recognizing the timing error is a key registry skill..
MR venography and flow quantification.
MR venography adapts the same three angiographic techniques to the slower, lower-pressure venous system.
2D time-of-flight MRV is well suited to slow venous flow because each thin 2D slice is refreshed with a fresh RF excitation,

limiting the in-plane saturation that would otherwise null slow-moving venous spins in a thick 3D slab; a saturation band placed on the arterial side of each slice nulls arterial inflow so only venous
signal remains.
Phase-contrast MRV uses a low VENC appropriate to venous velocities, typically well under arterial VENC settings, and additionally provides directional and quantitative flow data.
Contrast-enhanced MRV times acquisition to the venous phase, later than an arterial CE-MRA, and is flow-independent,
useful when slow or complex venous flow would otherwise degrade a non-contrast study.
Non-contrast venography has a well-known pitfall: pseudo-occlusion.
On 2D TOF, in-plane flow within the plane of a slice, or flow parallel to a long vessel segment, can saturate and mimic thrombosis.
Separately, a subacute clot containing methemoglobin is inherently T1-bright and can mimic patent, flowing blood, the reverse problem, a T1-bright false positive for patency.
Correlating with PC or contrast-enhanced venography, or with the clinical picture, resolves these pitfalls.
Phase-contrast techniques are also the workhorse for flow quantification outside pure angiography, most notably CSF flow studies,
for example at the cerebral aqueduct in suspected normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and vascular flow volume measurement.
In both cases, a through-plane PC acquisition perpendicular to the vessel or CSF-filled space is obtained with a VENC scaled to the expected peak velocity,
a region of interest is drawn over the structure on each cardiac phase, and volumetric flow is calculated as mean velocity multiplied by cross-sectional area, integrated across the cardiac cycle.
Key point: 2D TOF MRV limits in-plane saturation of slow venous flow because each thin slice gets a fresh excitation..
Key point: A saturation band nulls arterial inflow so 2D TOF MRV isolates venous signal..
Key point: Pseudo-occlusion on TOF venography comes from in-plane saturation (false positive for clot) or T1-bright subacute clot (false positive for patency)..
Key point: CE-MRV times acquisition to the venous phase and is flow-independent, useful when slow venous flow degrades non-contrast studies..
Key point: PC flow quantification (CSF or vascular) uses through-plane VENC and an ROI: flow equals mean velocity times cross-sectional area..
Worked example.
A patient with suspected dural venous sinus thrombosis undergoes 2D TOF MRV.
A segment of the superior sagittal sinus shows signal loss that raises concern for thrombosis, but that segment runs largely within the imaging plane over a long course.
Because in-plane flow is prone to saturation on 2D TOF, the technologist adds a phase-contrast or contrast-enhanced venogram for correlation.
The follow-up study shows normal flow through the segment, confirming the TOF finding was pseudo-occlusion from in-plane saturation rather than true thrombosis.
Memory hook: TOF venography pseudo-occlusion has two opposite causes: in-plane saturation looks falsely clotted, T1-bright clot looks falsely patent..
Memory hook: Flow quantification is just geometry: velocity from phase times area from the ROI equals volume per time..
Exam trap: A TOF venography signal void is not diagnostic of thrombosis by itself given the in-plane saturation pitfall; a second technique is expected..
Exam trap: PC flow quantification needs the imaging plane truly perpendicular to the vessel; an oblique plane underestimates velocity and biases the flow calculation..
The diffusion tensor and fractional anisotropy (FA).
Basic DWI treats diffusion as if it were the same in every direction.
In white matter that assumption breaks down.
Water inside and around myelinated axons moves easily along the fiber but is hindered across it, a property called anisotropic diffusion.
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) captures this by measuring diffusion along at least six non-collinear directions, plus a b0 image with no diffusion weighting,
and fitting the results to a 3x3 diffusion tensor for every voxel.
The tensor can be decomposed into three eigenvectors and three eigenvalues.
The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue points along the dominant diffusion direction, which in a coherent white matter tract lines up with the axons themselves.
From the eigenvalues, two summary numbers drive most clinical and research use.
Mean diffusivity (MD) is the average diffusion magnitude, independent of direction.
Fractional anisotropy (FA) is a unitless ratio from 0 to 1 that describes how directional the diffusion is.
An FA of 0 means diffusion is equal in all directions, isotropic, as in CSF.
An FA near 1 means diffusion is strongly restricted to one axis, as in a dense, coherently organized tract like the corpus callosum.
FA maps are commonly color coded by direction: red for left-right, green for anterior-posterior, blue for superior-inferior, with brightness scaled to the FA value itself.
Key point: White matter diffusion is anisotropic: faster along axons, hindered across them..
Key point: DTI requires at least 6 non-collinear diffusion directions plus a b0 image to solve the tensor..
Key point: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the tensor give the principal diffusion direction and its magnitude..
Key point: FA ranges 0 (isotropic, e.g.
CSF) to 1 (highly anisotropic, dense coherent tracts)..
Key point: Color FA maps use a standard convention: red left-right, green anterior-posterior, blue superior-inferior..
Worked example.
A color FA map through the centrum semiovale shows a bright red band running side to side.
This is the corpus callosum, whose fibers cross the midline, so their principal diffusion direction is left-right.
Immediately superior to it, a green band marks the cingulum bundle running front to back.
The color tells the direction; the brightness within that color tells how strongly organized the tract is.
Memory hook: Six directions plus a b0 is the minimum recipe to solve a tensor..
Memory hook: FA colors follow RGB axes: red left-right, green front-back, blue up-down..
Exam trap: Confusing FA (directionality of diffusion) with MD (average magnitude of diffusion); they answer different questions..
Exam trap: Assuming any single diffusion direction acquisition is DTI; true DTI needs the multi-direction tensor fit..
DTI tractography: mapping white matter tracts.
Tractography uses the voxel-by-voxel principal diffusion direction from DTI to reconstruct the paths of white matter tracts as streamlines.
The algorithm starts at a seed voxel and steps outward, following the principal eigenvector from one voxel into the next, building a line that approximates an underlying fiber bundle.
Deterministic tractography follows a single best direction at each step, producing one streamline per seed.
Probabilistic tractography instead models a distribution of possible directions at each voxel and samples repeatedly,
producing many streamlines that express confidence as streamline density rather than a single fixed path.
Tracking is stopped, or a streamline discarded, when FA drops below a set threshold or when the path bends more sharply than an allowed turning angle,
since both suggest the voxel no longer represents a single coherent fiber population.

The clinical payoff is presurgical mapping of eloquent white matter, such as the corticospinal tract, arcuate fasciculus, and optic radiations, so a neurosurgeon can plan an approach that avoids them.
The major limitation is crossing and kissing fiber populations within a single voxel.
A standard single tensor model cannot separate two fiber populations crossing at an angle, and partial volume averaging can make tracking stop early, drift onto the wrong tract,
or fail to continue through the crossing region.
Key point: Streamlines are built by following the principal eigenvector from voxel to voxel..
Key point: Deterministic tractography gives one path per seed; probabilistic tractography gives a distribution of likely paths..
Key point: FA threshold and maximum turning angle are the standard stopping criteria for a streamline..
Key point: Presurgical use includes mapping the corticospinal tract, arcuate fasciculus, and optic radiations..
Key point: Crossing and kissing fibers, plus partial volume averaging, are the main limitation of single tensor tracking..
Worked example.
Before resecting a lesion near the motor cortex, tractography is run to outline the corticospinal tract.
The reconstructed tract is displayed alongside the tumor on the surgical navigation system, showing the tract is displaced but not invaded.
The surgeon plans a corridor that stays lateral to the tracked fibers, reducing the risk of a postoperative motor deficit.
Memory hook: Streamlines just chase the biggest eigenvector, voxel after voxel..
Memory hook: Crossing fibers are the single tensor model's blind spot..
Exam trap: Treating a tractography reconstruction as a direct anatomic photograph rather than a model built on assumptions that can fail..
Exam trap: Forgetting that a low FA region, such as a crossing fiber zone, can prematurely terminate a real tract on the reconstruction..
Diffusion pitfalls: T2 shine-through, ADC, and b-value.
The classic diffusion pitfall is T2 shine-through.
Diffusion weighted images carry inherent T2 weighting, so a lesion with a very long T2, like a chronic cyst or an old infarct, can appear bright on high b-value DWI purely from that T2 signal,
with no true restriction present.
This mimics acute restricted diffusion and can mislead an unwary reader.
The fix is always to check the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map, which is calculated from at least two b-values and removes the T2 contribution,
leaving a purely quantitative map of diffusivity.
True restriction is bright DWI paired with a low, dark ADC.
Shine-through is bright DWI paired with an ADC that is bright or unremarkable, because diffusion there is not actually hindered.
The b-value itself sets how strongly the sequence is weighted toward diffusion.
A higher b-value increases diffusion contrast and lesion conspicuity but comes at the cost of lower signal to noise, and the longer TE it often requires can worsen geometric distortion,
while it also reduces the residual T2 contribution, which is why very high b-value images are less prone to shine-through than low b-value images.
Reading DWI and ADC together, rather than DWI alone, is the standard of practice for this reason.
Key point: T2 shine-through is bright high-b DWI from a long T2 lesion, not true diffusion restriction..
Key point: The ADC map removes T2 weighting and gives a quantitative diffusivity value per voxel..
Key point: True restriction: bright DWI with low, dark ADC.
Shine-through: bright DWI with bright or normal ADC..
Key point: Higher b-value increases diffusion weighting and conspicuity but lowers SNR and, via a longer TE, can increase distortion..
Key point: DWI should never be interpreted without its matched ADC map..
Worked example.
A chronic lacunar infarct from years earlier appears bright on the high b-value DWI image, raising concern for a new acute stroke.
The ADC map is reviewed and shows the same region is bright, not dark, confirming T2 shine-through from the old, gliotic, long T2 tissue rather than a new restricting lesion.
No acute intervention is warranted based on this finding alone.
Memory hook: Bright DWI is a question; the ADC map is the answer..
Memory hook: Shine-through shines on both DWI and ADC; true restriction only shines on DWI..
Exam trap: Calling a chronic lesion an acute infarct because it is bright on DWI without checking ADC..
Exam trap: Assuming a higher b-value is always better; it trades SNR and adds distortion for stronger weighting..
Advanced diffusion applications: DWI beyond stroke.
Diffusion imaging extends well past acute stroke into everyday problem solving across the body.
In the brain, restricted diffusion helps separate a pyogenic abscess, which restricts because its thick, viscous pus hinders water motion, from a necrotic or cystic tumor,
whose fluid center is typically less viscous and does not restrict.
Epidermoid cysts also restrict, unlike a simple arachnoid cyst, which follows CSF signal and diffusivity on every sequence, a distinction that is otherwise easy to miss on conventional imaging alone.
Densely cellular tumors, such as lymphoma and some high-grade or small round blue cell tumors,
restrict diffusion because their tightly packed cells leave little extracellular space for water to move through.
This makes DWI a useful adjunct for grading and for distinguishing cellular tumor from surrounding vasogenic edema, which does not restrict.
Outside the brain, whole-body diffusion weighted imaging with background suppression (DWIBS) is used in oncology for lesion detection and staging and for monitoring treatment response,
since a successfully treated tumor typically loses restriction as cellularity falls and ADC values rise.
This makes diffusion one of the few unenhanced, radiation free tools for tracking tumor response over time.
Key point: Abscess restricts (viscous pus); necrotic or cystic tumor center typically does not restrict..
Key point: Epidermoid cyst restricts diffusion; arachnoid cyst follows CSF and does not..
Key point: Densely cellular tumors like lymphoma restrict because of tightly packed cells and little extracellular space..
Key point: Whole-body DWI (DWIBS) supports oncologic lesion detection, staging, and treatment response monitoring..
Key point: A rising ADC after treatment generally signals falling tumor cellularity, a favorable response..
Worked example.
A suprasellar cystic mass is worked up with DWI to decide between epidermoid and arachnoid cyst before surgical planning.
The mass restricts diffusion, bright on DWI with a low ADC, confirming epidermoid rather than arachnoid cyst, which would have followed CSF signal throughout.
This diffusion finding directly changes the surgical approach, since epidermoid tumors require more meticulous capsule dissection.
Memory hook: Pus is thick, so an abscess restricts; necrotic tumor fluid usually does not..
Memory hook: Epidermoid acts like a solid on DWI; arachnoid cyst just acts like CSF..
Exam trap: Assuming every ring enhancing lesion with a restricting center is an abscess without considering cellular tumor..
Exam trap: Mixing up epidermoid and arachnoid cyst on conventional T1/T2 alone; DWI is what separates them..
Cardiac gating and triggering: ECG, VCG, and the R-wave.
Cardiac MRI requires synchronizing data acquisition with the heartbeat, since cardiac motion during a single TR would blur the image beyond usefulness.
The scanner uses ECG gating, most commonly a vectorcardiogram (VCG) lead set, to detect the R-wave and mark the start of each cardiac cycle.
VCG algorithms combine multiple lead vectors to reliably identify the R-wave peak even though the static magnetic field and pulsatile blood flow distort the surface ECG signal inside the bore.
Blood is a conductive fluid moving through the strong static field, and this motion induces a voltage across the aorta that is superimposed on the ECG trace,
most pronounced during systole and worsening at higher field strength.
This magnetohydrodynamic effect elevates and distorts the T-wave, sometimes mimicking or obscuring the R-wave,
which is why VCG-based detection algorithms rather than simple amplitude thresholds are required for reliable triggering.
Prospective triggering waits for the R-wave, then acquires a fixed set of k-space lines for a predetermined portion of the cardiac cycle,
leaving a gap near end-diastole before the next trigger to allow for heart rate variability.
Retrospective gating instead acquires data continuously throughout the entire R-R interval, tagging each line with its timing relative to the ECG trace,
then sorts and reconstructs images spanning the full cardiac cycle, including end-diastole.
Retrospective gating is generally preferred for cine function studies because it does not truncate late diastole and tolerates mild arrhythmia better,
since outlier beats can be rejected during reconstruction.
Because a single heartbeat does not contain enough time to fill k-space for a full set of cine frames, data are collected in segments across many consecutive heartbeats,
with each segment assigned to a specific phase of the cardiac cycle.
An arrhythmia rejection window discards data from beats whose R-R interval falls outside an accepted range around the patient's average heart rate,
preventing ectopic or premature beats from corrupting the reconstructed cine series.
Key point: VCG lead placement improves R-wave detection over conventional ECG inside the magnet..
Key point: The magnetohydrodynamic effect distorts the T-wave from pulsatile aortic flow in the static field, worst during systole..
Key point: Prospective triggering acquires a fixed window after each R-wave and skips end-diastole..
Key point: Retrospective gating covers the full R-R interval and is preferred for accurate function studies..
Key point: Arrhythmia rejection windows exclude beats with abnormal R-R intervals from cine reconstruction..
Worked example.
A patient's heart rate varies between 58 and 74 bpm during a short-axis cine acquisition.
The technologist sets a moderate arrhythmia rejection window so an occasional premature ventricular contraction does not corrupt the diastolic frames,
and chooses retrospective gating so end-diastolic volume is fully captured for ejection fraction calculation.
Memory hook: Prospective triggers after the beat and misses the finish line at end-diastole..
Memory hook: Retrospective records the whole race, then sorts the photos afterward..
Exam trap: Assuming prospective triggering is always preferable because it is simpler; it actually truncates end-diastole and suits function assessment poorly..
Exam trap: Forgetting that the magnetohydrodynamic effect worsens with higher field strength and faster flow rather than being fixed by better electrode contact..
Cine imaging and ventricular function.
Cardiac cine imaging is built on a balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP) sequence,
valued for its inherently bright blood pool signal that comes from the ratio of T2 to T1 rather than flow-related enhancement,
giving high and reliable contrast between the blood pool and myocardium regardless of flow velocity or direction.
bSSFP also delivers excellent temporal resolution and signal-to-noise per unit time, both essential for capturing wall motion accurately across the cardiac cycle.
Each cine frame is built from a small segment of k-space lines acquired during a limited window of the cardiac cycle,
repeated across roughly 8 to 16 consecutive heartbeats within a single breath-hold to assemble a full set of temporal phases, typically 20 to 30 frames per R-R interval.
Patients hold their breath at end-expiration for each slice to suppress respiratory motion,
since diaphragmatic movement between beats would otherwise misregister the heart from one segment to the next.
A short-axis stack of contiguous cine slices from the mitral valve plane to the apex allows the end-diastolic and end-systolic myocardial contours to be traced on every slice,
and volumes are summed using the method of discs, or Simpson's method, to calculate end-diastolic volume, end-systolic volume, stroke volume, and ejection fraction.
This slice-by-slice contouring approach avoids the geometric assumptions that limit echocardiographic ejection fraction estimates.
Regional wall motion is graded qualitatively across the cine frames using a standardized segmentation model, describing each myocardial segment as normal, hypokinetic, akinetic, or dyskinetic,
which helps localize the territory affected by prior infarction or ischemia before tissue characterization sequences are even reviewed.
Key point: bSSFP contrast comes from the T2/T1 ratio, giving bright blood without needing flow-related enhancement..
Key point: Cine frames are assembled from k-space segments acquired across many heartbeats within one breath-hold..
Key point: A short-axis stack from mitral valve to apex enables volumetric ejection fraction by Simpson's method..
Key point: About 20 to 30 cardiac phases per R-R interval are typical for smooth cine playback..
Key point: Regional wall motion is graded as normal, hypokinetic, akinetic, or dyskinetic..
Worked example.
A technologist prescribes a short-axis stack of ten contiguous 8 mm slices covering the left ventricle from base to apex, has the patient hold their breath for each slice,
and the software auto-contours the endocardial and epicardial borders at end-diastole and end-systole to calculate an ejection fraction of 62 percent, within normal range.
Memory hook: bSSFP for cine: balanced sequence, bright blood, because of T2/T1, not flow..
Memory hook: Short-axis stack, Simpson stacks the discs, no geometry guessing needed..
Exam trap: Confusing bSSFP bright-blood contrast with time-of-flight inflow enhancement; bSSFP brightness is intrinsic to the T2/T1 ratio and holds even with slow flow..
Exam trap: Assuming a single mid-ventricular slice can estimate ejection fraction; accurate volumetric EF requires the full short-axis stack, not one representative slice..
Myocardial tissue characterization: LGE and parametric mapping.
Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging is acquired roughly 10 to 15 minutes after contrast injection,
once gadolinium has washed out of normal myocardium but remains trapped in areas of scar or fibrosis due to expanded extracellular space and slower washout kinetics.
An inversion-recovery prepared gradient-echo sequence is used, with the inversion time (TI) selected to null the signal from normal myocardium,
so that any tissue retaining more gadolinium appears bright against a dark, suppressed normal myocardial background.
TI is not fixed; it must be adjusted for each patient and rechecked over the course of the exam because gadolinium continues to wash out during acquisition.
Most protocols include a TI scout sequence displaying several inversion times, letting the operator pick the one that makes normal myocardium appear darkest just before the LGE images are acquired.
The distribution of enhancement carries diagnostic meaning.
Subendocardial enhancement that extends toward the epicardium and follows a coronary artery territory is the hallmark of ischemic infarction,

since the subendocardium is the last tissue layer perfused and the first to suffer irreversible injury; enhancement can remain confined to the inner third of the wall or progress to full transmural inv
olvement depending on infarct size.
Enhancement confined to the mid-wall or epicardium, sparing the subendocardium and not respecting a coronary territory,
instead suggests a non-ischemic process such as myocarditis or non-ischemic cardiomyopathy.
Parametric mapping extends tissue characterization beyond LGE by measuring absolute T1 and T2 relaxation times pixel by pixel rather than relying on a nulled reference.
Native, pre-contrast, T1 mapping and extracellular volume calculation detect diffuse interstitial fibrosis that LGE can miss because it has no normal region to null against,
while T2 mapping identifies myocardial edema in acute processes such as myocarditis or recent infarction, since free water content raises T2 independent of contrast administration.
Key point: LGE images are acquired 10 to 15 minutes post-contrast, once gadolinium has washed out of normal myocardium but remains in scar..
Key point: TI is chosen to null normal myocardium so retained gadolinium in scar appears bright..
Key point: Subendocardial to transmural enhancement following a coronary territory indicates ischemic infarction..
Key point: Mid-wall or epicardial enhancement sparing the subendocardium suggests non-ischemic disease..
Key point: T2 mapping detects edema; native T1 mapping and extracellular volume detect diffuse fibrosis..
Worked example.
A patient with prior anterior chest pain undergoes LGE imaging showing bright signal spanning the full thickness of the anteroseptal wall in the left anterior descending territory,
consistent with transmural infarction and predicting poor recovery of contractile function in that segment even after revascularization.
Memory hook: LGE nulls the normal, so scar stands out; if it touches the endocardium, think ischemia..
Memory hook: T2 for wet tissue from edema, T1 mapping for the diffuse fibrosis LGE cannot null..
Exam trap: Picking a TI that nulls blood or fat instead of myocardium; the null point is specific to normal myocardial signal and shifts throughout the exam..
Exam trap: Calling mid-wall enhancement ischemic; enhancement that spares the subendocardium and ignores coronary territories points to a non-ischemic cause, not infarction..
Cardiac sequences and artifacts: black-blood, phase contrast, and banding.
Black-blood imaging uses a double inversion-recovery, or double IR,
preparation: a nonselective inversion pulse followed immediately by a slice-selective reinversion pulse restores longitudinal magnetization only within the imaging slice,
while blood outside the slice remains inverted and flows into the slice and is imaged at the null point of its inverted magnetization, appearing dark.
The result is dark, suppressed blood pool signal that sharply defines the myocardial and vessel wall borders, useful for anatomic evaluation of wall thickness, pericardium,
and masses where bright intraluminal signal would otherwise obscure the border.
Phase-contrast imaging encodes flow velocity into the phase of the MR signal using bipolar gradients, producing both a magnitude image and a velocity, or phase,
map that can quantify peak velocity and flow volume across a heart valve or great vessel.
The operator sets a velocity encoding value (venc) close to the expected peak velocity in the region of interest; a venc set too low causes velocity aliasing that wraps the phase signal,
while a venc set too high sacrifices velocity-to-noise sensitivity, so venc should be chosen based on the clinical question, such as a high venc for a stenotic aortic valve jet.
bSSFP cine sequences are vulnerable to dark banding artifact from off-resonance effects,
since the balanced gradient waveform requires a very uniform magnetic field and any local field inhomogeneity shifts the frequency response enough to create bands of signal loss.
These bands commonly arise near the lungs, at tissue interfaces, or from imperfect shimming, and can mimic or obscure pathology if they cross the myocardium.
Banding is minimized by performing a careful local shim over the heart and running a frequency scout to adjust the center frequency so the resulting band is pushed away from the region of interest,
ideally out into the lung or chest wall rather than across the ventricle.
For free-breathing acquisitions such as coronary MRA, navigator echoes placed over the right hemidiaphragm track its position in real time,
accepting data only when the diaphragm falls within a narrow gating window near end-expiration, suppressing respiratory motion without requiring a breath-hold.
Key point: Double inversion recovery nulls blood signal for black-blood anatomic imaging of the myocardium and vessel walls..
Key point: Phase-contrast imaging quantifies flow velocity through bipolar gradient encoding; venc should approximate expected peak velocity..
Key point: Venc set too low causes velocity aliasing; venc set too high reduces velocity sensitivity..
Key point: bSSFP banding artifact comes from off-resonance field inhomogeneity and is corrected with local shimming and frequency adjustment..
Key point: Navigator echoes track diaphragm position to gate free-breathing acquisitions such as coronary MRA..
Worked example.
For a patient with suspected aortic stenosis, the technologist prescribes a phase-contrast sequence through the aortic valve with venc set to 400 cm/s based on the expected high-velocity jet,
and separately notices a dark band crossing the inferior wall on the bSSFP cine, which resolves after rerunning the local shim and frequency scout centered on the heart.
Memory hook: Black-blood inverts twice, once for the whole body and once to save the slice, so blood washes out dark..
Memory hook: Banding lives where the field is bumpy; shim it, then scout the frequency to push it into the lung..
Exam trap: Setting venc too low to gain velocity sensitivity; that causes aliasing that wraps and misrepresents high-velocity jets as falsely lower or reversed..
Exam trap: Blaming banding artifact on patient motion; it is an off-resonance shimming problem specific to bSSFP, corrected with shim and frequency adjustment, not breath-holding..
MR spectroscopy basics: chemical shift and the spectrum.
Every proton in the body resonates at a frequency set by the main magnetic field, but the cloud of electrons surrounding each proton shields it slightly from that field.
Protons bound in different molecular environments, such as a proton on a fat chain versus a proton on a metabolite,
experience different degrees of electron shielding and therefore precess at slightly different frequencies.
This small frequency separation is called chemical shift, and it is the entire physical basis of magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
Because chemical shift is proportional to field strength, it is expressed as a ratio in parts per million (ppm) rather than in hertz,
which keeps the scale consistent whether the study is acquired at 1.5T or 3T.
A proton spectrum plots signal amplitude on the vertical axis against this ppm frequency axis, running conventionally from high ppm on the left to low ppm on the right.
Each peak on that axis corresponds to a specific metabolite or group of chemically similar protons,
and the area under a peak reflects the relative concentration of that metabolite within the sampled tissue.
Single-voxel spectroscopy collects one spectrum from a single, operator-placed cubic region of interest, giving a fast, high signal-to-noise measurement of that one location.
Chemical-shift imaging, also called MRSI or multi-voxel spectroscopy, instead samples a grid of voxels across a slab or slice,
producing a spectrum for every voxel and allowing metabolite maps to be generated across a lesion and its margins, at the cost of longer scan time and lower SNR per voxel.
Metabolite signals are roughly 10,000 times weaker than the signal from tissue water,
so without suppression the water peak would completely dominate the spectrum and bury every metabolite peak beneath it.
Robust water suppression, typically a chemical-shift selective saturation pulse applied before acquisition, is therefore mandatory.
Fat also produces a signal orders of magnitude stronger than most metabolites, so lipid suppression or careful voxel placement away from fat is equally important for a diagnostic-quality spectrum.
Key point: Chemical shift, from differing electron shielding around protons, is the physical basis of the MR spectrum..
Key point: The ppm scale is field-independent, so ppm positions are the same at 1.5T and 3T..
Key point: A spectrum plots signal amplitude versus ppm; peak area reflects relative metabolite concentration..
Key point: Single-voxel spectroscopy samples one region fast; MRSI/chemical-shift imaging samples a voxel grid for mapping..
Key point: Water and lipid suppression are mandatory because metabolites are about 10,000 times weaker than water..
Worked example.

A 45-year-old with a new enhancing frontal lobe lesion is sent for single-voxel MRS to help distinguish tumor from an infectious or demyelinating process; the technologist places the voxel centered on
the enhancing portion of the lesion, confirms the water suppression pulse is properly tuned on the pre-scan,
and reviews the resulting spectrum with the ppm axis running from about 4 ppm down to 0 ppm before the peaks are labeled.
Memory hook: Chemical shift is like an echo in different rooms: same shout, different room shapes the frequency you hear back..
Memory hook: ppm is the universal ruler: it reads the same no matter which scanner, 1.5T or 3T, is holding it..
Exam trap: Candidates sometimes assume ppm values change with field strength; they do not, because ppm is a ratio that cancels out field dependence..
Exam trap: Forgetting that fat, not just water, needs suppression leads to voxel placement errors near marrow or scalp fat..
Metabolites and clinical interpretation.
N-acetylaspartate (NAA) produces the dominant peak on a normal brain spectrum at about 2.0 ppm and is considered a marker of neuronal integrity and density.
NAA falls in almost any process that damages or destroys neurons, including tumor, infarct, and demyelinating disease,
so a reduced NAA peak is a nonspecific but reliable sign that normal neuronal tissue has been replaced or injured.
Creatine (Cr) appears at about 3.0 ppm and reflects cellular energy metabolism.
Because its concentration is relatively stable across many pathologic conditions, Cr is commonly used as an internal reference peak, with other metabolites reported as ratios to creatine,
such as Cho/Cr or NAA/Cr, rather than as absolute concentrations.
Choline (Cho) resonates at about 3.2 ppm and reflects cell membrane turnover, since it is a precursor and breakdown product of membrane phospholipids.
Rapidly dividing cells build and break down membrane at a high rate, so an elevated choline peak, and a raised Cho/NAA or Cho/Cr ratio, is a classic spectroscopic sign of neoplasm.
Lactate appears as a characteristic doublet at about 1.3 ppm and signals anaerobic glycolysis, seen in ischemia, necrosis,
and high-grade or rapidly growing tumors where blood supply cannot keep pace with metabolic demand.
Lipid peaks cluster in the same 0.9 to 1.3 ppm region and indicate tissue breakdown or necrosis.
Myo-inositol, at about 3.5 ppm, is a glial marker that can be elevated in low-grade glial proliferation and in early Alzheimer disease.
Put together, a spectrum showing elevated choline, decreased NAA, and a raised Cho/NAA ratio suggests neoplasm,
while the additional presence of lactate or lipid points toward necrosis or a higher-grade, more aggressive tumor.
Key point: NAA (~2.0 ppm) is a marker of neuronal integrity; it falls with neuronal injury from tumor, infarct, or demyelination..
Key point: Creatine (~3.0 ppm) is relatively stable and serves as the internal reference for metabolite ratios..
Key point: Choline (~3.2 ppm) reflects membrane turnover; elevated choline and a raised Cho/NAA ratio suggest neoplasm..
Key point: Lactate (~1.3 ppm doublet) signals anaerobic metabolism, seen in ischemia, necrosis, and aggressive tumor..
Key point: Lipids (~0.9-1.3 ppm) indicate necrosis; myo-inositol (~3.5 ppm) is a glial marker..
Worked example.
A spectrum obtained from a high-grade glioma shows a markedly elevated choline peak, a suppressed NAA peak, an elevated Cho/NAA ratio, and a prominent inverted lactate doublet at 1.3 ppm,
a pattern the radiologist correlates with tumor necrosis and uses to help guide the biopsy target toward the region of highest choline rather than the necrotic center.
Memory hook: NAA for Neurons Alive and Active; when it drops, neurons are in trouble..
Memory hook: Cho goes up when cells are dividing and chowing down on membrane, the signature of tumor..
Exam trap: Candidates confuse creatine's role: it is the reference peak, not the marker being measured for pathology..
Exam trap: A rising Cho/NAA ratio is often read as neoplasm, but without clinical context it is a nonspecific sign of increased cell turnover that can also occur with infection, inflammation,
or active demyelination..
Acquisition techniques: STEAM, PRESS, and echo time.
Localized single-voxel spectroscopy relies on one of two pulse sequence families to select signal from a single volume while suppressing signal from everywhere else.
STEAM (stimulated echo acquisition mode) uses three 90 degree pulses, one along each gradient axis, to generate a stimulated echo from the intersection of the three slices.
Because a stimulated echo carries only half the available signal compared with a spin echo, STEAM delivers roughly half the SNR of PRESS,
but its use of only 90 degree pulses allows a shorter minimum echo time,
useful when the goal is to detect short-T2 metabolites or J-coupled compounds such as myo-inositol and glutamate that would otherwise decay before a longer echo.
PRESS (point-resolved spectroscopy) uses one 90 degree pulse followed by two 180 degree refocusing pulses along the three orthogonal planes.
Because it produces a true spin echo rather than a stimulated echo, PRESS delivers roughly twice the SNR of STEAM at a matched voxel size and TE,
which is why PRESS is the more commonly used sequence in clinical practice, particularly for smaller voxels or lower field strength studies where SNR is already limited.
Echo time has a strong effect on the appearance of the spectrum.
A short TE (around 30 to 35 ms) shows more metabolite peaks, including myo-inositol, glutamate, and glutamine,
because these compounds have short T2 values and would otherwise decay before a longer echo time could capture them, but the tradeoff is a rolling,
less flat baseline that can make quantification harder.
A long TE (commonly 135 to 144 ms, or sometimes 288 ms) produces a cleaner, flatter baseline that more clearly displays NAA, creatine, choline, and lactate,
at the cost of losing the shorter-T2 metabolite signals.
Long TE acquisitions have one additional diagnostic advantage: because of J-coupling between the lactate methyl protons and the adjacent methine (CH) proton,
the lactate doublet at 1.3 ppm characteristically inverts below the baseline at TE values around 135 to 144 ms, then returns above the baseline at very long TE such as 288 ms.
This predictable inversion is a useful confirmation that a peak at 1.3 ppm is truly lactate and not overlapping lipid, which does not invert.
Regardless of technique, careful voxel placement away from bone, fat, and air, combined with high-order shimming to achieve a narrow linewidth,
is essential for a spectrum that can be reliably interpreted.
Key point: STEAM uses three 90 degree pulses (stimulated echo), giving shorter minimum TE but about half the SNR of PRESS..
Key point: PRESS uses 90-180-180 (spin echo) pulses, giving higher SNR, and is the more commonly used clinical sequence..
Key point: Short TE shows more metabolites, including myo-inositol, but has a rolling, harder-to-quantify baseline..
Key point: Long TE (commonly 135-144 ms) gives a cleaner, flatter baseline highlighting NAA, Cr, Cho, and lactate..
Key point: The lactate doublet characteristically inverts below baseline at TE around 135-144 ms, confirming its identity..
Worked example.
For a suspected pediatric posterior fossa tumor, the protocol includes both a short-TE acquisition to screen for myo-inositol and other short-T2 metabolites,
and a long-TE (144 ms) PRESS acquisition; the long-TE spectrum shows an inverted doublet at 1.3 ppm,
confirming lactate rather than overlapping lipid contamination and supporting a diagnosis of a metabolically active, possibly necrotic mass.
Memory hook: STEAM has three 90s and half the signal; PRESS has 90-180-180 and packs twice the punch..
Memory hook: Lactate flips upside down around TE 135 to 144, like it is doing a handstand to prove its identity..
Exam trap: Candidates often assume higher TE always means better quality; long TE actually loses short-T2 metabolites even as the baseline flattens..
Exam trap: An inverted peak at 1.3 ppm is sometimes misread as an artifact; the lactate inversion is expected at long TE around 135 to 144 ms, not at short TE..
Pitfalls and spectral quality.
The single greatest determinant of spectral quality is magnetic field homogeneity within the voxel.
A good higher-order shim narrows the linewidth of every peak, keeping adjacent metabolite peaks distinct and allowing accurate measurement of peak height and area.
A poor shim broadens each peak, and when linewidths broaden enough, closely spaced peaks, such as glutamate and glutamine overlapping NAA, merge into an unresolvable hump,
making the spectrum difficult or impossible to interpret reliably.
Incomplete water suppression leaves a residual water signal that can swamp the baseline and distort the shape and apparent height of nearby metabolite peaks,
especially the peaks nearest the water resonance such as choline.
If the suppression pulse is mistuned or the shim is poor, the residual water hump can be mistaken for baseline drift or can obscure a genuine metabolite abnormality.
Voxel contamination from tissue outside the intended region of interest is one of the most common technologist-controllable pitfalls.
A voxel placed too close to the skull, scalp, or facial fat picks up an intense lipid signal that bleeds into the 0.9 to 1.3 ppm region, obscuring or mimicking the lactate doublet.
A voxel that includes bone, air, or a portion of CSF or ventricle introduces additional susceptibility effects,
dilutes the metabolite signal with fluid or air that contains essentially no measurable metabolites, and further degrades the local shim.
Finally, patient motion during a spectroscopy acquisition, which typically takes several minutes, shifts the voxel relative to the anatomy mid-scan and can smear or duplicate peaks,
while a voxel that is made too small to avoid these contaminants sacrifices signal-to-noise to the point that peaks are lost in noise.
Careful voxel placement well away from bone, fat, and air interfaces, patient immobilization, and attention to shim quality before acquisition begins are the practical keys to a diagnostic spectrum.
Key point: Good higher-order shim gives narrow, well-resolved peaks; poor shim broadens and merges adjacent peaks..
Key point: Incomplete water suppression leaves residual signal that can swamp the baseline near choline and creatine..
Key point: Voxel contamination from adjacent fat, such as skull or scalp, can mimic or obscure the lactate doublet..
Key point: Including CSF or ventricle in the voxel dilutes metabolite signal and worsens local shim quality..
Key point: Patient motion and undersized voxels both degrade spectral quality, the former by misregistration and the latter by low SNR..
Worked example.
A spectrum obtained near the skull base shows an unexpected broad hump under 1.3 ppm and poorly resolved NAA and creatine peaks; on review,
the voxel was placed too close to the temporal bone and adjacent fat, and the shim report shows a wider than expected linewidth,
prompting the technologist to reposition the voxel further from bone and fat and reshim before repeating the acquisition.
Memory hook: Shim narrow, peaks stand tall and separate; shim wide, peaks slump together..
Memory hook: Fat next door drowns out the lactate signal, so keep the voxel away from the skull and scalp..
Exam trap: A broad hump around 1.3 ppm from adjacent lipid contamination is easily mistaken for a true lactate doublet unless a long-TE inversion check is performed..
Exam trap: Candidates sometimes shrink the voxel to avoid contamination without recognizing that this trades contamination risk for a significant loss of SNR..
BOLD contrast: neurovascular coupling.
Functional MRI localizes brain activity using the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) effect,
an indirect marker of neuronal activity based on local blood chemistry rather than the electrical signal itself.
When a region of cortex becomes active, its metabolic demand rises,
and the vascular system responds with an overcompensating increase in local cerebral blood flow that exceeds the actual oxygen consumed.
The result is a paradoxical local rise in the ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated hemoglobin within and around the active tissue.
Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic and creates local field inhomogeneities that dephase spins, shortening T2* and, to a lesser extent, T2.
Oxyhemoglobin is diamagnetic and has little effect on the surrounding field.
Because active tissue ends up with relatively less deoxyhemoglobin, there is less dephasing, T2* lengthens slightly, and the T2*-weighted signal rises by a few percent in that region.
This small signal increase, not a decrease, is what fMRI detects as activation.
Because the effect depends on T2* changes, fMRI is acquired with T2*-weighted gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (GRE-EPI),
which is fast enough to sample the whole brain repeatedly and sensitive to the susceptibility differences the BOLD effect produces.

The vascular response is sluggish compared to the neuronal event that triggers it: the hemodynamic response function typically peaks about 4 to 6 seconds after a brief stimulus and then returns toward
baseline over several more seconds.
BOLD is therefore an indirect, delayed, low-amplitude surrogate for neuronal activity, not a direct measurement of it.
Key point: BOLD signal reflects local blood oxygenation, not neuronal firing directly..
Key point: Active cortex shows increased blood flow that outpaces oxygen extraction, raising the oxy to deoxy hemoglobin ratio..
Key point: Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic and dephases spins; oxyhemoglobin is diamagnetic..
Key point: Less deoxyhemoglobin means less T2* dephasing, so active regions show a signal increase..
Key point: BOLD is acquired with T2*-weighted GRE-EPI; the hemodynamic response peaks 4 to 6 seconds after the stimulus..
Worked example.
A technologist runs a finger-tapping fMRI paradigm and shows the radiologist a color activation map over the precentral gyrus.
The radiologist asks why the activated voxels appear brighter rather than darker on the T2*-weighted images,
and the technologist explains that increased flow to the tapping-related motor cortex washes out deoxyhemoglobin faster than it is produced,
so the paramagnetic dephasing effect drops and the local signal rises.
Memory hook: More flow, less deoxy, more signal: activation lights up on BOLD..
Memory hook: Deoxyhemoglobin is the villain of T2*; oxyhemoglobin is harmless..
Exam trap: Do not assume active brain regions show a signal drop; the overcompensating blood flow makes them brighter, not darker, on T2*-weighted images..
Exam trap: BOLD reflects hemodynamics with a several-second lag, not the instant of neuronal firing, so it cannot resolve activity on a millisecond timescale..
Task-based fMRI: paradigms and analysis.
Task-based fMRI compares brain activity during a controlled task against a baseline or control condition to identify regions engaged by that task.
The two common paradigm designs are block design and event-related design.
In a block design, the task and rest conditions alternate in extended epochs, for example 20 to 30 seconds of finger tapping followed by 20 to 30 seconds of rest, repeated several times.
This produces a large, sustained hemodynamic response with high signal-to-noise ratio and is the more robust and common approach for clinical presurgical mapping.
In an event-related design, brief individual stimuli are presented, and the hemodynamic response to each discrete event is modeled separately, often with randomized or jittered timing.
This design offers more flexibility, such as sorting trials after the fact by correct versus incorrect responses,
but each individual response has lower amplitude and statistical power than a sustained block, so more repetitions and longer scan times are typically needed.
Analysis is usually performed with a general linear model (GLM), which correlates the measured time course of each voxel against a predicted hemodynamic response derived from the task timing.
Voxels whose signal fluctuations match the predicted response are flagged as statistically active.
Because thousands of voxels are tested simultaneously,
a correction for multiple comparisons is applied before the resulting statistical map is thresholded and overlaid on a high-resolution anatomic image.
The single largest source of spurious or lost activation in task fMRI is patient head motion,
since even small movements between the task and rest epochs generate signal changes that can swamp the true BOLD effect.
Key point: Block design alternates extended task and rest epochs, giving a strong, robust signal favored clinically..
Key point: Event-related design models responses to brief individual stimuli, offering flexibility but lower power..
Key point: The general linear model (GLM) correlates each voxel time course with a predicted hemodynamic response..
Key point: Statistical activation maps require correction for multiple comparisons before thresholding..
Key point: Head motion is the dominant confounder in task-based fMRI..
Worked example.
For presurgical language mapping in a patient with a frontal glioma,
the neuroradiology team chooses a block design alternating word-generation and rest blocks rather than a single-word event-related task, because the sustained block produces a stronger,
more reliable activation map over Broca's area despite the patient's limited attention span.
Memory hook: Block design: long and strong.
Event-related: short and flexible..
Memory hook: GLM: the model predicts the wiggle, the voxel either matches it or does not..
Exam trap: Event-related designs are not simply better because they are more flexible; they trade signal strength and statistical power for that flexibility..
Exam trap: A statistically active voxel on an uncorrected map may just be noise; multiple-comparisons correction is required before a map is clinically meaningful..
Resting-state fMRI and functional connectivity.
Resting-state fMRI is acquired while the patient lies quietly without performing any task, typically simply told to relax with eyes open or closed and stay awake.
Rather than looking for signal changes tied to a stimulus, this technique measures spontaneous, low-frequency BOLD fluctuations, generally in the range of about 0.01 to 0.1 Hz,
that occur continuously across the brain even at rest.
The key finding is that distant brain regions whose spontaneous fluctuations rise and fall together over time are considered functionally connected,
meaning they are part of the same working network even though they may be anatomically far apart.
One well known example is the default mode network, a set of regions including the posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex that are more active at rest than during an external task.
Other established networks include sensorimotor, visual, and executive control networks.
Two common analysis approaches are seed-based correlation, in which the time course of a chosen reference region is correlated against every other voxel in the brain,
and independent component analysis (ICA), which decomposes the whole data set into separate spatial patterns of correlated activity without requiring a predefined seed.
Resting-state fMRI is especially useful in patients who cannot reliably perform a task, such as young children, sedated patients, or patients with cognitive impairment,
since no active cooperation is required beyond staying still.
Key point: Resting-state fMRI requires no task; the patient simply rests while spontaneous BOLD fluctuations are recorded..
Key point: Relevant fluctuations occur at low frequency, roughly 0.01 to 0.1 Hz..
Key point: Regions with correlated time courses are termed functionally connected, forming networks..
Key point: The default mode network is the classic example, more active at rest than during task engagement..
Key point: Analysis uses seed-based correlation or independent component analysis (ICA)..
Worked example.
A pediatric patient who is sedated for a separate reason has resting-state fMRI added to the protocol so the team can still map sensorimotor and language networks for surgical planning,
since a task-based paradigm would be impossible under sedation.
Memory hook: Resting-state: no task, no problem; the brain still talks to itself..
Memory hook: Fire together, wire together: correlated time courses define a network..
Exam trap: Resting-state fMRI does not eliminate motion sensitivity; the patient still must stay still even though no task is performed..
Exam trap: The default mode network is more active at rest, not during task performance; do not reverse this relationship..
fMRI acquisition and pitfalls.
Functional MRI acquisition demands speed, since the whole brain must be sampled repeatedly, typically every 1 to 3 seconds (the TR), to track the slow hemodynamic response over the course of a run.
This is achieved with fast gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (GRE-EPI),
which fills an entire slice of k-space after a single excitation and provides strong T2* weighting to make the sequence sensitive to the small susceptibility changes that underlie the BOLD effect.
The same susceptibility sensitivity that makes EPI useful for BOLD also makes it vulnerable to artifact.
At air-tissue interfaces, especially near the orbitofrontal and anterior temporal lobes close to the sinuses and skull base,
local field distortion causes geometric warping and regions of signal dropout, sometimes obscuring true activation in those areas entirely.

Patient motion is a critical technical concern because the true BOLD signal change is only a few percent; even sub-voxel head motion between frames can generate apparent signal changes of similar or gr
eater magnitude, either mimicking activation that is not real or masking activation that is real.
Motion correction (realignment) and censoring of severely corrupted frames are standard preprocessing steps.
Physiological noise from cardiac pulsation and respiration also contaminates the BOLD time course and is typically modeled or filtered out.
Clinically, the leading application of task-based fMRI is presurgical mapping of eloquent cortex, such as primary motor and language areas,
so the surgical team can plan a resection of a tumor or epileptic focus while minimizing damage to critical function.
Key point: fMRI uses fast T2*-weighted GRE-EPI with a TR of about 1 to 3 seconds to sample the whole brain repeatedly..
Key point: EPI's susceptibility sensitivity causes distortion and signal dropout near air-tissue interfaces..
Key point: Orbitofrontal and anterior temporal regions are classic sites of EPI dropout..
Key point: Head motion is critical because true BOLD changes are only a few percent of signal..
Key point: Presurgical eloquent-cortex mapping (motor, language) is a major clinical application..
Worked example.

A presurgical fMRI for a left temporal lobe tumor shows unexpectedly poor activation in the anterior temporal lobe near the task region; the technologist recognizes this may reflect EPI susceptibility
dropout near the skull base and temporal bone rather than a true absence of language function, and flags it for correlation with other mapping methods.
Memory hook: EPI is fast but touchy: great for BOLD, bad near air..
Memory hook: A few percent signal, a few pixels of motion: fMRI has almost no room for error..
Exam trap: Signal dropout near the orbitofrontal or temporal lobes on fMRI is often mistaken for absent function; it may simply be a susceptibility artifact of EPI..
Exam trap: Do not assume a single motion-corrupted frame is harmless; because true BOLD changes are only a few percent, small motion can fully mimic or erase activation..
Quantitative mapping: why measure relaxation times.
A conventional weighted image reports signal intensity in arbitrary units; the brightness of a pixel depends on scanner gain, coil sensitivity, and window and level settings,
so the same tissue can look different on two different scanners or even on the same scanner on different days.
A quantitative map instead assigns each pixel a physical value, the T1 or T2 relaxation time in milliseconds, that is a property of the tissue itself.
Because that number does not depend on receiver gain or display settings, it is reproducible and can be compared across scanners, field strengths, and time points in the same patient.
T1 mapping is generated by acquiring a series of images at multiple inversion times, or by acquiring images at several flip angles with a known repetition time,
and fitting the signal recovery curve at each pixel to the known T1 recovery equation.
T2 mapping uses a multi-echo spin echo acquisition; the signal measured at each echo time is fit to an exponential decay curve, and the decay constant becomes the T2 value for that pixel.
The result of either fit is a parametric map, commonly displayed with a color scale, in which the pixel value is not a signal intensity but the measured time constant itself.
Key point: Weighted images show arbitrary signal intensity; quantitative maps show an absolute T1 or T2 value in milliseconds..
Key point: T1 maps are built from multiple inversion times or variable flip angle acquisitions fit to the recovery curve..
Key point: T2 maps are built from multi-echo acquisitions fit to an exponential decay curve..
Key point: Quantitative values are reproducible and comparable across scanners and follow-up exams..
Key point: Parametric maps are typically displayed with a color scale where color encodes the measured time constant..
Worked example.
A cardiac MRI protocol includes a native T1 map before contrast; the septal myocardium measures 1020 ms on a 1.5T scanner.
Because this is an absolute value rather than a windowed signal intensity, the same 1020 ms reading obtained six months later on a repeat study can be directly compared to detect diffuse fibrosis,
something a conventional T1-weighted image could not do reliably.
Memory hook: Weighted equals look, quantitative equals number..
Memory hook: Multiple TI or flip angles builds T1; multiple echoes builds T2..
Exam trap: Do not confuse a T1-weighted image with a T1 map; only the map reports an actual millisecond value per pixel..
Exam trap: A single-echo or single-TI image cannot generate a quantitative map; the fit requires multiple data points per pixel..
T2*, R2*, and susceptibility mapping.
A multi-echo gradient echo acquisition measures signal decay across several echo times and fits it to produce a T2* map.
Because gradient echo signal loses coherence faster than spin echo signal in the presence of local field inhomogeneity, T2* is always shorter than or equal to T2.
The reciprocal of T2*, called R2* (R2* equals 1 divided by T2*), rises whenever local field inhomogeneity increases.
Iron is strongly paramagnetic, so tissue iron deposition creates local field distortion and shortens T2*, which raises R2*.
This makes R2* mapping the standard noninvasive method for quantifying liver iron overload, such as in hereditary hemochromatosis or chronic transfusion,
and for estimating brain iron deposition in deep gray matter structures.
Quantitative susceptibility mapping, or QSM, solves an inverse problem using the phase data from a gradient echo acquisition to calculate the underlying magnetic susceptibility of each voxel.
Because calcium is diamagnetic while iron and blood breakdown products are paramagnetic, QSM can distinguish a calcified lesion from one containing iron or hemorrhage,
a distinction that magnitude images and conventional T2* maps cannot make reliably.
Key point: Multi-echo gradient echo signal decay is fit to produce a T2* map..
Key point: R2* equals 1 divided by T2* and increases as local field inhomogeneity increases..
Key point: Iron is paramagnetic, so tissue iron raises R2*, the standard noninvasive marker of liver and brain iron overload..
Key point: QSM calculates magnetic susceptibility from gradient echo phase data, not magnitude..
Key point: QSM separates diamagnetic calcium from paramagnetic iron or blood products, which magnitude imaging cannot do..
Worked example.
A patient with a history of multiple transfusions for thalassemia undergoes an R2* liver protocol.
The measured R2* is markedly elevated, corresponding to a high estimated liver iron concentration,
prompting adjustment of chelation therapy; a conventional T2-weighted image could show low signal in the liver but could not quantify the iron burden or track it reliably over time.
Memory hook: R2* is the reciprocal of T2*: more field distortion, more R2*..
Memory hook: Iron has unpaired electrons, paramagnetic; calcium's electrons are all paired, diamagnetic; QSM tells them apart by susceptibility sign..
Exam trap: Do not say T2* mapping alone can distinguish calcium from hemorrhage; both cause signal loss on T2* but only QSM separates them by susceptibility sign..
Exam trap: Remember R2* rises with iron, so a high R2* value means more iron, not less; do not invert the relationship..
Quantitative diffusion, fat, and fingerprinting.
The apparent diffusion coefficient, or ADC, map is a quantitative measurement of water diffusion expressed in units of square millimeters per second.
It is computed by acquiring diffusion-weighted images at two or more b-values and fitting the signal decay at each pixel to the diffusion equation.
Tissue in which water motion is restricted, such as a hypercellular tumor or an acute infarct, shows a low ADC value, while freely diffusing water shows a high ADC value.
Proton density fat fraction, or PDFF, is a quantitative measurement of the fraction of signal attributable to fat, expressed as a percentage.
It is derived from a multi-echo Dixon acquisition that separates and corrects the water and fat signals for confounding factors such as T2* decay,
and it is used clinically to quantify liver steatosis or vertebral marrow fat content.
MR fingerprinting uses a pulse sequence with pseudorandomly varying flip angles and repetition times so that each tissue produces a unique signal evolution over time.
That measured signal curve is matched against a large precomputed dictionary of simulated curves to derive T1, T2, and proton density simultaneously in a single rapid acquisition.
A related technique, synthetic MRI, uses one such quantitative acquisition to retrospectively generate any conventional weighted contrast, such as T1-weighted or T2-weighted images,
without rescanning the patient.
Key point: The ADC map is quantitative, expressed in mm2/s, and computed from diffusion images at two or more b-values..
Key point: Restricted diffusion produces a low ADC value; free diffusion produces a high ADC value..
Key point: PDFF is a percentage fat fraction derived from a multi-echo Dixon acquisition..
Key point: MR fingerprinting matches a unique pseudorandom signal evolution against a dictionary to yield T1, T2, and proton density at once..
Key point: Synthetic MRI reconstructs multiple weighted contrasts from a single quantitative acquisition..
Worked example.
A patient with suspected nonalcoholic fatty liver disease undergoes a multi-echo Dixon acquisition; the calculated PDFF is 18 percent, consistent with moderate hepatic steatosis.

This percentage can be tracked on follow-up imaging to monitor response to dietary or medical treatment, unlike a qualitative assessment of liver brightness on a single in-phase and out-of-phase pair.
Memory hook: Low ADC, tight cells: restriction slows the water down..
Memory hook: Fingerprinting matches a signal fingerprint to a dictionary to get T1 and T2 in one pass..
Exam trap: A single b-value DWI acquisition cannot generate a true ADC map; the fit needs at least two b-values..
Exam trap: Do not confuse PDFF with simple fat suppression; PDFF is a quantitative percentage, not a qualitative signal suppression technique..
Breast MRI technique and protocol.
Breast MRI is performed with the patient prone in a dedicated bilateral breast coil, which allows the breasts to hang dependent, away from the chest wall,
and minimizes respiratory motion in the field of view.
The coil design permits simultaneous imaging of both breasts for direct comparison and, on many systems, allows image-guided biopsy in the same position used for diagnostic imaging.
The protocol balances high spatial resolution with high temporal resolution so that small lesions can be characterized both by shape and by how quickly they enhance.
A T2-weighted sequence is obtained first to evaluate cysts, lymph nodes, and fluid-containing structures,
then a dynamic T1-weighted gradient-echo series is acquired once before contrast and repeatedly after gadolinium injection to capture the enhancement pattern over time.
Fat suppression, or subtraction of the precontrast series from each postcontrast series, is mandatory.
Breast tissue is fat-rich, and without suppressing that signal, enhancing lesions would be obscured by bright background fat.
Subtracted images isolate the tissue that took up contrast, making even small enhancing foci conspicuous.
Common indications include annual high-risk screening for women with an elevated lifetime risk of breast cancer,
extent-of-disease staging in a patient with a newly diagnosed cancer to detect additional foci or multicentric disease, evaluation of silicone implant integrity,
and problem-solving when mammography and ultrasound findings are inconclusive.
Key point: Dedicated bilateral breast coil, patient positioned prone.
