Key point: T2-weighted series plus dynamic pre- and postcontrast T1 gradient-echo series.
Key point: Fat suppression or subtraction is mandatory to reveal enhancing lesions.
Key point: High spatial and temporal resolution are both required.
Key point: Indications: high-risk screening, staging, implant evaluation, problem-solving.
Worked example.
A 42-year-old BRCA1 carrier presents for her annual screening breast MRI.
She is positioned prone in the dedicated breast coil, and the technologist confirms fat-suppressed T2 and dynamic contrast-enhanced T1 sequences are queued,
with the power injector timed to begin the first postcontrast acquisition immediately after the gadolinium bolus.
Memory hook: Prone in the coil, contrast tells the whole story..
Memory hook: No fat suppression, no lesion conspicuity..
Exam trap: Do not confuse breast MRI positioning with mammography positioning; MRI is prone, not upright..
Exam trap: Fat suppression or subtraction is not optional; it is required on every postcontrast series..
Dynamic contrast enhancement kinetics.
The dynamic series produces a time-signal intensity curve for each enhancing region, described in two phases.
The initial phase, also called wash-in, reflects how quickly the tissue takes up contrast immediately after injection and is characterized as slow, medium, or rapid.
The delayed phase describes what happens to signal intensity after that initial peak.
A Type 1 persistent curve continues to rise through the delayed phase and favors a benign process.
A Type 2 plateau curve levels off after the initial rise and is considered indeterminate.
A Type 3 washout curve rises rapidly and then declines, a pattern that is suspicious for malignancy.
Malignant tumors tend to show rapid wash-in followed by washout because of tumor angiogenesis, which produces immature, leaky vessels, and arteriovenous shunting,
which delivers and clears contrast faster than normal tissue.
This combination of rapid uptake and rapid efflux is the kinetic signature radiologists look for in a suspicious lesion.
Kinetics are never interpreted alone.
Morphology, meaning the shape, margins, and internal enhancement pattern of a lesion, is combined with the kinetic curve type to reach a final assessment,
since some benign lesions can show washout and some cancers can show a persistent curve.
Key point: Wash-in phase is graded slow, medium, or rapid.
Key point: Type 1 persistent favors benign, Type 2 plateau is indeterminate, Type 3 washout is suspicious.
Key point: Rapid wash-in and washout reflect angiogenesis and arteriovenous shunting in malignancy.
Key point: Kinetics alone are not diagnostic; morphology must be considered together.
Key point: Overlap exists: benign lesions can wash out and cancers can persist.
Worked example.
A spiculated mass in the upper outer quadrant shows rapid wash-in in the first minute after contrast, followed by a decline in signal on the delayed images.
The radiologist documents a Type 3 washout curve combined with irregular margins, favoring malignancy, and recommends biopsy.
Memory hook: Up fast, down fast: think cancer.
Up and stays up: think benign..
Memory hook: Type 1 rises, Type 2 plateaus, Type 3 washes out, in order of rising suspicion..
Exam trap: Do not assume a plateau curve is benign; Type 2 is indeterminate, not reassuring..
Exam trap: Do not read kinetics in isolation; morphology and kinetics together drive the final assessment..
Background parenchymal enhancement, morphology, and BI-RADS.
Background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) is the normal enhancement of fibroglandular tissue that occurs regardless of any lesion, and it is graded as minimal, mild, moderate, or marked.
BPE is driven by hormonal status and fluctuates with the menstrual cycle, being lowest in the second week (the late follicular phase).
Because marked BPE can obscure small lesions or mimic abnormal enhancement, screening exams are ideally timed to the second week of the menstrual cycle,
when hormonal stimulation and background enhancement are at their lowest.
This timing improves lesion conspicuity and reduces false-positive findings.
Enhancing findings are described as either a discrete mass, a three-dimensional lesion with a defined shape and margin, or non-mass enhancement, an area of enhancement without a corresponding mass,
often following a ductal or segmental distribution.
Morphology descriptors include the mass margin, such as smooth, irregular, or spiculated, and the internal enhancement pattern, such as homogeneous, heterogeneous, or rim enhancement.
Findings are ultimately assigned a BI-RADS category, the same standardized system used in mammography, ranging from BI-RADS 1 for a negative exam and BI-RADS 2 for a benign finding,
through BI-RADS 3 for a probably benign finding that warrants short-interval follow-up, BI-RADS 4 for a suspicious finding that warrants biopsy,
and BI-RADS 5 for a finding highly suggestive of malignancy.
This shared language allows consistent communication of risk across modalities.
Key point: BPE is graded minimal, mild, moderate, or marked, and is hormonally driven.
Key point: Timing screening MRI to the second week of the cycle minimizes BPE.
Key point: Enhancement is classified as mass or non-mass enhancement.
Key point: Morphology descriptors include margin and internal enhancement pattern.
Key point: BI-RADS categories standardize risk communication across breast imaging modalities.
Worked example.
A 35-year-old with dense breasts is scheduled for a high-risk screening MRI.
The scheduler confirms her last menstrual period began 8 days ago, placing the exam in the second week of her cycle, and the resulting images show only minimal background parenchymal enhancement,
allowing confident evaluation of the fibroglandular tissue.
Memory hook: Week two, BPE low, lesions show..
Memory hook: Mass has a shape, non-mass is just a smear of enhancement..
Exam trap: Do not confuse BPE grade with the breast density categories used in mammography; they are separate scales..
Exam trap: Do not schedule high-risk screening MRI during the premenstrual week, when BPE peaks and false positives rise..
MRCP technique.
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) relies on a heavily T2-weighted acquisition with a very long TE, often 800 milliseconds or more,
so that only slow-moving or static fluid retains signal.
Bile within the gallbladder and bile ducts, along with pancreatic-duct fluid, stays bright, while solid organs, fat, and flowing blood lose signal and appear dark.
Two complementary sequence types are used together.
Thin-section single-shot fast spin echo images are acquired through the biliary tree to provide detailed cross-sectional anatomy,
while a thick-slab radial projection sequence collapses the fluid-filled ducts into a single cholangiogram-like image similar to a conventional ERCP view.
Acquisition is performed with breath-holding or respiratory triggering to limit motion blur, since the ducts are small and easily degraded by respiratory motion.
No intravenous contrast is required for standard MRCP because the technique depends entirely on the intrinsic T2 signal of stationary fluid.
When duct distention is inadequate or subtle ductal pathology is suspected, secretin can be administered intravenously to stimulate pancreatic exocrine secretion,
transiently distending the pancreatic duct and improving visualization of strictures, duct disruption, or anomalous pancreaticobiliary union.
Key point: Heavily T2-weighted with very long TE isolates static fluid signal..
Key point: Thin-section single-shot fast spin echo plus thick-slab radial projection are acquired together..
Key point: Breath-hold or respiratory triggering controls motion given the small caliber of the ducts..
Key point: No intravenous contrast is needed for standard MRCP..
Key point: Secretin transiently distends the pancreatic duct to improve stricture and leak detection..
Worked example.

A patient with intermittent right upper quadrant pain and mildly elevated liver enzymes undergoes MRCP; the thick-slab projection shows a filling defect at the distal common bile duct that persists on
every radial projection, and the thin-section source images confirm a well-defined low-signal focus outlined by bright bile, consistent with choledocholithiasis rather than a transient flow artifact.
Memory hook: MRCP: no needle, just a long echo, since it needs no contrast, only a very long TE..
Memory hook: Pair thin slices with thick slab to recall the two complementary sequence types acquired together..
Exam trap: Do not confuse standard MRCP with contrast-enhanced MR cholangiography using hepatobiliary agents; standard MRCP is a non-contrast T2 technique..
Exam trap: A single thick-slab image alone is insufficient for diagnosis; thin-section source images must be reviewed to exclude artifact..
Hepatobiliary contrast agents.

Gadoxetate disodium and gadobenate dimeglumine are gadolinium-based agents with a property beyond typical extracellular distribution: a fraction of the injected dose is taken up by functioning hepatocy
tes through organic anion transporters and then actively excreted into bile.
This dual behavior produces a conventional dynamic extracellular phase followed by a delayed hepatobiliary phase,
which occurs around 20 minutes after injection for gadoxetate and roughly one to two hours for gadobenate because of its lower hepatocyte uptake fraction.
On the hepatobiliary phase, normal liver parenchyma enhances strongly because hepatocytes concentrate the agent.
Lesions that contain functioning hepatocytes with a patent biliary connection, such as focal nodular hyperplasia, retain contrast and remain bright relative to background liver.
Lesions that lack functioning hepatocytes, including most metastases and hepatocellular carcinomas, and simple cysts (which never contain hepatocytes),
fail to take up the agent and appear dark against the enhancing liver, which sharpens lesion conspicuity and aids characterization.
Because the agent is excreted into bile, the hepatobiliary phase also opacifies the intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts,
allowing functional assessment of biliary anatomy and detection of a bile leak when contrast is seen extending outside the expected ductal course, such as after cholecystectomy or hepatic resection.
Key point: Gadoxetate and gadobenate are partly excreted into bile via hepatocyte uptake..
Key point: Gadoxetate hepatobiliary phase occurs around 20 minutes; gadobenate takes one to two hours..
Key point: Focal nodular hyperplasia retains contrast and stays bright on the hepatobiliary phase..
Key point: Most metastases and hepatocellular carcinoma lack functioning hepatocytes and stay dark..
Key point: The hepatobiliary phase opacifies bile ducts and can localize a postoperative bile leak..
Worked example.
A young woman with an incidental hypervascular liver mass undergoes gadoxetate-enhanced MRI; on the 20 minute hepatobiliary phase the lesion is isointense to bright relative to surrounding liver,
confirming functioning hepatocytes and a patent biliary connection, which supports focal nodular hyperplasia rather than a hepatic adenoma or metastasis.
Memory hook: FNH keeps the light on, since it has working hepatocytes and stays bright at 20 minutes..
Memory hook: Gadoxetate: the hepatobiliary phase arrives at twenty minutes..
Exam trap: Do not assume every liver lesion washes out on delayed imaging; hepatobiliary-specific agents behave oppositely from extracellular agents for lesions such as FNH..
Exam trap: Scanning the hepatobiliary phase too early, before hepatocyte uptake peaks, can cause a benign lesion to be misread as non-uptaking..
MR enterography.
MR enterography evaluates the small bowel, most often to assess known or suspected Crohn disease, by combining luminal distention with dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging.
Patients drink a large volume of biphasic oral contrast, a solution that appears bright on T2-weighted images and dark on T1-weighted images,
which distends the bowel loops and allows the wall to be assessed separately from the lumen on both sequence types.
An antiperistaltic agent, typically glucagon, is given just before imaging to suppress bowel motion and peristaltic artifact, improving image sharpness for wall assessment.
After the antiperistaltic agent takes effect, dynamic post-gadolinium T1-weighted images are obtained through the abdomen and pelvis to characterize bowel wall enhancement.
Findings of active inflammation include mural thickening, increased mural enhancement relative to adjacent normal bowel, mucosal hyperenhancement,
and restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging.
These features help separate an actively inflamed segment, which may respond to medical therapy, from a chronic fibrotic stricture,
which typically shows only mild enhancement and a thickened but less avidly enhancing wall and may instead require surgical management.
Key point: Chiefly used for Crohn disease evaluation of the small bowel..
Key point: Large-volume biphasic oral contrast distends the lumen, bright on T2 and dark on T1..
Key point: Glucagon or another antiperistaltic agent suppresses bowel motion before imaging..
Key point: Dynamic post-gadolinium T1 imaging characterizes bowel wall enhancement..
Key point: Mural thickening, hyperenhancement, and restricted diffusion indicate active inflammation over chronic fibrosis..
Worked example.
A teenager with known Crohn disease and worsening abdominal pain undergoes MR enterography; a terminal ileal segment shows marked mural thickening, layered hyperenhancement after gadolinium,
and restricted diffusion, favoring an actively inflamed segment amenable to escalated medical therapy rather than a fixed fibrotic stricture.
Memory hook: Glucagon calms the gut so the bowel holds still for imaging..
Memory hook: Bright on T2, dark on T1 for the oral contrast: biphasic flips between sequences..
Exam trap: Do not mistake a fibrotic stricture, which enhances only mildly, for active inflammation, which enhances avidly and restricts diffusion..
Exam trap: Skipping the antiperistaltic agent leaves peristalsis that can mimic wall thickening or obscure true pathology..
Pitfalls and applications: MRCP and body MRI.
Several pitfalls can degrade MRCP interpretation.
Pneumobilia, air within the bile ducts after sphincterotomy or biliary-enteric surgery, produces a signal void that can mimic a stone or filling defect,
as can flow-related signal loss from turbulent bile motion.
Duct pulsation transmitted from the adjacent hepatic artery can also create a linear artifact across the common duct.
Overlapping fluid-filled bowel loops adjacent to the pancreatic head or distal common bile duct can obscure the ducts on the thick-slab projection.
Correlating the thick-slab images with the thin-section source images helps distinguish true filling defects, which persist and have a defined margin, from artifact,
which shifts position or configuration between sequences.
Elsewhere in body MRI, susceptibility artifact from bowel gas, surgical clips, or other metallic hardware degrades image quality on gradient-echo and diffusion sequences,
an important consideration in postsurgical abdominal and pelvic imaging.
Respiratory motion remains a persistent challenge for upper abdominal imaging and is managed with breath-hold techniques, respiratory triggering, or navigator-based sequences.
For hepatobiliary contrast studies, correct timing of the hepatobiliary phase is essential; imaging too early, before hepatocyte uptake and biliary excretion peak,
can cause a lesion with normal function to be misclassified as non-enhancing, leading to an incorrect diagnosis.
Key point: Pneumobilia and flow-related voids can mimic a stone on MRCP; correlate thick-slab with thin-section images..
Key point: Duct pulsation artifact from the adjacent hepatic artery can cross the common bile duct..
Key point: Overlapping fluid-filled bowel can obscure the pancreaticobiliary ducts..
Key point: Susceptibility from bowel gas or surgical clips degrades gradient-echo and diffusion images..
Key point: Correct hepatobiliary phase timing is required or lesion characterization fails..
Worked example.
A postoperative patient after sphincterotomy has a rounded filling defect near the distal common bile duct on the thick-slab MRCP image,
but the thin-section source images show the defect shifts position between adjacent slices and corresponds to an air bubble rather than a fixed stone, avoiding an unnecessary ERCP.
Memory hook: Air moves, stones stay, to separate pneumobilia from a true calculus..
Memory hook: Too early misses the liver, for hepatobiliary phase timing errors..
Exam trap: Treating any filling defect on the thick-slab image alone as a stone without checking the thin-section source images..
Exam trap: Assuming metallic susceptibility only affects gradient-echo sequences; it also disrupts diffusion-weighted imaging..
Multiparametric protocol and zonal anatomy.
Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) of the prostate combines three sequence types into one study: high-resolution T2-weighted imaging for anatomy,
diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with an apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map for cellularity, and dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) imaging for vascularity.
The exam is typically performed at 1.5T or 3T, with or without an endorectal coil, though 3T without a coil is now the common approach at high-volume centers.
The prostate is divided into zones that behave differently on imaging and carry different cancer risk.
The peripheral zone (PZ) forms the posterior and lateral gland and is where the majority of clinically significant cancers arise; on T2-weighted images it is normally bright,
so a focal area of low signal stands out against that background.
The transition zone (TZ) surrounds the urethra centrally and is the site of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), which causes it to enlarge and develop a heterogeneous, nodular appearance with age.
High-resolution, small field-of-view T2-weighted imaging in at least two planes is the anatomic backbone of the exam.
It defines zonal anatomy, the capsule, and adjacent structures such as the seminal vesicles and neurovascular bundles,
and it provides the framework onto which the functional DWI and DCE findings are mapped.
Key point: mpMRI combines T2-weighted anatomy, DWI/ADC, and DCE imaging in a single exam..
Key point: Peripheral zone (PZ) is the posterior and lateral gland, normally T2-bright, and the most common site of cancer..
Key point: Transition zone (TZ) surrounds the urethra and enlarges with benign prostatic hyperplasia..
Key point: Performed at 1.5T or 3T; an endorectal coil is optional and used less often at 3T..
Key point: Small field-of-view, high-resolution T2-weighted imaging in multiple planes anchors the anatomic interpretation..
Worked example.
A 62-year-old man with an elevated PSA undergoes a 3T mpMRI without an endorectal coil.
High-resolution T2-weighted images show a normal, homogeneously bright peripheral zone on the left and a rounded area of low signal in the right posterolateral peripheral zone,
prompting further evaluation with DWI/ADC and DCE at that site.
Memory hook: PZ is posterior, peripheral, and the usual site of prostate cancer; TZ is central and gets BPH with age..
Memory hook: T2 draws the map; DWI and DCE color it in..
Exam trap: Do not assume an endorectal coil is required; many 3T exams are performed with a surface coil only..
Exam trap: Do not confuse the transition zone, which is BPH-prone and central, with the peripheral zone, which is cancer-prone and posterolateral; each has its own normal T2 appearance..
Diffusion, ADC, and sequence dominance.
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with its accompanying apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map is the single most important functional sequence in prostate mpMRI.
DWI is acquired at multiple b-values, and a high b-value image, typically 1400 or higher, either directly acquired or calculated from lower b-value data, is used to highlight restricted diffusion.
Clinically significant prostate cancer is densely cellular, which restricts the free movement of water molecules.
Restricted diffusion appears as focal high signal on the high b-value image and as focal low signal, meaning a low ADC value, on the ADC map.
A lesion that is bright on high-b DWI and correspondingly dark on ADC is the classic signature of significant disease, and the two images should always be read together rather than in isolation.
Sequence dominance differs by zone.
In the peripheral zone, DWI and ADC are the dominant sequence for assessment, meaning they carry the most weight in scoring a lesion.
In the transition zone, T2-weighted morphology is the dominant sequence, with DWI playing a supporting role.
Knowing which sequence leads in which zone is essential for correctly applying the PI-RADS system described next.
Key point: DWI/ADC is the most important functional sequence in prostate mpMRI..
Key point: High b-value DWI, about 1400 or greater, is acquired or calculated to emphasize restricted diffusion..
Key point: Restricted diffusion equals high signal on high-b DWI plus low signal on the ADC map..
Key point: DWI/ADC is the dominant sequence for scoring lesions in the peripheral zone..
Key point: T2-weighted imaging is the dominant sequence for scoring lesions in the transition zone..
Worked example.
On a suspicious right peripheral zone focus identified on T2, the high b-value DWI shows marked focal hyperintensity and the ADC map shows a matching focal area of low signal.
Because DWI/ADC is dominant in the peripheral zone, this concordant restriction pattern is the primary driver of an elevated suspicion score, independent of the T2 appearance alone.
Memory hook: Bright on high-b, dark on ADC, that is restricted diffusion and that is suspicious..
Memory hook: DWI drives the peripheral zone; T2 drives the transition zone..
Exam trap: Do not call restriction from the high b-value image alone; the ADC map must show a matching low value to rule out T2 shine-through..
Exam trap: Do not apply DWI as the dominant sequence in the transition zone; T2 morphology leads there, with DWI as a supporting feature only..
PI-RADS assessment.
The Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System, version 2.1 (PI-RADS v2.1), assigns each lesion a score from 1 to 5 that reflects the probability of clinically significant cancer,
with 1 being very low probability and 5 being very high probability.
The score is built from the dominant sequence for the zone in which the lesion sits, with a secondary sequence used to refine borderline cases.
In the peripheral zone, the DWI/ADC appearance sets the baseline score.
Dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) imaging serves as a tiebreaker: a peripheral zone lesion that scores an equivocal 3 on DWI/ADC is upgraded to a 4 if there is early,
focal enhancement that corresponds to the same location on DWI.
Diffuse or symmetric enhancement does not qualify; the enhancement must be focal and must match the DWI finding.
In the transition zone, T2-weighted morphology sets the baseline score.
A suspicious transition zone lesion is typically lenticular or non-circumscribed and homogeneously low in T2 signal, resembling an erased charcoal smudge.
This contrasts with a typical BPH nodule, which is usually well-circumscribed with a visible capsule, sometimes described as looking like a walled-off marble.
Key point: PI-RADS v2.1 scores each lesion 1 to 5 for the likelihood of clinically significant cancer..
Key point: In the peripheral zone, DWI/ADC sets the score and DCE can upgrade an equivocal 3 to a 4..
Key point: The DCE upgrade requires early, focal enhancement matching the DWI location, not diffuse enhancement..
Key point: In the transition zone, T2 morphology sets the score..
Key point: A suspicious transition zone lesion is lenticular, non-circumscribed, and homogeneously dark on T2, unlike a well-defined BPH nodule..
Worked example.
A peripheral zone lesion shows moderate restriction on DWI/ADC, earning an initial score of 3.
DCE images show early focal enhancement at the same location, so the radiologist upgrades the final PI-RADS assessment to 4, triggering a recommendation for targeted biopsy.
Memory hook: PZ: DWI scores it, DCE can bump a 3 to a 4 if it lights up focally and early..
Memory hook: TZ: a charcoal smudge suggests cancer, a walled-off marble suggests BPH..
Exam trap: Do not use DCE to upgrade a transition zone lesion; the DCE tiebreaker rule applies only to the peripheral zone..
Exam trap: Do not upgrade based on any enhancement; only early, focal enhancement matching the DWI abnormality moves a PZ score from 3 to 4..
Pitfalls and applications.
Post-biopsy hemorrhage is bright on T1-weighted images and can obscure a true lesion or mimic one on T2 and DWI,
so mpMRI is generally delayed roughly 6 to 8 weeks after a prostate biopsy to let the blood products clear.
If imaging cannot be delayed, a pre-contrast T1-weighted sequence should be reviewed first to identify hemorrhage before interpreting the other sequences.
Prostatitis and BPH nodules are common mimics of cancer.
Prostatitis can cause wedge-shaped or diffuse low T2 signal and mild diffusion restriction in the peripheral zone that overlaps with malignancy,
while BPH nodules in the transition zone can show low ADC values that overlap with significant disease; correlating morphology, symmetry, and clinical history helps separate these from true tumor.
DWI is technically demanding and prone to susceptibility-related distortion near rectal gas, hip prostheses, or other metal, which can blur or displace the apparent lesion location.
Despite these pitfalls, mpMRI has become central to prostate cancer management: it guides targeted MR-ultrasound fusion biopsy to sample suspicious areas directly,
and it assesses local staging features such as extracapsular extension and seminal vesicle invasion that influence treatment planning.
Key point: Post-biopsy hemorrhage is T1 bright and can mimic or obscure disease..
Key point: Imaging is typically delayed 6 to 8 weeks after biopsy to let hemorrhage resolve..
Key point: Prostatitis and BPH nodules both mimic cancer on T2 and DWI/ADC..
Key point: Rectal gas and metal such as hip prostheses cause susceptibility distortion on DWI..
Key point: mpMRI guides MR-ultrasound fusion biopsy and stages extracapsular extension and seminal vesicle invasion..
Worked example.
A patient scanned only 3 weeks after a prostate biopsy shows extensive T1-bright signal throughout the peripheral zone.
The radiologist recommends repeating the mpMRI in 6 to 8 weeks once the hemorrhage has resolved, since the blood obscures reliable assessment of the zone.
Memory hook: Blood is bright on T1, so wait 6 to 8 weeks before you trust the picture..
Memory hook: Fusion biopsy hits what mpMRI finds; staging asks whether it broke out of the capsule..
Exam trap: Do not interpret a recently biopsied prostate without checking pre-contrast T1 for hemorrhage first..
Exam trap: Do not assume every area of restricted diffusion is cancer; prostatitis and BPH nodules can restrict diffusion too..
Metal artifact reduction.
Metal implants such as arthroplasty hardware, screws, and surgical clips create severe local field inhomogeneity through susceptibility artifact.
This produces signal voids where the field is most disrupted, geometric distortion that displaces anatomy from its true position,
and a characteristic bright rim of signal pile-up immediately adjacent to areas of signal dropout.
Fat suppression is also affected: spectral, or chemical-shift, fat saturation relies on a narrow, uniform range of resonant frequencies and fails near metal,
leaving unwanted fat signal or producing patchy suppression.
Basic scan parameter adjustments reduce artifact severity without specialized sequences.
Increasing receiver bandwidth widens the frequency range each pixel represents, so a given field-induced frequency shift spans fewer pixels,
which shrinks the frequency-encode misregistration caused by field distortion.
Using a short TE limits the time available for spins to dephase before readout.
Spin echo or fast spin echo sequences are preferred over gradient echo because the 180 degree refocusing pulse compensates for much of the field inhomogeneity that gradient echo cannot correct.
For fat suppression near metal, STIR should replace spectral techniques because STIR suppresses fat based on T1 relaxation time rather than a narrow resonant frequency,
so it remains reliable despite field inhomogeneity.
Thinner slices, smaller voxels, and aligning the frequency-encode direction along the long axis of the hardware, rather than across it, further limit distortion.
When conventional adjustments are not enough, dedicated metal artifact reduction sequences correct distortion more directly.
View-angle tilting (VAT) applies a compensating gradient during readout to correct in-plane distortion.
SEMAC, slice-encoding for metal artifact correction, adds an extra phase-encoding step in the slice direction to correct through-plane distortion,
resolving the true location of misplaced slice signal.

MAVRIC acquires the volume across multiple offset frequency bins to sidestep slice distortion; the hybrid MAVRIC-SL adds slice encoding and view-angle tilting to correct both in-plane and through-plane
distortion.
These techniques are standard for postoperative arthroplasty imaging, where accurate assessment of the bone-implant interface, periprosthetic fluid,
and adjacent soft tissue depends on controlling metal-induced distortion.
Key point: Susceptibility artifact near metal causes signal voids, geometric distortion, and bright pile-up next to dropout..
Key point: High bandwidth and short TE reduce metal artifact by limiting dephasing time and frequency misregistration..
Key point: Use STIR instead of spectral fat saturation near metal because STIR is not frequency-selective..
Key point: Fast spin echo is preferred over gradient echo because refocusing pulses compensate for field inhomogeneity..
Key point: VAT, SEMAC, and MAVRIC are dedicated sequences that correct in-plane and through-plane distortion for arthroplasty imaging..
Worked example.
A patient with a total hip arthroplasty is referred for MRI to evaluate suspected periprosthetic infection.
The technologist selects a fast spin echo protocol with high receiver bandwidth, short TE, and STIR for fluid-sensitive fat-suppressed contrast,
then adds SEMAC to control through-plane distortion so the periprosthetic collection and bone-implant interface can be evaluated with confidence, instead of relying on spectral fat saturation,
which would fail adjacent to the hardware.
Memory hook: STIR near steel: swap spectral fat saturation for STIR whenever hardware is in the field..
Memory hook: SEMAC slices, MAVRIC bins, VAT tilts: three fixes for through-plane, frequency-bin, and in-plane distortion..
Exam trap: Choosing spectral, or chemical-shift, fat suppression near metal is a common wrong answer; STIR is correct because it does not depend on a narrow resonant frequency..
Exam trap: Test writers may pair reducing metal artifact with gradient echo as a distractor; gradient echo worsens metal artifact and fast spin echo is the correct choice..
Cartilage and quantitative MSK mapping.
Routine morphologic evaluation of articular cartilage relies on fat-suppressed proton-density or T2-weighted sequences, which depict cartilage thickness, surface contour,
and focal defects such as fissures or full-thickness loss.
These sequences show established structural damage well but are less sensitive to the earliest stages of cartilage degeneration,
when the tissue looks morphologically intact but is already biochemically abnormal.
Quantitative mapping techniques target that earlier stage.

T2 mapping generates a pixel-by-pixel map of T2 relaxation time across the cartilage; collagen matrix disorganization and increased water mobility that precede visible fibrillation raise T2 values in t
he affected region.
T1-rho mapping, T1 in the rotating frame, is sensitive to proteoglycan content specifically, so a drop in proteoglycan concentration, an early event in osteoarthritis,
is detectable as a T1-rho change before any morphologic abnormality appears.
Both techniques allow regional comparison against normal reference values rather than a simple visual read.
Delayed gadolinium-enhanced MRI of cartilage (dGEMRIC) takes a different approach: an intravenous gadolinium-based contrast agent is administered, and after a delay to allow equilibration,
the negatively charged contrast agent distributes into cartilage inversely to the concentration of negatively charged glycosaminoglycan.
Areas of glycosaminoglycan depletion accumulate more contrast and show shortened T1, so a calculated dGEMRIC index reflects glycosaminoglycan content and, indirectly, cartilage matrix health.
Key point: Morphologic cartilage imaging uses fat-suppressed proton-density or T2 sequences and shows established structural damage..
Key point: T2 mapping detects collagen disorganization and increased water mobility as regionally elevated T2 values..
Key point: T1-rho mapping is sensitive to proteoglycan loss, an early biochemical change that precedes morphologic damage..
Key point: dGEMRIC uses delayed gadolinium distribution, inversely related to glycosaminoglycan content, to grade cartilage matrix health..
Key point: Quantitative techniques detect degeneration before morphologic sequences show visible cartilage loss..
Worked example.
A 34-year-old runner with knee pain and a morphologically normal-appearing cartilage surface on fat-suppressed proton-density imaging undergoes T2 mapping,
which shows focally elevated T2 values in the weight-bearing femoral condyle,
indicating early collagen matrix disorganization that would not have been detected by standard morphologic sequences alone.
Memory hook: T2 tells collagen, T1-rho tells proteoglycan: separate the two relaxation targets by which matrix component they sense..
Memory hook: dGEMRIC: more contrast where glycosaminoglycan is gone, since distribution is inverse to concentration..
Exam trap: Do not reverse dGEMRIC's relationship; low glycosaminoglycan means high contrast uptake and shortened T1, not reduced signal..
Exam trap: T1-rho and T2 mapping are sometimes used interchangeably in distractors; T1-rho targets proteoglycan while T2 reflects collagen and water content..
Marrow and specialized sequences.
Normal adult bone marrow is predominantly fatty and therefore bright on T1-weighted images, which makes T1 the most sensitive screening sequence for marrow disease.
Any process that replaces or infiltrates fatty marrow, such as tumor, metastasis, leukemia, or lymphoma, lowers the T1 signal because it displaces fat with cellular or fibrous tissue.
Marrow edema from trauma, stress reaction, or osteomyelitis similarly lowers T1 signal.
Because low T1 signal alone is nonspecific, a STIR or fat-suppressed T2-weighted sequence is added to confirm that the T1 abnormality corresponds to true edema or replacement,
which appears bright once background fat signal is suppressed.
Chemical-shift imaging, acquired as in-phase and opposed-phase gradient echo pairs, assesses the fat content of marrow directly.
Normal or benign marrow that contains a mixture of fat and water, such as red marrow or benign compression fractures,
loses signal on the opposed-phase image relative to in-phase because fat and water signal cancel at the voxel level.
Marrow that has been fully replaced by tumor contains little or no fat, so it fails to drop signal on opposed-phase imaging,
a distinction that helps separate benign from malignant vertebral compression fractures.
Gradient echo sequences serve a different specialized role in marrow and joint imaging: their sensitivity to local field inhomogeneity produces pronounced signal loss, or blooming,
around hemosiderin deposits.
This is exploited to identify pigmented villonodular synovitis, where hemosiderin-laden synovial proliferation blooms markedly on gradient echo,
and to confirm prior intra-articular hemorrhage from trauma or hemophilic arthropathy.
Key point: T1 is the primary screening sequence for marrow disease because normal fatty marrow is bright and replacement or edema lowers signal..
Key point: STIR or fat-suppressed T2 confirms a T1 abnormality represents true marrow edema or replacement..
Key point: In-phase and opposed-phase chemical-shift imaging assesses marrow fat content and helps distinguish benign from malignant compression fractures..
Key point: Benign marrow with mixed fat and water drops signal on opposed-phase imaging; tumor-replaced marrow does not..
Key point: Gradient echo blooming from hemosiderin identifies pigmented villonodular synovitis and prior hemorrhage..
Worked example.
An oncology patient has a compression fracture on radiographs; T1-weighted MRI shows diffusely low marrow signal at the fracture level and multiple other vertebral bodies,
opposed-phase chemical-shift imaging shows no signal drop compared to in-phase, and STIR confirms diffuse marrow abnormality,
together indicating tumor infiltration rather than a benign osteoporotic fracture.
Memory hook: Fat is bright, fat leaving is dark: T1 signal tracks fatty marrow content directly..
Memory hook: No drop on opposed-phase, no fat left to drop: malignant marrow replacement fails to lose signal on opposed-phase imaging..
Exam trap: Low T1 marrow signal is nonspecific for malignancy; edema from trauma or infection produces the same finding, so STIR or clinical correlation is required..
Exam trap: Confusing which phase drops signal in benign marrow; benign fat-water marrow loses signal on opposed-phase, not in-phase..
Artifacts, applications, and pitfalls.
The magic angle artifact arises in highly ordered collagenous tissues such as tendons, ligaments, and to a lesser extent cartilage,
when a segment of the tissue is oriented at approximately 55 degrees to the main magnetic field.
At this angle, dipolar coupling between water molecules bound to the collagen matrix is minimized, which paradoxically increases T2 relaxation time and raises signal on short-TE sequences.
The artifact mimics tendinosis or a partial tear on proton-density or T1-weighted images obtained at short TE.
The key to recognizing magic angle artifact is that it is TE-dependent: because it results from an increase in the effective T2 rather than true tissue pathology,
the abnormal signal resolves or markedly diminishes on a long-TE, T2-weighted sequence.
True tendon pathology, such as a tear or tendinosis with mucoid degeneration, remains bright on both short-TE and long-TE images.
Confirming disappearance on a long-TE sequence is the standard way to distinguish the artifact from a real abnormality.

Near orthopedic hardware, the same principle discussed for metal artifact reduction applies clinically: spectral fat saturation fails and should be replaced with STIR to maintain reliable fat suppressi
on around a prosthesis.
Quantitative cartilage values from T2 or T1-rho mapping are not universal constants; they vary with pulse sequence design, echo spacing, and field strength,
so comparisons should use consistent protocols and, ideally, site-specific reference ranges.
Clinically, advanced MSK techniques are applied to assess arthroplasty complications such as periprosthetic osteolysis, component loosening, and adverse local tissue reaction,
and quantitative cartilage mapping is used in early osteoarthritis research and pre-surgical cartilage assessment.
Key point: Magic angle artifact occurs in ordered collagenous tissue near 55 degrees to the main field and raises signal on short-TE sequences..
Key point: Magic angle artifact resolves on long-TE, T2-weighted sequences, which distinguishes it from true tendon pathology..
Key point: True tendon tears or tendinosis remain bright on both short-TE and long-TE sequences, unlike the artifact..
Key point: Quantitative T2 and T1-rho cartilage values vary with sequence design and field strength, requiring consistent protocols for comparison..

Applications and pitfalls.
Quantitative mapping has moved from research into routine clinical protocols.
Cardiac MRI uses native T1 mapping and extracellular volume calculation to detect diffuse myocardial fibrosis and infiltrative disease, such as amyloidosis,
without requiring a comparison to normal myocardium.
Musculoskeletal imaging uses T2 mapping to evaluate cartilage health and early degeneration and to characterize edema.
Liver protocols use R2* and PDFF together to quantify iron and fat content in the same examination.
In the brain, T1 and T2 mapping support tissue characterization in demyelinating and neurodegenerative disease.
Several pitfalls limit quantitative accuracy.
T1 mapping is particularly sensitive to inhomogeneity of the B1 transmit field,
which causes the actual flip angle delivered to a voxel to differ from the prescribed value and skews the fitted T1; correction methods are needed to keep values reliable.
Relaxation times also depend on field strength, since T1 lengthens at higher field strength, so normal reference ranges established at 1.5T do not directly apply at 3T.
Patient motion and partial-volume averaging with adjacent tissue can corrupt pixel-level values,
and reproducibility across different scanner vendors and pulse sequence implementations remains imperfect,
so absolute numeric thresholds should be applied with caution and ideally compared against site-specific normal ranges.
Key point: Cardiac native T1 and extracellular volume detect diffuse fibrosis and infiltrative disease without needing a comparison region..
Key point: T2 mapping is used for cartilage evaluation and characterizing tissue edema..
Key point: R2* and PDFF are combined in liver protocols to quantify iron and fat in one exam..
Key point: B1 transmit field inhomogeneity skews T1 mapping and requires correction..
Key point: T1 values lengthen at higher field strength, so normal ranges are field-strength specific..
Worked example.
A patient with suspected cardiac amyloidosis has a native myocardial T1 of 1150 ms at 1.5T, above the site's normal range,
and an elevated extracellular volume fraction; both point to diffuse infiltration even though the myocardium appears visually unremarkable on standard cine images.
The technologist confirms B1 shimming was applied and that the value was compared to the correct field-strength-specific reference range before it is reported as abnormal.
Memory hook: B1 off, T1 off: uncorrected transmit field skews the map..
Memory hook: Higher field, longer T1: normal ranges do not travel between 1.5T and 3T..
Exam trap: Do not apply a 3T normal T1 range to a 1.5T study or vice versa; relaxation times are field-strength dependent..
Exam trap: Do not assume all vendors' quantitative maps are interchangeable; standardization across platforms is still incomplete, so absolute thresholds need caution..
Applications and pitfalls.
Annual breast MRI screening, added to mammography, is recommended for women at high risk, generally defined as an estimated lifetime risk of breast cancer of about 20 percent or greater,
including known or suspected BRCA1 or BRCA2 carriers and women with a strong family history or prior chest radiation.
For patients with silicone implants, a dedicated silicone-specific protocol that suppresses both fat and water is added so the silicone itself becomes the source of signal,
separate from the fat-suppressed sequences used for parenchymal evaluation.
On these images, the linguine sign, collapsed, wavy lines of implant shell floating within the silicone, indicates an intracapsular rupture,
meaning the shell has failed but the silicone remains contained within the fibrous capsule.
Marked BPE is one of the most common pitfalls in interpretation, since intense background enhancement can obscure a true lesion or itself be mistaken for an abnormal finding.
Timing the exam to the second week of the menstrual cycle, as with screening protocols, is the primary strategy to reduce this source of error.
Breast MRI has very high sensitivity for detecting invasive cancer but comparatively limited specificity, meaning many benign findings also enhance.
This tradeoff means MRI generates a meaningful number of additional biopsies for findings that ultimately prove benign, a consequence that must be weighed against its value in high-risk populations.
Key point: High-risk screening applies to roughly 20 percent or greater lifetime risk, including BRCA carriers.
Key point: Silicone-specific sequences that suppress both fat and water assess implant integrity.
Key point: The linguine sign indicates intracapsular silicone implant rupture.
Key point: Marked BPE can obscure or mimic lesions; timing to the cycle reduces this.
Key point: High sensitivity with limited specificity means more biopsies of benign findings.
Worked example.
A 50-year-old with bilateral silicone implants and a palpable lump undergoes breast MRI with an added silicone-specific sequence.
The silicone-only images, which suppress both fat and water, show wavy, collapsed shell lines within the silicone of the left implant, confirming the linguine sign and an intracapsular rupture,
while the palpable finding itself proves to be a simple cyst.
Memory hook: Linguine floating in silicone means the shell inside has failed..
Memory hook: High sensitivity catches cancer, low specificity catches extra biopsies too..
Exam trap: Do not call a linguine sign an extracapsular rupture; linguine means the silicone is still contained within the capsule..
Exam trap: Do not treat every enhancing focus as cancer; limited specificity makes some benign biopsies an expected tradeoff..
